en: Preface to the Reprinted Revised and Determined *Zhi Guan* (Stopping and Contemplation), composed by Wu Kiji of Kaian. How marvelous!
This scripture for saving the world and clarifying the Way was not expected to circulate once again in the present age. May it reach the high officials and great lords...
If those in high office were to know of this book, they would certainly not reach the point of trusting slander to destroy [the Dharma].
If scholars and gentlemen were to know of this book, they would certainly not reach the point of establishing arguments to oppose and reject it.

If those who open the gate of Chan were able to read this book, would they dare to deceive themselves by claiming there is a "separate transmission outside the teachings"? If those who seek out the sutras and śāstras were able to read this book, would they dare to...
To become entangled by one's own conceptualization of names and characteristics is already a source of self-imprisonment;

how much more so, then, when one wishes to cause everyone within and beyond the narrow seas to keep this book in their homes, so that through its successive transmission and guidance, they may fully comprehend its meaning? Furthermore, who would be willing to crave the coarse and inferior five desires instead of seeking liberation early on?
These are all the general outlines of how disciples of the Inner Teaching protect and uphold the Dharma. Zigong was fond of...
Discernment clarifies the Way of Confucius; Mencius was as majestic as a towering crag. His merit is worthy of succeeding Yu. When measured by these words, who would say they are not true?
*Zhi Guan* (Cessation and Contemplation), Ten Major Chapters.

Preface to the *Biography of the Great Master Zhizhe* (also titled *Tiantai Dharma-Gate Treatise*).

Written by Hu Ze, Grand Master of the Household of the Middle Rank, Right Counselor of the Palace, Commissioner of Military and Civil Affairs for Hangzhou Prefecture, concurrently Commissioner for Encouraging Agriculture and Maritime Trade,
Marquis of the Upper Pillar State, and Recipient of the Purple Gold Fish Bag, who exhorted others to provide the means for its carving and circulation.

Cui Yucái (style name: Hujun), Chamberlain for the Imperial Household and Vice Director of the Department of Topography in the Ministry of Rites, stationed at Nanjing, donated his stipend to carve the woodblocks.
These two gentlemen were renowned worthies of the central court; we have retained their names as they were in the original edition to show that we do not forget our origins.
The General Principles of Tiantai *Zhi-guan*, Composed by Liang Su, Academician of the Hanlin Academy and Acting Right Assistant for Deficiency, of Anding.
As for what *zhi* (calm abiding) and *guan* (insight) are: they are that which guides one to the principle of all phenomena and returns one to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
What is the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)? It is the fundamental nature of things. That things cannot return [to their original state] is caused by obscurity and movement.
To illuminate obscurity is called clarity; to arrest movement is called stillness. Clarity and stillness are the essence of cessation (*śamatha*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

In the causal stage, they are called cessation and contemplation; in the resultant stage, they are called wisdom (*jñāna*) and concentration (*samādhi*). In the causal stage, they are called practice.
The "fruit" refers to accomplishment; the "practitioner" is one who practices this, and the "accomplished one" is one who realizes it. How profound!
The Sage perceived that delusion is sufficient to ruin one's will and movement is sufficient to lose one's direction; thereupon, he ceased and observed it.
Quiescent yet luminous, he enables movement to be quiescent and quiescence to be luminous. By relying on mutual dependence, he establishes the dharmas;
by transcending dependence, he illuminates the wood. He sets up the great chariot to govern with rectitude and mounts upon great affairs to wield sovereign power.

He gauges the waxing and waning within the field of non-duality and inspires all within the realm of the three teachings. Reaching the ultimate subtlety, he exhausts his nature; reaching the ultimate complexity, he...
To embody the spirit: if we speak of what is near, even a single hair’s worth of goodness can be communicated; if we speak of what is far, the gate of the double mystery can be glimpsed.
Use the ultimate roundness to make things round, and nothing will be partial; use the ultimate reality to make things real.
In things there is no such thing as "randomness. The Sage cites their words in order to demonstrate; he expands their categories in order to inform.
He treats them with ease and gentleness so that they may seek them for themselves; he provides models and encourages deliberation so that they may arrive at them on their own.

This is the origin of the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). Now, what are the Three Truths? They are simply "the One. What are emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the middle (*madhyama*)? They are also "the One."
These are merely designations. "Emptiness" and "provisionality" are terms for mutual relativity; "the Middle Way" is a name for attaining oneness.
These are explanations based on discursive thought, not the ultimate principle of reaching oneness. Reaching oneness is precisely the three; reaching the three is precisely oneness.

It is not so because they are joined together, nor is it so because they give rise to one another. It is not a matter of numerical categories, nor is it a forced designation. It is the principle of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, that which is spoken and transmitted is the "trace" (ji); the underlying principle is called the "root" (ben), and the trace is called the "branch" (mo).
The root is the ground reached by the Sage; the branch is the teaching manifested by the Sage.
By proceeding from the root to manifest the traces, there arise the categories of small and great, common and distinct, sudden and gradual, manifest and secret, and provisional.

It is reality; it is the fixed and the unfixed. By following the traces back to the source, it becomes the One and the Great, the Perfect and the Real, the Non-abiding and the Middle, the Sublime and the Ultimate Truth. These are the three aspects of the One.
That which is called "emptiness" is spoken of in terms of penetrating all phenomena. That which is called "provisionality" is spoken of in terms of establishing all phenomena.
It is so. That which is the "Middle" is that which articulates the wondrousness of all phenomena. In shattering all delusions, nothing is more preeminent than emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
In establishing all phenomena, nothing is more preeminent than the provisional (*upāya*). In ultimately realizing all natures, nothing is greater than the Middle.
If one takes up the "Middle," there is no dharma that is not the Middle. If one takes up the "Provisional," there is no dharma that is not provisional.
If one takes up the "Empty," there is no dharma that is not empty. To perfect these is called the Three Virtues; to cultivate them is called the Three Contemplations. To state their essential point:

is this not the teaching of the Sage who exhausts the profound, investigates the subtle, and fully realizes principle and nature? It causes those who are obscure to become clear and those who are obstructed to become unimpeded. Once they are unimpeded—
Awakening. When one awakens, one arrives at the ultimate. When one arrives, it is eternal. When it is eternal, it is exhaustive. Clarity then illuminates. Illumination then transforms.

Transformation then completes. When completed, all is One. The Sage has a means by which he encompasses the myriad dharmas without error, pervades the myriad kalpas without omission, sustains the sands of the Ganges without attachment, and returns to the state of non-existence without being nothing. He gives this a provisional name: [The title of the text follows here]
The Buddha is forcibly designated as "Awakened" (Buddha). Upon investigating its essential meaning, is this not the supreme and most wondrous virtue of liberation and sovereign mastery?
Such is the achievement of the three contemplations. That which is called "Perfect and Sudden" (Yuantun) is neither gradual nor indeterminate.
This refers to the meaning of the ten chapters of the treatise. The ten chapters expand upon the beginning and end; they are the gateway through which one attains the Way.

The five summaries present the grand framework; they are the ferry for cutting across the stream. The ten objects are the mechanisms that trigger practice and the truths upon which contemplation is established.
The ten vehicles are the cultivation of wondrous function and the gateways for initiating practice. One should rest in right contemplation and...
The reason one finally perceives the objective realm is that its meaning is complete therein. The reason other factors are omitted is that they are not essential to the practice.
What is a vehicle (*yāna*)? It is that which carries things and moves them forward. What is "ten"? It is that which accomplishes the task of carrying.
To know the wondrous nature of the realm and reach it without acting is the pinnacle of virtue. This is simply by riding upon the One; why rely on the Nine?
These Nine are nothing other than the doctrine of mutual generation, which is the path trodden by those who have not yet arrived.

Therefore, one who gives rise to the mind does so with no place from which to give rise; one who settles the mind settles it with no place to settle; one who shatters the pervasive [delusion] shatters it with no place for the pervasive to exist.
It refutes [other views]. From here, even reaching the other vehicles (*yāna*), all are taught out of necessity.
As for distinguishing their doctrinal categories and organizing them into chapters and headings: to expand upon them is not prolixity; to unify them is not brevity.
They are like linked rings that cannot be untied; like strung pearls that cannot be confused; like suspended mirrors that cannot be obscured. Like...
The flowing stream cannot be dammed; the many gates of the House of Meaning are not for disputation. Examining the scriptures to substantiate the principles is no empty talk.
Discerning the relative depth of the four teachings has its source in fact; establishing the causal conditions of a single matter leaves no principle unaddressed.

Alas! Are the *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation) not the scriptures for saving the world and clarifying the Way? Were it not for one whose sagely wisdom is transcendent and peerless, standing alone and eminent—who else could have composed them?
Were it not for one who is brilliant and profoundly penetrating, grasping the meaning while forgetting the symbols—who else could have understood them?
Yet people today exclusively rely on chapters and sentences, following the literal words to explain them; how remote and pedantic this is!

(“Ní” is alternatively read as “lòu”). Some claim that the inconceivable realm and inconceivable phenomena both belong to the domain of the ultimate sages, such that even the Perfected Persons at the stage of Equal Enlightenment have not yet fully exhausted them.

If an ordinary person, with a mind subject to arising and ceasing and the three delusions raging vast and unbridled, attempts to infer the supreme and wondrous principle through verbal discourse, it is like a vinegar-fly attempting to describe the Great Peng, or a summer insect debating the winter frost.

"Ice. Its invisibility is clearly evident. Now, the teachings on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* consist of tens of thousands of characters; to discuss the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*) at such length provides no benefit to beginners.

How could this be compared to remaining in quietude, where one cultivates for oneself until the realization arrives naturally? Why must one make premature planning one's business? This is most certainly not so.
For what is called the realm of the supreme sages—how could it be separated from the ordinary by vast distances or remote frontiers? It is not far removed from the common person.

The realm of phenomena is utterly transcendent (one version reads "profoundly remote"), yet it is nothing other than this single nature. To attain it is called awakening; to lose it is called delusion. It is but a single principle.
Through delusion one becomes an ordinary person; through awakening one becomes a sage. It is the deluded who create separation for themselves; the principle itself is not separated.

That which is lost is lost of its own accord; its nature is not lost. The practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is intended to distinguish between differences and similarities and to investigate the sacred and the divine, thereby causing all sentient beings to align their true nature with the principle.
Aligning one’s true nature with the principle is the means by which one traverses the path of awakening and reaches the wondrous realm.
If one does not understand this teaching, then into what shall one’s learning enter, and where shall one’s efforts be applied? What is the use of wisdom?
What is it that has been initiated? It is like one who is blind and ignorant of the light of the sun and moon, yet travels through a place of profound peril;
how could the instances of his stumbling, falling, and tumbling be fully recounted? Alas! Since the Sage passed away long ago, no worthy sages have appeared.
Those of common and deluded nature possess nothing more than consciousness. Consequently, they allow demonic and heterodox deceptions to flourish, with various factions burning fiercely together.

Amidst these empty clamors, there are those who create pits and traps; some are so bound by the literal words of the texts that they dare not move, while others drift upon vast, surging waves and cannot find stillness.
Some venture too far and willingly refuse to arrive, while others are so near that they mistake it for their own very bodies.
Among these, there are those who take a withered tree to be meditative concentration; those who take a hollow sound to be wisdom; those who take running about against the Way to be skillful means;
those who rely on ghosts and spirits to claim supernatural penetration; those who let their minds wander to call it expansiveness; those who rarely speak to call it secrecy;
and those who transmit things secretly through teeth and tongue to call it oral instructions. All such as these—
[They] established themselves as patriarchs and made their lineages into families; they contravened the classics and deviated from the sages, yet those in ignorance did not perceive it.
Confucius had a saying: "I know why the Way has not been clarified—it is because of entanglement with external things. Alas!

From the passing of the Great Master Zhizhe in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty until the Jianzhong era of our present dynasty, nearly two hundred years have elapsed. By means of these writings...
Tradition holds that there were five masters in total. The first was Guanding; the next was Jin Yunwei;
the next was Dongyang Xiaowei; the next was Master Lang of Zuoxi; and the fifth was Master Ran of Jingxi.
Among his fellow disciples, [Zhi]ding was foremost in wisdom and understanding; he was able to follow his master’s instructions and compile this book.
This was likely because he did not prioritize literary elegance. At times it is overly verbose, and at other times it is crude.

During the era of the two Empresses (Wu Zetian and Empress Wei), it was merely sealed and transmitted, and thus its Way did not spread. It was only during the Tianbao period that Zuoxi first propagated its exegesis and made it known.
Those who [truly understand this] are indeed few. Jingxi [Zhiyi] extensively compiled biographies and records totaling hundreds of thousands of words to encompass the remaining Dharma;
his diligence was exhaustive. Yet after Jingxi’s passing, those who truly understood his teachings were but three or four people.
An ancient said: "To know by birth is the highest; to know through learning is next; to learn because of distress is yet another level. Now, as for one born...
Those who know it through innate nature are those possessing the virtue of their original nature (*xingde*). Those who know it through study are those with profound celestial faculties (*tianji*).
However, if one’s sensual desires are deep and one’s ears and eyes are obstructed, then even with study one cannot know it; this is the lowest grade.
Now, students are internally afflicted by obscuration and externally enslaved by distraction; they spend a lifetime unable to master its texts, and after several years they still cannot grasp it.
As for its deficiencies: the elaboration of literary style is like shackling one's feet with fetters; the entanglement of phrasing is like having chaff and dust blown into one's eyes.
Because teachers who lack the power of true analogy instruct disciples who fail to grasp the teachings, it is no wonder that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* have not yet been made magnificent in this age.
You, sir, have long been grieved by this; you have thus straightened the grand framework and grasped the essential pivot. As for its principles—
Regarding what has been preserved, that which was urgent for the teachings—some parts were rearranged, some were expanded upon;
where the meaning was circuitous or the phrasing was vulgar, some were excised, while others were refined. In general, nine out of ten instances of such superficial flaws have been cured.
Regarding the appropriateness of expansion or brevity, I have retained one out of three. This is intended to dispel my own vulgar stagnation and to guide the ignorant;
as for bequeathing this to others, how could I dare? If those of like vision and practice do not condemn me for my lack of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, then there is nothing hidden from you.

The Jianzhong era, the first *jiǎzǐ* year of the Upper Prime (*shàngyuán*), marks the commencement of this editorial work; after three years, when the celestial position was at the ford of Xīmù, the task was completed.
(This refers to Master Liang’s revision and determination of the *Zhǐguān*, for which he composed the *Tǒnglì* to follow it—much like Wang Fǔjì’s *Lüèlì* appended to his commentary on the *Yījīng*.

I have now carved this private preface and placed it at the beginning, so that those who peruse it may first recognize the structural framework and thus remain unhindered in their practice when encountering the text.)
Preface to the *Cessation and Contemplation Revised and Determined* (Xiūzhǐguān shāndìng),
Scroll One: Liang Dynasty Account of the Origins.
Initially, the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai transmitted the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* from Mount Nanyue: first, the gradual; second, the indeterminate;
and third, the perfect and sudden. All three are Mahāyāna teachings that take the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) as their object and are equally termed *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

Although the gradual method also recognizes the true reality from the outset, because the true reality is difficult to reach, the gradual approach is easier to practice. One first cultivates the precepts of taking refuge, thereby ceasing the three evil destinies and attaining...

First, one cultivates the three wholesome paths; next, one cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to cease the scattered net of the desire realm and reach the path of the form and formless realms.

Next, one cultivates the untainted (*anāsrava*) to cease the prison of the three realms and reach the path of *nirvāṇa*. Next, one cultivates loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*) to cease self-realization alone and reach the path of the Bodhisattva.
Finally, one cultivates the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) to cease the partiality of the two extremes and reach the eternally abiding Middle Way. This proceeds from shallow to deep, as follows:
Ascending the rungs of the ladder constitutes gradual *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. As for "indeterminate," there is no separate underlying intent;

it merely refers to the alternation between the preceding gradual and the subsequent sudden, moving further forward and further back, mutually shallow and mutually deep, whether in terms of phenomena (*dharma*) or principle (*tattva*).

Whether calming and contemplation constitute *śamatha*, or illumination and stillness constitute *vipaśyanā*, it is like a diamond jewel placed in the sunlight, which possesses no fixed color or form. This is called the indeterminate.

Regarding *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*: for those of the Perfect and Sudden [teaching], one initially takes the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) as the object. As the objective sphere is engaged, it is immediately the Middle; there is nothing that is not real. One binds the conditions to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

In a single thought-moment, the Dharma-realm is such that every form and every fragrance is none other than the Middle Way. It is likewise with one’s own realm, the Buddha-realm, and the realm of sentient beings.

The aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*) are all thusness (*tathatā*); there is no suffering to be abandoned. Ignorance and the afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves bodhi; there is no accumulation (*samudaya*) [of suffering].
It can be severed. Extremes and deviance are all rectified in the Middle Way. There is no path to be cultivated; birth-and-death is itself nirvana.

There is no cessation to be realized. There is no suffering and no accumulation; therefore, there is no mundane world. There is no path and no cessation; therefore, there is no supramundane world. It is a single, pure reality with no further distinct phenomena.
The quiescence of the dharma-nature is called *śamatha* (calm abiding); its constant illumination within that stillness is called *vipaśyanā* (insight). From the beginning until—
Afterward, there is neither duality nor distinction. Just as one with supernatural powers soars through the air, this is called the Perfect and Sudden (yuantun) *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

For the sake of those with the three types of faculties, three Dharma-gates are taught and three analogies are cited; the gradual and the indeterminate methods are set aside and not discussed here. Now, following the sutras, I shall directly clarify the Perfect and Sudden.
As the Wondrous Virtue (Mañjuśrī) and Worthy Head (Samantabhadra) of the *Avataṃsaka* said: "When a Bodhisattva first resolves the mind within birth and death..."
At that time, they seek enlightenment single-mindedly, firm and immovable.

The merit of even a single thought of theirs is so deep and vast, without limit or bound, that even if a Tathāgata were to explain it in detail, it could not be exhausted throughout an entire kalpa. Having heard this perfect Dharma, these Bodhisattvas give rise to perfect faith.
Establishing the perfect practice, abiding in the perfect stage, one adorns oneself with perfect merit and establishes sentient beings through perfect power and function.
How does one hear the perfect Dharma? One hears that birth-and-death is itself the Dharmakāya, afflictions are themselves Prajñā, and karmic bonds are themselves liberation.
Although there are three names, there are no three substances; although it is a single substance, three names are established. This is...
The three are identical to the one mark; in reality, there is no difference between them. The Dharma-body is ultimate; Prajñā and liberation are likewise ultimate.
When Prajñā is pure, the others are also pure; when liberation is sovereign, the others are also sovereign. Hearing all dharmas is also like this;
this is called hearing the perfect dharma. What is perfect faith? It is to believe that all dharmas are simultaneously empty, simultaneously provisional, and simultaneously [middle].
In the midst [of this], there is no one, two, or three, yet there are one, two, and three. That there is no one, two, or three is the negation of one, two, and three;
that there are one, two, and three is the illumination of one, two, and three. With neither negation nor illumination, all are ultimately pure and sovereign.

Hearing the profound, one is not afraid; hearing the vast, one does not doubt; hearing that which is neither profound nor vast, one possesses courage in mind. This is called perfect faith. Thus it is said.
What is Perfect Practice (*pariṇata-caryā*)? It is the resolute seeking of Bodhi without turning toward anything else;

the perfect cultivation of the Three Truths without being stilled by the infinite or moved by the finite, entering directly into the Middle Way—this is called Perfect Practice. What is the Perfect Stage (*pariṇata-bhūmi*)?
It refers to the moment of entering the First Abode (*prathama-vihāra*), wherein one abode is all abodes, all are ultimate, all are pure, and all are sovereign. This is...
This is called the Stage of Perfection (*paripūrṇāvasthā*). What is meant by "the adornment of perfect mastery"? That sutra explains the characteristics of mastery in detail:
one may enter meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) through this faculty and emerge from it through that faculty; or enter through one faculty and emerge through all faculties;
or enter and emerge simultaneously through a single faculty; or neither enter nor emerge; and so on, even down to a single atom (*paramāṇu*).

The same applies to all directions. To explain in detail: within a single sense-faculty and a single object, there is simultaneous entry and exit, simultaneous dual entry and exit, and simultaneous non-entry and non-exit.
It is like the sunlight pervading the four continents; while it is dawn in one direction, it is already midday in another.
On one side it is evening, on the other side it is midnight; in a single day, four different phenomena are seen simultaneously. The sovereign mastery of the Bodhisattva is likewise so.

This is called the "Adornment of Perfect Sovereignty. How does he perfectly establish sentient beings? Sometimes by emitting a single ray of light, he can cause sentient beings to obtain immeasurable benefit;
sometimes they obtain the benefit of the simultaneous identity of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle; or [he causes them] to enter and emerge [from meditative states].
There is no entering or exiting, nor any increase; it is thus throughout walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
For those with the karmic affinity, it is as if they were beholding light with their own eyes; for those without the affinity, they remain blind and cut off from it.

It is like a dragon king who, while sending forth various thunder, lightning, clouds, and rain—vertically reaching through the six heavens and horizontally spanning the four continents—remains unmoved and unshaken within his own palace. The Bodhisattva is likewise; he does not move.
The Dharma-nature possesses various divine functions; this is called the establishment of sentient beings through the power of perfect efficacy.

If even the initial stage of the Bodhisattva path (the First Abode of Initial Resolve) can be thus, how much more so for the middle and later stages? Question: It may be granted that such is the case for what is induced by the Perfect and Sudden [teachings].

However, regarding the Gradual and the Indeterminate, what scriptural evidence is there? Answer: The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "He turned the Wheel of Dharma three times throughout the great chiliocosm; yet that wheel was originally..."
The coming [of the Buddha] is eternally pure; that devas and humans attain the Way serves as its testimony. Thus the Three Jewels appear in the world;
this is the beginning of the gradual teaching. It is further said: "The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind."
"Sometimes there is fear, sometimes joy; sometimes revulsion arises, and sometimes doubt is severed—this is the meaning of the indeterminate teaching.
Furthermore, it says: 'The Dharma is neither existent nor non-existent; all phenomena arise through causes and conditions. There is no self, no creator, and no experiencer;
yet the karma of good and evil does not perish. This is the meaning of the sudden teaching. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* speaks of "gradual practice."

The gradual training and the gradual path demonstrate the progressive nature [of realization]. Furthermore, it is said that when a mani jewel is wrapped in various colors and placed in water, it takes on the color of whatever object it encounters;

this demonstrates its indeterminate nature. Moreover, it is said that from the very first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), one immediately sits upon the terrace of enlightenment, turns the wheel of Dharma, and delivers sentient beings; this demonstrates the sudden nature. The Lotus Sūtra states: "Such a person should..."
"By means of this Dharma, one gradually enters the Buddha-wisdom. This proves the gradual [approach]. Furthermore, it says:

"If one does not believe in this Dharma, then within other profound Dharmas, one provides instruction, benefit, and joy. This proves the indeterminate [approach]. Furthermore, it says: "Directly abandoning expedient means, he speaks only of the Unsurpassed Way.
This proves the sudden [approach]. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "From milk comes curd, and so on until clarified butter (*ghṛta*). This is the gradual [approach]. Moreover, [it continues:]...
If poison is placed in milk, the milk immediately kills a person; even if poison is placed in clarified butter (*ghṛta*), the clarified butter kills a person—it is not fixed.
Furthermore, on the Snowy Mountains there is a herb called "Patience" (*kṣānti*); if a cow eats it, she immediately produces clarified butter—it is sudden.
The *Avataṃsaka* says: "When the Dragon King Sāgara rains from the sea like the pouring of a chariot axle, the rest of the earth cannot endure it. The *Vimalakīrti* says:

"Those who enter this room smell only the fragrance of the merits of all Buddhas. The *Śūraṅgama* says: "If one pounds ten thousand kinds of incense into pellets and burns even a single atom of them, the full array of their fragrances is present.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* says: "By means of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), one knows all things."
Dharma. One should study the *Prajñāpāramitā*. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Those who wish to hear the complete path [should study] the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtras*.
For example, it is like a person bathing in the great ocean who should know that they are using the waters of all rivers; this is the meaning of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*).
These are all the dharmas upon which the Tathāgatas of the three periods rely as their teachers. Because the Dharma is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal. Such is the text; it cannot be otherwise.
To cling to the literal text is to bring harm upon oneself. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Whether one perceives the Prajñā or does not perceive it, all are bound and all are liberated.
An objector asks: "The quiescent mark of all dharmas cannot be expressed in words. The *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra* says: "Arising and arising cannot be spoken of;
even non-arising and non-arising cannot be spoken of. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "That which is spoken is without speaking and without..."
[Question: It is shown that those who hear the Dharma neither hear nor attain it. Such a person cannot speak; this Dharma is unspeakable. If so, how can it be shown to others? [Answer:
This merely cites one side [of the argument] and does not understand its essential purport. According to the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, because there are causes and conditions, it can indeed be spoken.

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, it is taught for the sake of sentient beings through the causes and conditions of skillful means (*upāya*). Furthermore, the Tathāgata always relies upon two [aspects].
He preached the Dharma with clarity. Vimalakīrti, the nature of words is itself liberation. If this is so, how could there be an absolute absence of speech?
To compete over whether one speaks or remains silent is to fail to understand the intent of the teaching; it distances one further from the principle. Apart from speech there is no principle;

apart from the principle there is no speech. Thus, speech is non-speech, and non-speech is speech. Being neither two nor distinct, reality is suchness within phenomena—this is the very essence of the teaching.
It is thus. Nowadays, people’s faculties are dull; therefore, profound insight is difficult to attain. Since the eye relies upon the sense-field of form, relying on written texts makes it easy.

If one becomes attached to the literal text, it will cause harm; one must know that the text is not the text itself. One should realize that all texts are neither text nor non-text, and be able to gain all understanding from a single word.
Now, this is opened into ten chapters as follows: 1. General Meaning; 2. Explanation of Names; 3. Essence.
1. Characteristics; 2. The Four Means of Integration; 3. The Partial and the Perfect; 4. Expedient Means; 5. Right Contemplation; 6. Retribution; 7.

The Arising of the Teaching; 8. The Pointing to the Ultimate Refuge. Since beginningless time, sentient beings have been shrouded by delusions, failing to realize that ignorance is itself enlightenment.
Now I shall awaken them; therefore, it is called "Great Meaning" (*Dàyì*). Once one knows that ignorance is itself clarity, there is no further movement; this is called "Cessation" (*Śamatha*).
When there is luminous and vast purity, this is called "Insight" (*Vipaśyanā*). To hear the name and attain its essence—this essence is the encompassing of all phenomena (*dharmas*).

These phenomena have both partial and perfect aspects. Through the understanding of these partial and perfect aspects, skillful means (*upāya*) arise. Once skillful means are established, right insight is perfected, and one shall obtain the wondrous fruition. Thus the teaching is initiated.
Instructing others, we shall together return to eternal quiescence. Such is the meaning of the sequence of the ten chapters. Regarding the general purport:

first, as for the "General Purport of Calming and Contemplation" (*Zhiguan Danyi*), it encompasses the beginning and the end; its meaning is broad and difficult to perceive. Now, I shall briefly set forth five points, namely: the arousal of the great [aspiration].

The mind cultivates great practices, realizes great fruits, tears asunder the great net, and returns to the Great Abode. Those who wish to resolve their minds to practice should first distinguish between what is right and what is wrong.
There are ten characteristics of a non-virtuous mind: if one's thoughts are moment by moment fixed upon greed, hatred, and delusion;

if these cannot be restrained from returning nor extracted once they have arisen; and if they give rise to the ten unwholesome deeds of the highest degree, such as those of the Pañcāśatikas—this is the arousal of a hell-bound mind.

While walking along a path smeared with fire, if one’s mind, moment by moment, desires many followers and seeks them greedily without ceasing—like the ocean swallowing rivers or like fire consuming wood—one gives rise to the ten unwholesome actions of medium degree, such as Devadatta inciting the multitude; this is the arousal of an animal-like mind.

They tread upon paths smeared with blood. If their minds, moment by moment, delight in wickedness, flattery, and seductive artifice, or harbor secret malice and envy, yet still seek renown far and wide and compare themselves to sages and saints, they give rise to the ten unwholesome actions of the lowest grade.

Like Māgandiya, they give rise to a demonic mind and tread upon paths smeared with knives. If their minds, moment by moment, constantly desire to surpass others, exalting themselves and disparaging others.
Externally manifesting benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom, one gives rise to a lower-grade wholesome mind and practices the path of asuras.

If one’s mind, in every thought-moment, delights in worldly pleasures while still directing one's will toward practicing benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom, this gives rise to a middle-grade wholesome mind and leads to the human realm.
If his mind, in every thought-moment, perceives that the three evil realms are purely suffering, that the human realm is a mixture of suffering and pleasure, and aspires toward celestial bliss,
causing the six sense organs not to go out and the six sense objects not to enter, this gives rise to a superior grade of wholesome mind and leads to rebirth in the heavenly realms.
If his mind, in every thought-moment, desires great majesty and power such that all actions of body, speech, and mind are followed and obeyed, this is the arousal of desire.

If one’s mind dwells on the state of a world-ruler (*cakravartin*) and practices the path of Māra, yet in every thought-moment desires to benefit others through wisdom, eloquence, and sagacity such that nothing remains unperceived—this is the arousal of the worldly-wise mind (*lokajñāna-citta*), practicing the path of the Nirgranthas.

If one’s mind dwells in every thought-moment upon the bliss of the third dhyāna, and that bliss is held as paramount within—this is the arousal of the Brahma-mind, practicing the path of the meditative absorptions of the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpya-dhyāna*). If one’s mind dwells in every thought-moment knowing what is wholesome...

The wheel of evil is that from which the noble ones (ārya) have departed. The destruction of evil arises from pure wisdom (*prajñā*); pure wisdom arises from pure meditation (*dhyāna*); and pure meditation arises from pure precepts (*śīla*).
One who esteems these three dharmas gives rise to the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) and practices the path of the two vehicles (*yāna*).

Whether in terms of the mind or the path, those [who do so] are not many; they are briefly said to be ten. Furthermore, nine types [of beings] are within birth and death (*saṃsāra*), like silkworms binding themselves; the final one is *nirvāṇa*.

[The character] "pan" [is used]. It is like a roe deer emerging alone. Furthermore, nine dharmas pertain to the worldly truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and its origin (*samudaya-satya*), while the final one pertains to the supramundane truths of the path (*mārga-satya*) and cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Although there may be skillful means (*upāya*) without great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and though the defiled and pure, or the ultimate and conventional, differ, now all are distinguished as pairs.
If you grasp this intent, then throughout all sense organs and objects, the three karmas, and the four modes of conduct, you should employ this contemplation in every instance.

Examine this: the meaning of the ten "non-" [categories] can thus be seen. Having already discarded what is non-true, one should clearly realize what is true; this is precisely the reality (*tattva*).
The dharmas of reality are immeasurable, but for now, they shall be briefly manifested through three dharmas: namely, the Four Noble Truths, the Four Great Vows, and the Six Stages of Bodhi.

Regarding the Four Noble Truths, according to the "Chapter on Holy Practice" (*Ārya-caryā*) in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, there are four kinds: namely, arising-and-ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*), no-arising, no-cessation, and neither-arising-nor-ceasing.
Arising and ceasing, immeasurable, and unconditioned. Regarding "arising and ceasing": suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are the causes and effects of the mundane;
the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*) are the causes and effects of the supramundane. Suffering undergoes the transition of the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*);

the origin flows as the four mental states (*citta*). The path is easily subverted by its opposites; cessation is the extinction of existence back into non-existence. Although both the mundane and the supramundane are subject to transformation, they are thus called "arising and ceasing."
Regarding the Four Noble Truths: that which is "unborn" means that suffering is without affliction and all things are empty. How could emptiness itself dispel emptiness? Form is itself emptiness;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so. As for "origination," there is no aggregation, meaning that both cause and effect are empty;

how could they possibly combine? This applies likewise to all afflictions throughout their course. As for the "path," it is non-dual, meaning there is neither a remedy nor that which is to be remedied.
Since even emptiness does not possess even one [dharma], how could there be two? Dharmas are fundamentally not so; now they do not cease.
Because they are neither ignited nor extinguished, they are called the "Unborn Four Truths. Regarding "immeasurable": suffering and its accumulation have immeasurable characteristics.
If even a single realm is immeasurable, how much more so the ten realms? Only the eye of wisdom of a Bodhisattva can penetrate them. The Path and Cessation likewise possess immeasurability.
Characteristics refer to the distinctions between the skillful and unskillful means of analyzing the substance, the indirect and direct, the long and short, and the provisional and real;
these differences are manifold. Such skillful means can extinguish the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); such skillful means can extinguish the *rajas-aṇu* and ignorance (*avidyā*).

There are those that are correct and those that are auxiliary, each without confusion; therefore, they are called the "Infinite Four Truths. That there is no creator is because they are all the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Truths. Furthermore, the four truths are separately explained as the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Suffering (*duḥkha*) consists of seven branches: consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Accumulation (*samudaya*) consists of five branches: ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*).

The skillful means that counteract these links of dependent origination is called the path (*mārga*). The cessation of everything from ignorance through old age and death is called cessation (*nirodha*). Therefore, the Great Sūtra speaks of four types of twelvefold dependent origination.
Regarding the conditions: by observing with inferior wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a śrāvaka; by observing with middling wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;

by observing with superior wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a bodhisattva; and by observing with the highest-of-the-high wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a Buddha. Furthermore, the treatise states:
For disciples of sharp faculties, he teaches that the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) possess the characteristic of being neither arising nor ceasing.

For disciples of dull faculties, he teaches that the twelve links of dependent origination possess the characteristic of arising and ceasing. One should know that the Truths (*satya*) and dependent origination are identical in essence, differing only in name.

In various sutras, it is clarified that the arousal of the bodhicitta is not uniform: some arise through inference, some through contemplating the Buddha, some through hearing the Dharma, and some through seeing the [Buddha-]lands.

Among the disciples of the Master, some observe the cultivation of various practices, while others observe the endurance of various sufferings; such instances are numerous, yet they can all give rise to a single realization.
Here, I shall briefly illustrate this principle with two or three examples. First, regarding the investigation through reasoning:

if one were to claim that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is inherently so by its own celestial nature—that it cannot be defiled by accumulation (*saṃudaya*), cannot be afflicted by suffering (*duḥkha*), cannot be traversed by the path (*mārga*), and cannot be purified by cessation (*nirodha*)—then [this would be a misconception].
It is like clouds enshrouding the moon; they do not obstruct one another. Only after the afflictions (*kleśa*) have been dispelled does one perceive the *dharmatā*.

As the Sūtra says: "Cessation is not the ultimate truth; through cessation, one realizes the Truth. If even cessation is not the Truth, how could the [other] three truths be so? Within affliction there is no bodhi.

Within Bodhi there are no afflictions; one should contemplate this truthfully. To seek the Buddha-way above and to transform sentient beings below is called "inferring the Four Noble Truths of Arising and Ceasing to give rise to the Bodhicitta" (the first).

If one says that the Dharma-nature is not different from suffering and its accumulation, but that one fails to see the Dharma-nature because of delusion regarding suffering and its accumulation—just as when water freezes into ice, there is no separate ice apart from it—one must realize that suffering and its accumulation are non-existent.

Suffering and its accumulation are themselves the dharma-nature. If even suffering and accumulation are thus, how much more so are the Path and Cessation? As the Sūtra says: "Afflictions are themselves Bodhi;

Bodhi is itself afflictions. To contemplate in this manner, seeking the supreme above and transforming those below, is called "arousing the mind by inferring the Four Truths as non-arising" (the second).
If one considers that the dharma-nature is called the "true mark," it is already beyond the reach of the Two Vehicles, let alone...
Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) perceive a pure dharma existing separately beyond the two extremes, as illustrated by the ten parables in the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*.

This is called "arousing the mind through the investigation of the immeasurable Four Noble Truths" (the third). If one were to claim that the *dharmatā* and all phenomena are non-dual and undifferentiated, then ordinary beings already possess it;
how much more so the followers of the Two Vehicles? To seek the holy apart from the ordinary is like avoiding space while seeking space. As the Sūtra says: "Birth-and-death is itself Nirvāṇa."
A single form and a single fragrance are none other than the Middle Way; this is called generating the bodhicitta by investigating the unconditioned Four Noble Truths.
Indeed, by investigating a single dharma, one immediately penetrates the Dharma-realm, attaining ultimate fulfillment and reaching the further shore both horizontally and vertically;
only then is it called the perfection of generating the bodhicitta (the fourth). Next, regarding generating the mind upon beholding the Buddha’s marks: if one sees the Tathāgata as a father...
The mother gives birth to a physical body whose features are radiant and luminous; among all that is above and below heaven, there is nothing to compare with it.

"May I realize this so as to deliver sentient beings"—this is called the aspiration for Buddhahood arising from beholding a response-body Buddha (nirmāṇakāya). If one sees the Tathāgata, one knows that the Tathāgata has no "Tathāgata-ness."

To see the marks and signs as not being marks and signs—wherein both the Tathāgata and his marks and signs are like empty space, and within that emptiness there is no Buddha, much less marks and signs—to see the Tathāgata as not being the Tathāgata is precisely to see the Tathāgata; to see the marks and signs as not being marks and signs is to see all marks.
"May I realize this and thereby deliver sentient beings"—this is called generating the mind through beholding the supreme. If one sees...

The physical form of the Tathāgata is like a pure, bright mirror; there is nothing he does not see. Each of his marks and secondary characteristics is such that neither ordinary beings nor sages can fathom their limits;
even Brahmā cannot see the crown of his head, and Maudgalyāyana cannot exhaust the range of his voice. A treatise states: "The formless, supreme essence is an adornment that transcends all adornment.
May I realize this. This is called the arousal of the mind upon seeing the Reward Buddha (*vipākabuddha*). If one sees the [Dharmakāya]...
Come! Know that the Tathāgata’s wisdom profoundly penetrates the characteristics of both sin and merit, universally illuminating the ten directions.

His subtle and wondrous Dharma-body is endowed with the thirty-two marks; each and every mark and excellence is the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). May I realize this—this is called generating the mind [of enlightenment] by perceiving the marks of the Buddha-dharma.
Generating the mind by seeing the Buddha’s supernatural transformations follows the same principle. Next is generating the mind upon hearing the Dharma.
If one hears the single phrase "arising and ceasing," one immediately knows that all mundane and supramundane phenomena arise and cease anew, shifting from moment to moment;
that precepts, wisdom, liberation, and tranquility alone are true. Or, upon hearing "arising and ceasing," one immediately understands that the Four Noble Truths are all non-arising and non-ceasing:
in emptiness there are no thorns, so how can they be pulled out? Who suffers? Who accumulates [defilements]? Who practices? Who realizes? Subject and object are both tranquil.
Yet there is nothing that is not pure. If one hears of arising and ceasing, one immediately understands that arising and ceasing contrasted with non-arising and non-ceasing constitute duality;
that which is neither arising and ceasing nor non-arising and non-ceasing is the Middle Way. This Middle Way is pure, standing alone beyond both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

Alternatively, upon hearing of arising and ceasing, one immediately understands arising and ceasing, non-arising and non-ceasing, and that which is neither arising and ceasing nor non-arising and non-ceasing.

Simultaneously illuminating both arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing—being three while being one, and one while being three—the secret mysteries of the Dharma-realm are ultimately and fully perfected.
Thus, within the single phrase "arising-and-ceasing," these four interpretations are established; this is called generating the aspiration for enlightenment through hearing the Dharma.
This extends even to hearing such terms as "non-arising," "immeasurable," and "unconditioned. One should understand them all by applying this same principle.

If one grasps this intent, one will know that a single phrase contains all phrases without further obstruction. Fearing that this may still be difficult to clarify, it is further explained by a verse from the Treatise (*śāstra*).

The Treatise says: "Phenomena produced through causes and conditions—I declare these to be emptiness. Since they are said to be produced through causes and conditions, how can they be identical to emptiness? [This requires] waiting for...

Only when one analyzes causes and conditions to their exhaustion does one finally realize emptiness (*śūnyatā*). To point to that very emptiness as being "immediately empty" and also call it a "provisional name" (*prajñapti*) means that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) cannot exist independently;
they must rely on various conditions. Because they depend on conditions, they are provisional. This is not the "provisionality" of employing skillful means (*upāya*).

Furthermore, calling this the meaning of the "Middle Way" (*madhyamā pratipad*) means that being free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism is called the Middle Way; it is not the Middle Way of the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*). If one understands it in this way...

Although the three phrases are all empty, they do not yet constitute "immediate emptiness" (*jìkōng*); how much less so for the provisional (*jiǎ*) and the middle (*zhōng*), which are merely the meaning of the four truths of arising and ceasing.

If the dharmas of dependent origination do not require analytical deconstruction for their essence to be empty, yet one cannot attain the provisional and the middle—then even if one speaks of the provisional and the middle, these all conform to entry into emptiness.
Why? Because all dharmas are immediately empty due to the absence of a self as a master; the provisional is likewise immediately empty.
Because it is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*), the Middle Way is also emptiness. Because it is free from the two extremes, this is the meaning of the Four Noble Truths as non-arising.

If one were to say that emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are identical, then these three are distinct: they are all empty because they lack a master; they are all provisional because they exist only as names;
and they are all the middle because they are the true, the responsive, and the real. However, this is only according to their sequential order.

This accomplishes the meaning of the four noble truths of immeasurability. If one says that emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are identical—being three yet one without mutual obstruction—all are the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
To realize emptiness is to realize the provisional and the middle; they are neither before nor after. This accomplishes the meaning of the four noble truths of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
One should know that hearing a single dharma and giving rise to various understandings and establishing various vows is called "arousing [the bodhicitta]."

Regarding the bodhicitta: although the causes for generating the mind—such as the practice of contemplating suffering by the disciples of a pure land—are distinct, this example may serve to clarify them.
In order to make these practices and vows manifest, they are next explained through the four great vows.

Now, the mind does not arise in isolation; it must depend on conditions. The mental faculty (*manas*) serves as the cause, and the objects of the dharma (*dharmāyatana*) serve as the condition. The mind that arises from these...

All phenomena that arise—roots and objects—are shifting and unstable, not remaining for even a single moment. Form is like a bubble, sensation like foam, perception like a flame, mental formations like a city, and consciousness like an illusion.
The three realms are impermanent; they are a basket of pervasive suffering. As the four mountains close in, there is no place to escape.

One must therefore concentrate one’s mind upon precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom to sever the flow of all existence. As the Sūtra says: "In the past, I and you did not see the Four Truths."
Truths. Therefore, one revolves for a long time; this gives rise to compassion and the four great vows to uproot suffering and bestow happiness.

This is precisely the meaning of Śākyamuni seeing the plowing and tilling, and Maitreya observing the collapsing terrace. Because one clearly understands the Four Truths, it is not the ninefold bondage;
because one can give rise to the great vows, it is not the single liberation. Neither bondage nor liberation—this is called the manifestation of the truth.
The Right Bodhicitta (Part One). One merely observes the arising of a single thought-moment; that which gives rise [to phenomena] and that which is given rise to are both immediately empty.
They have no self-nature, no other-nature, no common nature, and no causeless nature. They do not abide within, without, or in between, nor do they exist eternally of themselves.
There is only a name, which is called "mind. This word does not abide, yet it is not non-abiding. It does not...

Because it can be attained, it is called "non-arising. The *Siddhārthasamuccaya* states: "Suffering is non-arising; origination is non-combination; the path is non-dual; cessation is non-birth. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"Understanding that suffering is without suffering, and so on, up to understanding that cessation is without cessation, yet there is the True Dharma (Tattva)."

Since accumulation (*saṃskāra*) is itself emptiness, one should not be like a thirsty deer pursuing a mirage. Since suffering (*duḥkha*) is itself emptiness, one should not be like a deluded monkey reaching for the moon in water.
Since the Path (*mārga*) is itself emptiness, one should not say, "I practice that which is emptiness," nor "I do not practice that which is not emptiness."
As for the parable of the raft: even the Dharma should be relinquished, how much more so that which is not the Dharma.

Since cessation is itself emptiness, one should not say that it is sentient beings or their life-span who, having ceased here, realize cessation there. Since birth-and-death is itself emptiness, how could it be abandoned?
Since nirvana is itself emptiness, how could it be attained? As the Sūtra says: "I do not wish to allow that within the dharma of non-arising there be the cultivation of the path."

There are those who have attained the fruits [of the path]. By analogy, one should also say that within the dharma of non-arising (*anutpāda*), there are no five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) or the three poisons (*triviṣa*).

It is merely out of compassion for sentient beings that one gives rise to vows to uproot the two kinds of suffering and bestow the two kinds of happiness. Because one has realized the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of suffering and its origin (*samudaya*), there are not nine bonds;

because one has realized the emptiness of the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*), there is not a single liberation. This is what is meant by being neither bound nor liberated, giving rise to true correctness.

The Bodhicitta (Part Two). One observes only the arising of a single thought-moment; as soon as a thought arises, it is provisional. This mind of provisional names is the root of both delusion and liberation.
It is said that the Four Noble Truths possess immeasurable aspects, yet the three realms contain no separate dharmas; they are produced solely by this one mind.

The mind is like a skilled painter, creating the various five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). That is to say, such views and attachments constitute the signs of the light and heavy accumulations within the realms, as well as the signs of the light and heavy accumulations outside the realms.

Such birth and death constitute the signs of the light and heavy suffering of the *pariccheda* (segmented) existence, as well as the signs of the light and heavy suffering of the *pariṇāma* (transformative) existence.
When this mind turns back and gives rise to liberation, it is like a painter washing away all his [traces].
The form is painted with fine colors. This refers to the contemplation of the body as impure, up to the contemplation of the mind as impermanent.
Such factors of the path (mārga-aṅga) lead circuitously to the city of transformation (nirmita-pura). One contemplates the body as empty of self, up to contemplating the mind as empty of self.
Within emptiness, there is neither impermanence nor impurity. Such factors of the path lead directly to the city of transformation. One contemplates the body as impure; that which is impure is...
Emptiness. ... up to contemplating that the dharma-nature of the body is neither pure nor impure, neither empty nor non-empty;

contemplating the mind is likewise. In this way, the factors of the path wind through to the place of treasure. One contemplates that the dharma-nature of the body is neither pure nor impure, illuminating both purity and impurity simultaneously;
up to contemplating that the dharma-nature of the mind is both permanent and impermanent, illuminating both permanence and impermanence simultaneously.
In this way, the factors of enlightenment lead directly to the place of treasure. When such a person extinguishes [defilements] through the vision of the truths, it is called the first fruit;

when they extinguish them through contemplation, it is called the third fruit. When such a person extinguishes them through vision, it is called the stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*); when they extinguish them through contemplation, it is called "thinning," "detachment," or "having accomplished" (*kṛtāvin*).

Even up to the point of eradicating the residual habits (*vāsanā*), one is called a Pratyekabuddha. When such a person extinguishes both vision and contemplation, it is called the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*); when they extinguish the dust-like sands [of afflictions], it is called the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*).

The Ten Transferences. The extinction of ignorance is termed the Ten Grounds, Equal Enlightenment, and Sublime Enlightenment. When this person extinguishes the afflictions of views, thoughts, and the sands of dust, it is termed the Ten Faiths;
the extinction of ignorance is termed the Ten Abidings, and so on until the extinction of the path of discrimination at Equal Enlightenment and Sublime Enlightenment.
These sixteen gates are distinct, yet all Buddha-dharmas are as clear as looking into the palm of one's hand, without any error or deviation; they all arise from the mind.
Contemplate this single mind; it can penetrate unspeakable minds, unspeakable dharmas, and that which is unspeakably neither mind nor dharma.
Ordinary people bound by the nine fetters do not perceive or know this, like a wealthy man who is blind and sits within his own treasury, moving about therein.

They are wounded by the precious objects themselves. Those of the Two Vehicles are like those suffering from a feverish illness; they perceive the rare treasures as ghosts, tigers, dragons, and snakes, and abandon them and flee.
For more than fifty years, they wander in hardship and distress. Although their states of being bound or liberated differ, both have lost the unsurpassed treasure of the Tathāgata.

Therefore, one should give rise to the vow of compassion to pull others from suffering and bestow happiness upon them; this is what is meant by "neither bound nor liberated" as the manifestation of the True.

The Right Bodhicitta (Part Three). Next, when the sense faculties and their objects encounter one another, the single thought-moment that arises is simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way.
Whether it be the faculty or the object, both are the Dharma-realm; both are ultimately empty; both are the Tathāgatagarbha; both are the Middle Way.

What is meant by "simultaneously empty"? It is empty because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). What is meant by "simultaneously provisional"? It is provisional because they arise despite lacking intrinsic nature. What is meant by...
This is precisely the Middle Way. It does not depart from the Dharma-realm, yet it is entirely the Middle. It is not three, yet it is three; it is three, yet it is not three.
It is neither conjoined nor dispersed, yet it is both conjoined and dispersed. It is neither non-conjoined nor non-dispersed. It is neither vertical nor horizontal; it is inconceivable.
Oneself, the Buddha, and all sentient beings are likewise so. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. Contemplate this.
Yi said: "To seek bodhi while being deluded regarding the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas) is to mistake that which is already detached for something else;

there is no such thing as bodhi. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* says: 'The liberation of the Tathāgata should be sought within the mental activities of sentient beings. Sentient beings are themselves bodhi;
they cannot be further attained. They are themselves nirvāṇa; they cannot be further extinguished. If this is so for a single mind, it is the same for all minds."
All phenomena are likewise so. The *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra* states: "Vairocana pervades all places;

one should know that all phenomena are themselves the Buddha-dharma, for they are the Tathāgata’s dharma-realm. Sometimes "emptiness" is cited as the starting point of the discourse, meaning ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
Sometimes "conditioned existence" is cited as the starting point, meaning that within a single atom there is a great trichiliocosm scripture. Or, sometimes the "middle" is cited.
This constitutes the starting point of discourse: namely, that not even a single form or a single fragrance is anything other than the Middle Way.

If one attains this understanding, then the moment a single thought arises, it already encompasses the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma. That birth-and-death is itself nirvana is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
That a single defilement is itself the eighty-four thousand defilements—that afflictions are themselves awakening—is called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). One by one...
The gates of defilement (*kleśa*) become samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and the various pāramitās; thus, ignorance becomes clarity, just as melting ice becomes water—it is not a separate entity.
Within a single thought-moment, all are universally and fully present. It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*):
to say it has jewels is incorrect, and to say it has no jewels is likewise incorrect. It cannot be known by the mind.
It cannot be distinguished by words. Sentient beings, within these phenomena that are not bound, conceive thoughts of bondage;

within these phenomena that are not liberated, they diligently seek liberation. For this reason, one gives rise to compassion and arouses the great vows to extract them from both sufferings and bestow upon them both joys.
Therefore, it is called "neither bound nor liberated" generating the true and correct bodhicitta (the fourth). Furthermore, according to these four bodhi-...

The mind is directed solely toward the Four Noble Truths. Of these, the first three are provisional (*upāya*), while the last one is real (*tattva*). The provisional does not encompass the real; rather, the real encompasses the provisional.
It is like a skilled physician who possesses a secret formula that subsumes all other prescriptions;

this *agada* medicine combines the efficacy of all other drugs. This constitutes the "Great Matter" (*mahāntam artham*). Because this single reality is not false and the single path is pure, it is called [the Great Matter].

First: Its nature is vast and expansive, possessing great capacity for inclusion. It is that which is mounted by those of great wisdom, great severance, and great personhood; therefore, it is called "Great.
The Buddhas of the three periods attain the Way by means of this and deliver sentient beings by means of this; therefore, it is called "Phenomenon" (Dharma).

Sentient beings invoke the Buddha through this as a cause, and the Buddha responds to them through this as a condition; therefore, it is called "Cause and Condition" (Hetu-pratyaya). Furthermore, this is not...
The method of practice: This is not something created by Buddhas, devas, or humans. The eternal object is signless; the eternal wisdom is without objective conditions.

One takes the signless object as the condition for signless wisdom, and takes the signless object as the characteristic of signless wisdom. Wisdom and object are merged into one, yet they are spoken of as "object" and "wisdom."
This is called non-action; this is called the inconceivable. The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states: "To shatter all arousal is called arousing the bodhicitta.
One arouses the bodhicitta while constantly following the characteristics of bodhi. It is an arousal without arousal, a following without following.
Furthermore, it transcends all arousal and transcends all following; it simultaneously illuminates and shatters both arousal and following—this is called the inconceivable. [The preceding section.]
The first three are observed by superior, middling, and inferior wisdom; the latter one is observed by the most superior wisdom. The former three are common, while the latter one is uncommon.
The former three correspond to the small, medium, and great [stages]; the latter one corresponds to the great-of-the-great and the supreme-of-the-supreme.
The most perfect among the perfect, the reality among realities, the definitive meaning among definitive meanings, the profound among the profound, and the sublime among the sublime.
To thus discern the provisional and recognize the real while generating the bodhicitta is to be of the lineage of all Buddhas.
It is like a prince born already possessing the regal marks and features; it is like the cry of a kalaviṅka chick within its shell, which is already supreme; it is like the sinew of a lion.
It is like the milk of a lion, like the arrow of Nārāyaṇa, and like a wish-fulfilling jewel.

If one understands this mind, one will spontaneously attain *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Being without arousal and without obstruction is *vipaśyanā*; its nature being quiescent is *śamatha*. The *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* states:
A bhikṣu asked the Buddha, "What kind of bhikṣu is able to receive offerings? The Buddha said, "The bhikṣu who..."

“[Included in] the number [of the Saṃgha], practicing the work of the Saṃgha, and obtaining the benefits of the Saṃgha—such a person is able to receive offerings. Those who are candidates for the four fruits are the number of the Saṃgha;

the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the work of the Saṃgha; and the four fruits are the benefits of the Saṃgha. The bhikṣu asked: “If one generates the mind of the Mahāyāna, what then? The Buddha said:

“If one generates the mind of the Mahāyāna seeking all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), one does not fall into the number [of the Saṃgha], does not practice the work [of the Saṃgha], and does not [obtain the benefits].”
He obtained benefits and was able to receive offerings. The bhikṣus asked him in astonishment for the reason why. The Buddha said:

"This person receives robes and spreads them across the great earth; he receives morsel food as vast as Mount Sumeru. You should know that the ultimate fruit of the Hīnayāna does not equal the initial resolve of the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, the *Tathāgataguhyaka-sūtra* says: "If a person has committed the ten grave evils, yet is able to know..."
The Tathāgata has taught the Dharma of causes and conditions: it is without self, person, sentient being, or life-span; it is without arising and without cessation;
it is without defilement and without attachment; its original nature is pure. Furthermore, regarding all phenomena, one knows their originally pure nature, understands and realizes them with faith.
I do not say that such a person will fall into the evil realms. Why is this? Because phenomena have no accumulation, and phenomena have no gathering of afflictions. One.
All phenomena are neither born nor do they abide; they arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and having arisen, they pass away.
All fetters and afflictions likewise arise and then cease. It is impossible for anything to transgress or to abide [permanently]. It is like a dark room that has remained so for a hundred years.
If, when a lamp is lit, one says that the darkness will not depart even though one is the master of the room and refuses to leave, this sutra possesses the aforementioned four types of bodhicitta.
If the merit of the first thought-moment of bodhicitta can already destroy grave offenses, how much more so for the second, third, and fourth?

Now, a practitioner who possesses both wisdom and faith, upon hearing that a single thought-moment is itself Buddhahood, will not slander it because of their faith, nor will they doubt it because of their wisdom.

One need not fear. In this way, every thought from the first to the last is without exception truly real. If one lacks faith, one will distance oneself by speculating that the realm of the sages is beyond one's reach.
If one lacks wisdom, one will give rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*), claiming oneself to be equal to the Buddha.

In such cases, both the beginning and the end are erroneous. For this reason, it is further clarified through the six stages of *bodhi*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* uses the analogy of a burning wick.

This serves as an analogy. It is not that the beginning is separate from the beginning, nor that the end is separate from the end. Although the six names differ, their essential meaning does not vary. These are:

the identity of principle (*li-ji*), the identity of name (*ming-zi-ji*), the identity of practice (*guan-xing-ji*), the identity of resemblance (*xiang-si-ji*), the identity of partial truth (*fen-zhen-ji*), and the ultimate identity (*jiong-jing-ji*).

Regarding the "identity of principle" (*li-ji*): the mind is itself the *tathāgatagarbha*. As previously stated regarding the three truths and the one truth—it is neither three nor one; it is the original...

It exists inherently; therefore, it is called "the principle-as-awakening" (*li-ji-pútí*). It is also called "the principle-as-stillness-and-contemplation" (*li-ji-zhìguān*). That which is quiescent is called "stillness" (*zhì*);

that which is illuminating is called "contemplation" (*guān*). Regarding "the name-as-awakening" (*míngzì-ji-pútí*): although the principle is inherently identical [to awakening], one is unaware of it in daily life.

Now, for the first time, having heard the meaning of the single reality (*yīshí-yì*), one penetrates and understands it through its names and words, realizing that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are entirely the Buddha-dharma. This is...
Names are themselves bodhi; they are also the śamatha and vipaśyanā of names.

As for the practice of contemplation being itself bodhi, it is merely hearing the name and speaking it aloud, like a worm eating wood that happens to form the shape of characters; yet the worm does not know whether these are characters or not.
One must clearly contemplate with the mind, ensuring that wisdom accords with principle, such that one’s words accord with one’s actions and one’s actions accord with one’s words;

this is called "contemplative practice as bodhi," and it is also called "contemplative practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā. Regarding "likeness as bodhi": the more one contemplates, the clearer it becomes;
the more one rests, the more tranquil it becomes. Thus, all worldly activities for livelihood and production do not contradict the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
[This] is the "Backward" [stage]. As the Sūtra says: "The purification of the six sense organs is called 'semblance' Bodhi, and is also called 'semblance' Calm Abiding and Insight.
Regarding "partial true" Bodhi: by the power of semblance contemplation, one breaks through ignorance, perceives the Buddha-nature, opens the secret treasury, and manifests True Suchness;
this is termed the Stage of Initial Resolve up to Equal Enlightenment. It is like the period from the first day of the moon to the fourteenth day.

Light descends as a circle; darkness descends to its end. Whether manifesting the eight phases of enlightenment or appearing through the universal gate (*samantamukha*), this is called "partial true bodhi" and is also termed "partial true *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
As for "ultimate bodhi," when the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) undergoes one final transformation, it enters Wondrous Enlightenment (*tathāgata-samyaksambodhi*).
The light of wisdom becomes perfectly full; this is Great Nirvāṇa. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Beyond this, there are no words that can be spoken. This is...
This is called ultimate Bodhi, and it is also called ultimate śamatha-vipaśyanā. To illustrate this collectively through metaphors:

suppose a poor person has a treasure trove in their home but is unaware of its existence. A knowledgeable friend points it out to them; they clear away the weeds and filth, dig it up, gradually approach the hoard, open it, and finally obtain and utilize it.
Six meanings can be seen here. Question: For what purpose are the six stages of "immediacy" (ji) explained in relation to the Perfect [Teaching]? Answer:

Yuan Guan [Zhiyi] states that all dharmas are categorized as the "six stages of identity. Therefore, according to the principle of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), he employs the six stages of identity to judge the levels of all phenomena.
Other teachings are not like this, and thus he does not employ them. Previously, he excluded the ten non-Buddhist paths based on the ascent and descent within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

Furthermore, he discussed the cleverness or clumsiness, and the depth or shallowness, of wisdom regarding the Four Noble Truths. Finally, he clarified the great vows and practices, and subsequently... [the text continues with the subsequent section].
Sixth, the stages are distinguished; as they progress through increasingly subtle and wondrous levels, this Dharma becomes manifest.
One should know that the divine pearl lies within the nine abysses, beneath the jaws of the black dragon; only those with resolve and virtue can obtain it.

Next is the cultivation of the Great Practice (*mahācaryā*). Now, one who wishes to ascend to the sublime station cannot do so without practice; therefore, following the arousal of the Great Mind, we shall discuss the cultivation of the Great Practice.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Furthermore, I see sons of the Buddha cultivating various practices; the methods of practice are numerous, but now I shall briefly clarify four kinds of samādhi:

first, constant sitting (*nityaparyaṅka*); second, constant walking (*nityacaṃkrama*); third, half-walking and half-sitting (*ardhacaṃkramārdhaparyaṅka*); and fourth, neither walking nor sitting (*anucaṃkramānaparyaṅka*)."
"Samādhi" means the concentration of rectitude and stability. The *Śāstra* states: "The abiding of the virtuous mind in a single place without movement is called samādhi.

This "single place" refers to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). "Abiding without movement" refers to correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*). Regarding "constant sitting," according to the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*:
Both sūtras name this the *Ekavyūha-samādhi*. To cultivate this samādhi, one should reside in a single quiet chamber or a secluded place, sitting upon a single seat.
One should make a vow before sitting: for a period of ninety days, one shall sit upright, facing toward the direction of whichever Buddha one chooses, remaining unmoving and without leaning.
If one becomes utterly exhausted from sitting, or is beset by illness, or overcome by the veil of drowsiness, [one may rest].
If internal and external obstructions cannot be dispelled, one should single-mindedly recollect a single Buddha and invoke the Buddha’s name to sustain the mind.

It is said that because the power of mindfulness is strong, the obstructions will immediately dissolve. Once evil thoughts have departed, one should exclusively bind the conditions to the *dharmadhātu*.
