A single thought of the *dharmadhātu* binds the conditions to form *śamatha*; a single thought forms *vipaśyanā*. One contemplates that all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma, and is thus free from...

Regarding the two extremes of existence and non-existence, one dwells in non-dwelling. To be able to contemplate in this way—just as all Buddhas dwell in the quiescent dharma-realm—is to contemplate the Tathāgata.
When contemplating the Tathāgata, one does not designate the Tathāgata as "Tathāgata";
there is no such thing as a Tathāgata who is a Tathāgata, nor is there any wisdom of a Tathāgata that can know the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata and the wisdom of the Tathāgata are non-dual.

Characteristics do not abide in the directions, nor are they separate from the directions. They are neither of the three periods of time nor not of the three periods of time. They are neither defiled nor pure.
One contemplates the characteristics of sentient beings as being like the characteristics of all Buddhas. The measure of the realm of sentient beings is equal to the measure of the Buddha-realm.

Seeing no ordinary dharmas, how could one abandon them? Seeing no holy dharmas, how could one grasp them? It is the same for birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, and for defilement and purity. This is the contemplation of characteristics.
They give birth to the true Buddha-dharmadhātu. They contemplate that greed, anger, and ignorance are all practices of quiescence and immovability;
they are neither the phenomena of saṃsāra nor the phenomena of nirvāṇa. Without abandoning various views, and without abandoning the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), they cultivate the Buddha-way.

This is neither the cultivation of the path nor the non-cultivation of the path; this is called correctly abiding within the dharmadhātu of afflictions. Furthermore, they contemplate that for those whose karma is heavy, there is no escape.

The five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) are themselves awakening (*bodhi*). Awakening and the five heinous crimes have no distinct characteristics. There is no one who awakens, no one who knows, and no one who discriminates.
They are indestructible; they are fundamentally without intrinsic nature. They are neither cause nor effect. All karmic conditions abide within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
This is what is meant by contemplating karma as the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). By means of this principle, all phenomena may be understood. Thus one practices.
One who hears this and is neither startled nor terrified must have long planted the roots of virtue under hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas.
You should know that such a person has already seen the Buddha and abides in the stage of non-retrogression, fully possessing the six *pāramitās*.

Next is the *Samādhi of Constant Walking*, which is extracted from the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*; this is translated as "The Buddha Standing. Regarding "The Buddha Standing," there are three meanings, namely: Buddha... [text truncated]

Through the power of majesty, the power of samādhi, and the practitioner’s own fundamental merit, one is able to see the Buddhas of the ten directions standing before them within meditative concentration;
therefore, it is called "The Standing of the Buddha. When practicing this samādhi, one should avoid evil associates and always dwell in solitude.
Cease all adornment of the *bodhimaṇḍa*. Bathe, change your robes, and devote yourself exclusively to the practice of the Way for a period of ninety days.
Invite one enlightened master who is proficient in both the inner and outer Vinaya to serve as your guide; serve him with a mind free from resentment or anger.
Constantly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha without ceasing in body or speech, while also mentally contemplating that this Buddha resides ten million *yojanas* away.
Within a jeweled hall upon a jeweled ground across billions of lands, he established the objective field by manifesting the thirty-two subtle marks and signs.

Furthermore, he contemplated that the Buddha is not attained from the mind, nor is he attained from the body. One does not use the mind to attain the Buddha’s form, nor does one use the form to attain the Buddha’s mind.
Why is this? As for the mind, the Buddha has no mind; as for form, the Buddha has no form. Even if one seeks wisdom within oneself, it cannot be found.
Since even a self cannot be found, how could there be any views? All phenomena are fundamentally non-existent; they destroy the root and sever the source.
(First) It is like seeing seven treasures, relatives, and so forth in a dream; upon waking, one searches for them, but not a single thing remains. One should recollect the Buddha in this way.
Furthermore, it is like being hungry or thirsty and dreaming of obtaining fine food; upon waking, the belly is still empty. One should reflect that all phenomena are like dreams.
To recollect the Buddha in this manner is called "recollection according to suchness" (*tathatā*).

Just as an image in a mirror does not come from without nor arise from within, but appears by itself because the mirror is pure, so too when the practitioner’s form is pure, all things are pure, and the Buddha is seen.
(Part Two) Furthermore, one reflects: "From where has the Buddha come? I, too, have nowhere to go. What I contemplate, that I see"—thus [it is] the mind.
To become a Buddha: the mind sees itself; the mind sees the Buddha; the mind is the Buddha; the mind is the self. The mind sees the Buddha;

the mind does not know the mind, and the mind does not see the mind. Where the mind has conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), there is delusion (*moha*); where it is without conceptualization, there is *nirvāṇa*.

This Dharma is not something to be delighted in; it is all produced by thought. Even if thought arises, one thoroughly understands its emptiness. This is called the Seal of the Buddha (the third). The Treatise says:
Contemplating the Buddha of True Reality, one attains supreme power. One should know that this samādhi is the eye of all Buddhas;
all Tathāgatas are born from this Dharma. Next, regarding "half-walking and half-sitting," the Vaipulya Sūtra says: "Rotate one hundred and twenty times."
He sat back and reflected. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Whether that person walks or stands while reading and reciting this sutra, or sits and reflects upon this sutra.
Thus, one knows that both walking and sitting are employed as methods for the practice. For the most honored Vaipulya [teachings], one should do so at a secluded place of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
One should invite a master who is clear in the Vinaya to serve as teacher, receive the twenty-four precepts and the *dhāraṇīs*, and for seven days...
This constitutes one session. When the ten practitioners have returned, they perform the *svāhā* mantra until it is finished. Then, sitting back down, they contemplate the *Mahāpratisarā Dhāraṇī*.
The meaning of "dhāraṇī" is to ward off evil and uphold goodness; it is simply the Middle Way of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), which is the mark of quiescence (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*).
This mark of quiescence is empty; those who seek, those who attain, the real, and those who come—all are likewise entirely empty.
Within that which is sought by none, I therefore seek it. Where should one seek it? One seeks it within the six *pāramitās*. All Buddhas attain the Way through these very dharmas.

According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, a period of twenty-one days constitutes one cycle. The *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* states: "Dedicate yourself solely to reciting the Mahāyāna;

even if you do not enter *samādhi*, repent of the offenses of the six sense organs during the six periods of day and night. The *Anle-xing-pin* (Chapter on the Practice of Peace and Bliss) says: "Regarding..."
All dharmas have no activity; they neither proceed nor are they differentiated. In these two sutras, the facts and the principles complement one another, their essential purport being no different.

When there is wondrous realization, both are abandoned. Furthermore, the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* states: "If one wishes to eliminate the sins of incalculable births and deaths in the space of a single finger-snap;
if one wishes to give rise to the bodhicitta and enter nirvana without severing the afflictions... [The text continues: "...not..."
Those who have detached from the five desires and purified their faculties, and who wish to attain the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, should practice this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

They should cause this wisdom of emptiness to correspond with the mind. One should contemplate that the supreme and unsurpassed skillful means, which is the mother of all bodhisattvas, is obtained through reflection on the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
All transgressions are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can eliminate them. Those who are able to uphold this sūtra [shall achieve this].
This is precisely what constitutes seeing me. "Neither walking nor sitting" means that, in reality, one practices while walking, sitting, and in all activities.

Master Nanyue named this "following one's own intention. Whenever the intention arises, one immediately cultivates samādhi. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* calls this the "Awakening Intention Samādhi" (*bodhy-anga-samādhi*).
When mental factors arise, one reflects back and does not perceive the source of movement or stillness; therefore—

It is called "enlightened mind" (*bodhicitta*). Furthermore, since the root of all phenomena is ultimately created by the mind, it is simply designated as "mind" (*manas*) as the starting point of discourse.
That which perceives objects and distinguishes them from wood or stone is called "heart-mind" (*citta*). Next, that which deliberates following the heart-mind is called "intention" (*manas*).

That which illuminates and discriminates is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). To differentiate in such a manner is to fall into the inversions of thought, perception, and view; this is not yet termed "enlightenment. As for enlightenment:
One knows that within the mind there is neither intention nor non-intention; neither consciousness nor non-consciousness.
Within intention there is neither mind nor non-mind; neither consciousness nor non-consciousness.
Within consciousness there is neither intention nor non-intention; neither mind nor non-mind. Mind, intention, and consciousness are not one.
Therefore, three names are established; because they are not three, one nature is taught. If names are non-names, then nature is also non-nature.

Because they are non-names, they are not three; because they are non-natures, they are not one. Because they are not three, they are not dispersed; because they are not one, they are not combined. Because they are not combined, they do not exist;
because they are not dispersed, they are not empty. Because they do not exist, they are not eternal; because they are not empty, they are not annihilated. If...

One does not perceive permanence or annihilation, nor does one ultimately perceive oneness or difference. Therefore, when contemplating the *manas*, it subsumes the *citta*, the *vijñānas*, and all phenomena.
For the direction of the human mind is either toward the wholesome or the unwholesome; if it does not incline toward the wholesome or the unwholesome, it is then indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Whether in motion or at rest, the myriad variations never transcend these three types. Now, first we shall proceed through various wholesome states for the purpose of contemplation; one should distinguish four [categories].

Fortune. For the mind-consciousness is formless; it cannot be discerned except through its characteristics. These are: the state before thought, the desire to think, the act of thinking, and the state after thinking.

If one penetrates these four characteristics, one immediately enters the single characteristic of non-characteristic. Someone may ask: "The state before thought is called the mind not yet having arisen;

the state after thinking is when the object of perception has already passed. Since these two states are without mind, how can they be observed? Answer: Although the state before thought has not yet arisen, it is not...

Ultimately, it does not exist. Although thoughts have already passed away, they are not eternally extinguished; because they continue in a succession, both [the past and the present] can be observed. Furthermore, it was asked:
"The past has already gone, the future has not yet arrived, and the present does not abide. If one is separated from these three times, there is no distinct mind.

How, then, does one observe the mind? The answer is: "If that which has already ceased, that which has not yet arrived, and that which does not abide are all unknowable, how could a noble one [observe them]?"
People know this. The Verse on the Mind of the Three Times says: "That which all Buddhas have taught is that although things are empty, they are not annihilated;

though they continue in succession, they are not eternal; and yet neither sin nor merit is lost. Once the practitioner knows these four characteristics, they should, according to whatever arises in their thoughts, use the wisdom of non-abiding to reflect back and observe them.
While virtuous matters are numerous, let us for now focus on the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). If there are various sensory objects that must...
Abandon the six types of sensation. If there are no external objects, one must still exercise the six functions; thus, the abandonment and the exercise together constitute twelve factors.
First, when the eye perceives a form, during the four stages—before seeing, the desire to see, the act of seeing, and having seen—the mind in these four exercises cannot be perceived.
Nor can it be said that it does not perceive. Furthermore, when reflecting back upon the mind that cognizes form, it does not come from without, nor does it emerge from within. Nor...
There is no interval; they do not exist eternally of themselves. One should know that the perception of form is ultimately empty and quiescent.

The form being observed is equal to emptiness; the observer is like one who is blind. This applies even up to the mind, which conditions dharmas: whether it has not yet conditioned them, is about to condition them, is currently conditioning them, or has already conditioned them, one reflects upon them as before.
This is called the contemplation of the six perceptions. One contemplates the eye, forms, emptiness, and clarity, each of which is devoid of seeing.
There is also no discrimination. Through the conjunction of causes and conditions, eye-consciousness arises. With eye-consciousness as a cause and condition, mind-consciousness arises.
When mind-consciousness arises, it is then able to discriminate. Dependent upon mind-consciousness, there is eye-consciousness; eye-consciousness is able to see forms. Having seen them, greed arises.
Being defiled by greed, one destroys the precepts—this constitutes the four stages of hell. Although the mind actually covets forms, one conceals it and says otherwise.
Thus it is. Regarding the four modes of the ghost realm: they give rise to attachment to form and calculate it as "self" and "mine. Regarding the four modes of the animal realm:

they regard their own form and the forms of others, considering themselves superior and others inferior. Regarding the four modes of the asura realm: they cultivate the five precepts and ten wholesome actions with respect to form. Regarding the four modes of the human and deva realms: [the same applies].
Contemplate the four phases of the mind: the arising and ceasing of mental states; that each moment of mind does not abide; that each moment of mind is subject to the three types of sensation;

that each moment of mind lacks autonomy; and that each moment of mind is dependent upon causes and conditions. Regarding the four phases of the two vehicles, one contemplates the afflictions of these four phases in both oneself and others, thereby giving rise to compassion and practicing the six perfections.

Furthermore, one contemplates that objects are not objects, remaining free from attachment to objects; and one contemplates that faculties are not faculties, [remaining free from attachment] to oneself.
Without attachment, one contemplates that a person cannot be found and that there is no recipient; these three things are all empty. This is called *dānapāramitā*.
This is what is meant by "giving without dwelling on form. It is like a person with eyes who, when the light of the sun shines upon them, sees various forms.
This is called signless *dāna* reaching the other shore. All dharmas tend toward *dāna*, thereby accomplishing the Mahāyāna. These are the four [perfections] of the Bodhisattva.
Contemplating the four modes of activity (*catur-yoga*) as equal to empty space is permanence (*nitya*). Not undergoing the four modes of activity is bliss (*sukha*).

Not giving rise to karma through the four modes of activity is self (*ātman*). Being unstained by the four modes of activity is purity (*śubha*). These are the four modes of activity of the Buddha-dharma (the four modes of activity common to all Buddhas).

Furthermore, although the four modes of activity are empty, within emptiness one perceives all varieties of the four modes of activity, even seeing them pervasively throughout the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
This is called the four modes of movement as provisional designations (*prajñapti*). If they were empty, they would not possess the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*).

The ten dharma-realms arise from causes and conditions; their essence is neither existent nor empty. Being neither existent, they simultaneously illuminate both emptiness and existence; the three truths are perfectly manifest, fully embodying the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

This is called the four modes of movement as the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). The observation of the five objects—sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas—and the five types of sensation is likewise thus. Next, observe...

Sixth, regarding those who practice giving: one observes that what has not been practiced, what is about to be practiced, what is currently being practiced, and what has already been practiced are all unfindable. One turns back to observe the awakening mind;
it is neither internal nor external, nor is it in between. It is ultimately empty and quiescent, yet by means of this mind, one is driven to act in ways that violate the precepts.
For deception; for retinues; for victory and defeat; for righteousness and yielding; for wholesome meditation; for *nirvāṇa*; for compassion; for provisional names; and for the Middle Way.
Within a single movement, these ten dharmas are fully present. Because the one is not fixed as one, it becomes ten;
because the ten are not fixed as ten, they become one. It is neither one nor ten, yet it is both one and ten, fully embodying the three [truths].
Truth. This applies even to standing, sitting, reclining, speaking, and acting. Furthermore, if one discusses each individual activity in terms of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*):
while walking, one contemplates sentient beings with compassion and loving-kindness, yet does not apprehend the mark of a "sentient being. Sentient beings feel no fear toward such a bodhisattva;
this is *dāna* (generosity) within walking. To cause no harm to sentient beings and not to apprehend the marks of sin or merit—this is *śīla* (ethical discipline).
This is called *śīla* (precept). When practicing, mental conceptions do not arise; there is neither agitation nor a place of abiding. This is called *kṣānti* (patience).
When practicing, one does not perceive lifting or placing the feet; there is no before or after, and no arising or ceasing. This is called *vīrya* (diligence).

One does not grasp at body or mind, and remains neither attached to nor distracted by saṃsāra or nirvāṇa. This is called *dhyāna* (meditation). When practicing, one knows the characteristics of the body to be like clouds and like...
Like a shadow, a dream, an illusion, or an echo, it is neither permanent nor discontinuous; it is neither bound nor liberated—this is called *prajñā*.
Furthermore, within the practice there is a state of tranquil concentration (*samādhi*). If one becomes defiled by this concentration, one will become greedily attached to the flavor of dhyāna;

this is the bondage of the bodhisattva. Now, when observing that even the mind itself does not exist, where could concentration reside? One should know that this concentration arises from inversion (*viparyāsa*). Thus should one contemplate with discernment.
This immediately breaks down fixed characteristics and arises through skillful means; this is the understanding of the bodhisattva.

Furthermore, when a practitioner has not yet attained realization, they may claim that the mind capable of observation is itself sublime wisdom. By exalting themselves through such wisdom, they instead create an obstruction to knowledge.
One should therefore reflect back upon the observing mind and find no place for it to abide. There is neither an observer nor a non-observer. Once the observer is empty, one is liberated from it.
Regarding visualization: the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states, "When mindfulness and conceptualization have been eliminated, one is then able to see Prajñā.

Such practice possesses the three samādhis: first, the observation that destroys all marks is the *śūnyatā-samādhi*; second, the observation that can destroy the mark of emptiness is called the *animitta-samādhi*;
and third, the observation that does not perceive an agent is called the *apraṇihita-samādhi*. This destroys the three inverted delusions and transcends them.
The three outflows (*āsrava*) are brought to completion as *pāramitās*, encompassing all phenomena. How could it be limited merely to the six perfections and the three samādhis?

The same applies to the other eleven matters. Furthermore, being cautious and pure regarding the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), and maintaining refined deportment (*īryāpatha*) during the six activities, is simply called "maintaining precepts" (*śīla-dhara*); it is not yet called "samādhi" nor a *pāramitā*. If one attains this...
Contemplating that ethical discipline (*śīla*) is self-perfected, and so forth—the meanings of patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom are all likewise.

Furthermore, regarding "following one's own intention through all evils": good and evil are not fixed. For instance, the various obscurations are considered evil, while the various perfections (*pāramitā*) are considered good;
yet, when contrasted with the Two Vehicles' departure from suffering, both are considered evil. Moreover, the Two Vehicles stop at their own deliverance alone.
It is not yet good. Only when the Bodhisattva’s six perfections possess the merit of universal salvation can they be called good.
Furthermore, although the six perfections are accompanied by compassion, they are like food stored in a vessel of poison; eating it kills the person. Thus, they remain evil.

It is only when the three vehicles equally sever [delusion] that it is called good. Moreover, even if they equally sever it, if one does not perceive the distinct principle and ignorance remains entirely intact, it is still not good.

"Good. The wisdom of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) is what is called "good. Furthermore, this separate wisdom still retains elements of expedient means (upāya) and thus has not yet attained the title of "ultimate reality.
As the Sūtra says: "All that precedes this is termed 'false view' (mithyādṛṣṭi). Falsehood is precisely evil. Only the Perfect Dharma (yuanfa) is good.

Thus, when discussing good and evil in this manner, their depths and shallows differ. Now, we must take the provisional (shi) as good and the various obscurations (āvaraṇa) as evil. [The preceding...]

Although one contemplates what is wholesome, the obscurations do not cease; whether it be stinginess or greed, anger or indolence, one should apply the wisdom of contemplation according to each specific obscuration.
As the Buddha taught, even householders can attain the Path: Aṅgulimāla was ever more murderous yet ever more compassionate;
Jīvaka and Mallikā were devoted solely to wine yet solely to the precepts; Vāsula was lustful yet practiced the Brahma-faring life; and Devadatta...
When the false views of Puṇyavardhana were thus corrected, one should know that evil does not obstruct the Path.

If a person’s craving and desire are so intense that their application of antidotes and efforts at subduing them only cause them to increase further, then for the time being one should allow them to follow their own inclinations. This is like a fishing net with a wheel:

if the fish is strong and the line is weak, one cannot pull it by force; rather, one must simply ensure the bait enters its mouth, and whether it is near or far, it will be caught before long. Regarding this—

The cultivation of contemplation for the obscuration is also like this. How does one contemplate? When sensual desire arises, one contemplates it clearly through four aspects: the state before desire, the state of desiring, the state of actual desire, and the state after desire has arisen.

One observes that from the state before desire, the desire to desire arises; and from the desire to desire, actual desire arises. From the state of actual desire, the desire to desire arises again. Thus, when the state before desire ceases, the desire to desire arises.
Does desire arise when it has not been extinguished? Does desire arise when it is both extinguished and not extinguished? Or does desire arise when it is neither extinguished nor not extinguished?
If desire were to arise while it has not yet been extinguished, would that mean it arises simultaneously with its cessation?

If it arises at the very moment of cessation, then arising and cessation are contradictory. If it arises after having already ceased, then its arising would be without a cause. If there is no desire...
Regarding that which is not extinguished yet desires to arise: is it identical to or distinct from [extinction]? If it were identical, then two characteristics of arising would exist simultaneously.
If it were distinct, it would likewise be without cause. If one claims that what has not yet been craved arises while being both extinguished and not extinguished:
if it definitely arises from extinction, then "not extinguished" is unnecessary; if it arises from non-extinction, then "extinguished" is unnecessary. It is not determinate.
If a cause gives rise to a determinate effect, then if their substance were one, their natures would be contradictory; if their substance were different, they would originally have no connection.
If you claim that it arises from that which is neither ceasing nor not ceasing, then as for this state of "neither," is it existent or non-existent?
If the "neither" is existent, how can it be called "neither"? If it is non-existent, how can that which is non-existent give rise to anything? As it is said:

These four lines are reversed: one does not perceive that unarisen desire has been extinguished, nor that desire is about to arise, nor that it both arises and does not arise, nor that it neither arises nor does not arise.
This is, for example, as previously explained regarding the contemplation of the obscuration of desire as ultimately empty and quiescent.

If the obscuration constantly arises, this contemplation constantly illuminates; yet one neither perceives the arising nor perceives the illumination, even while arising and illuminating. This is called...
Regarding the bait of the hook: furthermore, observe from where this obscuration arises. Does it arise from sensory objects (*viṣaya*)? Does it arise from conditions (*pratyaya*)?
Whether it be sound or form, whether in motion or at rest, observe its cause according to the place where it arises. Is it for the sake of violating the precepts? Is it for the sake of one's kin?
Or even for the sake of the Two Vehicles, Bodhisattvas, or the Buddha-dharma? When observing in this manner, there is no grasping toward sensory objects.

This means that while there is no agent within conditions, one simultaneously illuminates both existence and non-existence without mutual obstruction. One should know that obscuration and the essence and characteristics of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) are non-dual.
The *Caryāvatāra-sūtra* states: "Desire is itself the path; so too are hatred and delusion. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"By practicing what is not the path, one penetrates the Buddha-path. Sentient beings are themselves the characteristic of bodhi and the characteristic of nirvāṇa."
For those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), it is taught that liberation consists in abandoning lust, anger, and delusion.

For those without overweening pride, it is taught that the very nature of lust, anger, and delusion is itself liberation. To contemplate in this way is to contemplate the inconceivable principle of all evils.

Constantly cultivating contemplative wisdom in conjunction with the removal of obscurations is like the relationship between a form and its shadow; this is called the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-carita*).
Being able to ensure that all evils and worldly dharmas do not contradict the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is called the stage of semblance (*pratirūpa*).

Destroying the ignorance of obscuration and manifesting the vision of Buddha-nature is called the stage of partial realization (*pradeśa-tattva*). Exhausting the very source and bottom of all obscurations is called the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā*). Thus...
Up to the stages of the practice of contemplative wisdom obscured by anger, delusion, and so forth, it is all likewise [as previously explained].

Having clarified that good and evil follow one's own mind, one next clarifies that which is neither good nor evil. Now, that which is neither good nor evil is precisely the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Since the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) has no intention of its own to follow, how can it be an object of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*)? The *Mahā-śāstra* states: "Within the indeterminate, there is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Therefore, one should know that it can also serve as an object of contemplation. One contemplates whether this indeterminate is the same as or different from the wholesome and unwholesome.
If it were the same as the wholesome or the same as the unwholesome, it would not be called indeterminate. If it is different, does the determinate cease and the indeterminate arise? Determinate...
Is it that the indeterminate arises without ceasing? Or does it arise both ceasing and not ceasing? Or does it arise neither ceasing nor not ceasing?

Since even seeking a definitive answer (vyākaraṇa) is unattainable, how much more so the indeterminate? If it were identical to the definitive answer, they would be the same; if it were different from the definitive answer, they would be distinct. If they are not identical, there is no union;
if they are not different, there is no dispersal. If there is no union, there is no arising; if there is no dispersal, there is no ceasing. Thus it is.
When contemplating time, both the recorded and the unrecorded are like empty space. Furthermore, a single unrecorded dharma gives rise to the ten dharma-realms and all dharmas;
thus, within the unrecorded and non-path, one penetrates the Buddha-way, wherein nothing is not fully present. This can be understood by analogy with what preceded.
It is also said that obscuring the essence of the non-path is itself liberation; yet those of dull faculties and heavy obstructions, having heard these words, for the most part...
They sink once more. In the world, there are those who falsely interpret the meaning of the Mahāyāna emptiness (*śūnyatā*), like one who grasps a snake without protective charms.

Their former teachers may have cultivated wholesome dharmas, yet their power of contemplation was not perfected; they briefly attained a minor degree of concentration through unwholesome dharmas and mistook it for realization.
Claiming that all wholesome practices such as upholding the precepts are non-paths, they used this to teach others, causing unwholesome dharmas to proliferate everywhere.
This greatly deviates from the Buddha’s intention. When the Buddha stated that "lust is the path," he was merely referring to the intrinsic nature of lust.
Furthermore, knowing that a certain class of people would certainly be unable to cultivate meditation on wholesome objects, he led them to contemplate lust.

This is like a case where a patient has a severe illness for which various medicines are unsuitable; one simply administers Huanglong Decoction to treat it. Once taken, the illness is cured. This is what is meant by "lust."
This is the Way; the general meaning is as follows. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "I recall that Śrāvakas do not observe the faculties of others before preaching the Dharma.
If even those of the Two Vehicles are thus unsuitable, how much more so those who are spiritually deaf and blind, yet harbor the conceit of being teachers? Someone may ask:

"If the Middle Way and Right Contemplation unify the mind such that its application is self-sufficient, why rely on the manifold four kinds of samādhi and traverse through various good and evil states?"
When water is turbid, the pearl is obscured; when the wind is strong, waves arise. What benefit does this bring to clarity and stillness? Answer:
If one employs the contemplation of a single principle yet the mind is not unified, what can be done? This is a failure in one’s own practice.
Furthermore, since the faculties and natures of others differ, how could a single medicine cure all ailments? This is a failure in transforming others. Thus it is that—
The four kinds of samādhi are presented here in brief merely to encompass and support the various capacities of sentient beings; how could they be considered confused or chaotic? Someone may ask:
"If one is good at supporting the principle, one can cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; but if one is evil and contrary to the principle, how can one cultivate them? The answer is: Not so.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that there are four types of faculties with obstructions: first, those with sharp faculties and no obstructions; second, those with sharp faculties but with obstructions.

Those with dull faculties but no hindrances constitute the third case; those with dull faculties and hindrances constitute the fourth case. The first refers to disciples such as Śāriputra, who entered the Path upon hearing the Dharma once.
The second refers to those with sharp faculties but heavy karmic obstructions, such as King Ajātaśatru and Aṅgulimāla, whom evil could not defile.
Next, there are those whose three karmas are purely wholesome yet who do not accord with principle. Cūḍapanthaka was unable to recite a single verse for ninety days;

those who follow the latter category are all those who perform evil deeds and furthermore fail to practice cultivation. One should know that such people follow only the Way and do not calculate between good and evil.
As the Sūtra says: "To be lax regarding the precepts is not what is called being lax; it is to be lax regarding the Vehicle."
This is why they are called "Huan-er" (Slow-Ears); such is the meaning.
Furthermore, to clarify the pure and great karmic fruition of the Bodhisattva: by practicing in accordance with the Middle Way, one attains a perfect and wondrous fruition.
This principle will be explained extensively later in the eighth [chapter].

Furthermore, regarding "clearly tearing asunder the great net": if one’s contemplative wisdom is lucid, one penetrates the gradual and sudden teachings, like extracting a great thousand-fold scripture from a split atom, thereby knowing the dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

When transforming sentient beings, one contemplates their capacities and bestows the Dharma according to what they can endure, until at the time of attaining Buddhahood, one manifests through the universal gate. "Net" refers to the various *dharmaparyāyas*; it is so called because they are manifold.
The meaning [of this] is that, with respect to sentient beings, it has the sense of delusion; this meaning shall be explained in detail in the ninth [chapter].

Furthermore, regarding "returning to the Great Abode": the Buddhas appear for the sake of the single great cause and condition (ekamahākaruṇā-hetu-pratyaya), so as to cause sentient beings to equally perceive the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
Once they have perceived the Dharma-body, both the Buddha and sentient beings together return to the Dharma-body. Moreover, the Buddha speaks in various ways...
The Dharma causes all sentient beings to reach all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). Once they are fully endowed with all-knowledge, they likewise return to Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, the Buddha employs various skillful means to untie the bonds of sentient beings, liberating them all through the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
Once they have entered parinirvāṇa, they all return equally to liberation. As the Great Sūtra says:

"I shall place my children within the secret treasury, and I too shall not long remain outside it, but dwell therein myself. This is called the "point of return"; it is returning to the Great Abode. Furthermore, there are three kinds of Buddha-bodies.

These are the form body (*rūpakāya*), the dharma-door body (*dharmamukhakāya*), and the reality-body (*dharmatākāya*). As for their respective returns: the form body returns to liberation (*vimukti*); the dharma-door body returns to wisdom (*prajñā*);

and the reality-body returns to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Wisdom also has three types: the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The knowledge of the paths returns to liberation; all-knowledge returns to wisdom; and the knowledge of all aspects—
They return to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Liberation is also threefold: first, liberation from the bondage of ignorance; second, liberation from the bondage of grasping at signs;
third, liberation from the bondage of nescience (*avidyā*). Liberation from ignorance returns to liberation; liberation from grasping at signs returns to *prajñā*;

liberation from nescience returns to the Dharma-body. Furthermore, the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*) are neither three nor one; each is inconceivable. Why? If one were to say that the Dharma-body is merely the Dharma...
The body is not the Dharma-body. One should know that it is both body and non-body; it is neither non-body nor not non-body.
If one says that Prajñā is simply Prajñā, it is not Prajñā. One should know that Prajñā is both knowledge and non-knowledge; it is neither knowledge nor not non-knowledge.
If one says that liberation is simply liberation, it is not liberation. One should know that it is also liberation and non-liberation, neither liberation nor non-liberation.

The three virtues (triguṇa) are neither identical nor different; they do not obstruct one another, and the essence to which they return is the same. Therefore, it is called "the ultimate destination" (*nirvāṇa*). Furthermore, pointing is not pointing;
it is neither pointing nor non-pointing. Returning is not returning; it is neither returning nor non-returning. Each and every thing enters into this.
Within the Secret Treasury, the three virtues are quiescent; originally they possess no names.

Not knowing how else to designate them, we forcibly name them the Middle Way, the True Aspect, and the Dharma-body. We also forcibly name them the Knowledge of All Modes, Equal Great Wisdom, and Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, we forcibly name them the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, Mahāparinirvāṇa, and the Inconceivable Liberation.
Every single name and characteristic enters into the Secret Treasury. What is this taking refuge? To what place does one take refuge?

It is where the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases; it is eternally quiescent like empty space. This is called the true point of refuge. (End of Volume One, Original Edition)
Section Two: Explanation of Terms.
Now, names function to summon their corresponding realities. As a sutra says: "Prajñā is a single dharma; the Buddha speaks of it by various names.

Herein, I shall explain the application of the two terms *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) through two meanings: namely, relative and absolute. Regarding relative *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, there are three meanings for each.
Regarding the three meanings of *śamatha*: the meaning of cessation, the meaning of abiding, and the meaning of ceasing that which is not yet ceased.

"Cessation" refers to the resting of discursive thoughts. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "What is the cessation of objective conditions? It is for the mind to have nothing to apprehend. This is named according to that which is to be eliminated.

"Abiding" refers to the mind taking the ultimate principle as its object and remaining there without movement. As the *Ratnaketuparipṛcchā-sūtra* (Renwang jing) says: "The *prajñā* that enters into the principle is called..."

"Abiding" (sthiti) is so named in the sense of being able to cease [disturbance]. While the term "ceasing what does not abide" (anirodha-nirodha) may linguistically apply to the preceding [two types of cessation], its meaning differs greatly from those two.
First, it stills the movement of birth and death; second, it abides in the tranquility of nirvāṇa. Now, directly regarding the principle of the Truths (satya):
ordinary ignorance (avidyā) is itself the dharma-nature (dharmatā), and the dharma-nature is itself ignorance. Ignorance is neither ceasing nor non-ceasing.
Yet ignorance is termed "non-ceasing," while the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is neither ceasing nor non-ceasing; nevertheless, the nature of phenomena is termed "ceasing.
This is merely a discourse on the ceasing of the nature of phenomena in relation to the non-ceasing of ignorance. As the Sūtra says:

"The nature of phenomena is neither arising nor ceasing, yet it is called the quiescence of the nature of phenomena; the nature of phenomena is neither defiled nor pure, yet it is called the purity of the nature of phenomena. Thus one contemplates.
There are also three meanings: the meaning of piercing through, the meaning of penetrating through observation, and the meaning of observing in contrast to non-observation.

"Piercing through" means to pierce and destroy the afflictions with wisdom. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "To bore and dig through high ground. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "Using a sharp spade to cleave the earth."
This is named according to that which is negated. "Penetrating through contemplation" means to penetrate *tathatā* (suchness) by means of the wisdom of contemplation.
The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* states: "The mind at rest penetrates the source. This is named according to the contemplating subject.

Regarding "non-contemplation as opposed to contemplation," this also specifically refers to the principle of the truths (*satya*), wherein ignorance is itself the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), being neither contemplation nor non-contemplation; yet, ignorance is designated as the "dharma of non-contemplation."

The nature is neither contemplation nor non-contemplation, yet the dharma-nature is termed "contemplation. As the sutra says: "The dharma-nature is neither light nor darkness, yet the dharma-nature is called light.
Next is the illumination of cessation and contemplation through the transcendence of relativity; this is because it breaks down the three meanings of relative dependence.
If cessation were named according to that which is negated, then the name would arise from that [negated object], thereby falling into the nature of other-dependence. If it abides...
If "cessation" (śamatha) is named after that which it negates, then because the name arises from this [negation], one falls into the error of intrinsic nature (svabhāva).

If it is neither the object of cessation nor the principle of abiding, yet is designated as "cessation" because it is the cause for the wisdom of abandonment, then the name "cessation" arises from co-arising, and one thus falls into the error of common nature (sādhāraṇa-svabhāva).

If one claims that it is neither the negated nor the negator, yet is still "cessation," then one falls into the error of causelessness (ahetu). Since all four positions fall into error, Nāgārjuna correctly...
It is said: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another; they do not arise from both, nor without cause. Therefore, they are said to be unarisen.
How could the names "non-arising," "cessation," and "contemplation" be established based on the four propositions? To establish names based on the four propositions is to rely upon dependent arising.

It can be contemplated and spoken of; it arises from the fetters and delusions, and it can be broken and destroyed. Furthermore, that which arises from the four propositions is merely "arising-arising" (生生), not true cessation-and-contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).

If one ceases the views of seeing and thinking (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and abides in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), this is merely cessation-and-contemplation regarding arising and non-arising spoken in dependence upon arising.

If, by means of the empty mind, one emerges into the provisional (*nirmita*), ceasing the dust-like [delusions] and abiding in the conventional (*saṃvṛti-satya*), [this is true cessation-and-contemplation].
This principle refers to the discussion of non-arising arising based on the contrast between arising and non-arising; it is merely the śamatha and vipaśyanā of non-arising arising.
If one ceases ignorance and abides in the central principle, this is the discussion of śamatha and vipaśyanā based on the two extremes of existence and emptiness.

All of these involve mutual dependence and opposition; they are not yet even śamatha, let alone non-śamatha. They are still not even vipaśyanā, let alone non-vipaśyanā. Why? Because the elimination of attachments is not yet complete.

Language does not cease; the fruits of karma do not end. This is not the inconceivable Dharma. The inconceivable cuts off all dharmas such as karma, its fruits, and afflictions, so that none of them arise at all;
therefore, it is called "cessation" (*śamatha*). Yet even this cessation cannot be apprehended. Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is darkly identical to the object.
Since the object is already quiescent, how could there be contemplation? Furthermore, how can one discuss cessation by depending on what is neither non-cessation nor non-contemplation?
Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) depends upon cessation (*śamatha*) to be called "not cessation or contemplation. Cessation depends upon non-cessation to be called "neither cessation nor non-cessation.

When all such mutual dependencies are severed, it is neither conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). It is the path that transcends words; it is not the domain of mind or consciousness.

Its extinction is the extinction of extinction—this is called "absolute transcendence" (*juedai*). This absolute cessation and contemplation cannot be described; yet, because there are causes and conditions, it can also be described.
It can be explained. This explanation concerns *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. These names do not exist internally, externally, or in between;

nor do they inherently exist eternally. These names neither abide nor do they not abide; therefore, they are called "absolute *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*" and also "the *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* of the One Great Matter.
This Great Matter does not stand in contrast to small matters; it is like space, which is not named "great" because of a small space. *Śamatha*...

Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is also like this. It is not called "calm abiding and contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) because of delusion or confusion; there is nothing with which it can be contrasted. It is the solitary Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), transcending all relativity.

To transcend, and then to transcend that very transcendence—this is what is meant by "transcending relativity," as in the previous analogy of fire and wood. Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
That "all phenomena do not wait for one another, because they do not abide for even a single moment" is precisely its essential meaning.

This principle of non-reliance (or non-dependence) is sometimes termed "detachment," "non-abiding," "non-discrimination," "unconditioned," "quiescent cessation," or "meditative concentration" within the sūtras and śāstras.

All such terms as these are synonyms for cessation; their essence is utterly transcendent and great. Some are called "knowledge and vision," while others are called "wisdom, awakening, and illumination.
All such terms as these are synonyms for contemplation; their essence is utterly transcendent and great. Prajñā and liberation have many various names.

According to the various types of sentient beings, one establishes different terms within a single dharma. Furthermore, cessation (*śamatha*) is also called contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), because concentration is itself wisdom.

It is also called non-cessation, because the essence of concentration is empty. Contemplation is also called cessation, because illumination is itself quiescence. It is also called non-contemplation, because the essence of illumination is within [the nature of reality].
In various sutras, according to the conditions of those to be taught, a single dharma is emphasized to demonstrate the starting point of the meaning. This is the case with the *Śūraṅgama*.

Thus, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* discusses [the three natures] exclusively; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* discuss [them] exclusively from the perspective of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* discusses the complete fulfillment of the three dharmas.
One should know that each and every one of these is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and is the secret treasury (*guhyagarbha*).

Section Three: Explaining the Essence of Śamatha and Vipaśyanā. Now, the essence of the Dharma is difficult to manifest; I shall now clarify it through four points: first, the characteristics of the teaching; second, vision and wisdom; third, the objective realm;
and fourth, gain and loss. Regarding the characteristics of the teaching: the names "śamatha" and "vipaśyanā" are teachings that apply universally to both ordinary beings and sages. It is not...
One may seek the distinct essence by following its general name; therefore, they are distinguished by their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

If, for an ordinary person, that which is the object of cessation through wholesome states is the characteristic of calm (*śamatha*), and that which is produced by the practice of wholesome states is the characteristic of insight (*vipaśyanā*); furthermore, the four dhyānas and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are the characteristic of calm.

The six practices are the aspect of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); they all possess the aspect of being with outflows (*sāsrava*). If the two vehicles practice *dhyāna* through phenomena, it is the aspect of cessation (*śamatha*);
if they employ the wisdom of the Four Noble Truths, it is the aspect of contemplation. Although this brings about liberation from birth and death, it is a clumsy means of deliverance.

It merely analyzes form to enter emptiness and thus possesses the aspect of being without outflows (*anāsrava*); it is not the skillful means of deliverance discussed here. Cessation (*śamatha*) has three types: first, cessation that accords with reality; second, cessation according to [the specific] direction...

One then rests according to conditions. Third is resting by stilling the two extremes. Regarding "realizing the true nature": all dharmas arise from conditions; causes and conditions are empty and without a master.

By stilling the mind, one reaches the fundamental source; therefore, one is called a śramaṇa. Knowing that which is a provisional combination and an illusory transformation, its essence is emptiness, and emptiness is itself the truth.
Thus, it is named "stopping by realizing the true nature. Regarding "skillful means following conditions": if the three vehicles likewise [use]...
The path beyond words severs delusions and enters the Truth; yet that Truth is not otherwise. It is simply a matter of whether the residual habits of affliction have been exhausted or not.

For the followers of the Two Vehicles, realizing the essence of Truth requires no further expedient means. For Bodhisattvas, however, entering the realm of the provisional while knowing that emptiness is not [mere] emptiness, they distinguish between medicines and ailments;

thus it is termed "expedient means. Because they abide in conventional truth, it is called "cessation according with conditions" (*suiyuan zhi*). As for "resting from the two extremes," it refers to...

Birth-and-death as flux and nirvana as a fixed guarantee—both of these are one-sided extremes and do not accord with the Middle Way. Now, knowing that the conventional is not merely conventional, it is quiescent at the limit of the conventional;
yet one does not grasp it as non-conventional, for it is also quiescent at the limit of emptiness. This is called the cessation of the two extremes.
These three names for *śamatha* (calm abiding) are not seen in the sūtras or śāstras; they are now established in contrast to the three types of *vipaśyanā* (insight). The *Śāstra* states:
"The Bodhisattva, relying on the scriptural teachings, establishes these designations; this is called the 'gift of Dharma' (*dharma-dāna*). What fault is there in establishing such names?

Upon careful examination, these three *śamathas* appear similar to the three *śamathas* discussed in the *Vyākhyāyukti*, yet when analyzed according to the Three Truths (*trīṇi satyāni*), their characteristics are vastly different. Insight is likewise of three kinds. [From the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*...]

The *Luo jing* (Luo-chu-jing) states: "Entering emptiness from the conventional is called the contemplation of the two truths; entering the conventional from emptiness is called the contemplation of equality.

These two contemplations serve as the path of skillful means to enter the Middle Way and simultaneously illuminate the two truths. With every thought extinguished, one naturally flows into the ocean of sarvajñā (all-knowledge);
this is called the contemplation of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way. As for what are called the 'two truths,' it refers to the contemplation of the conventional..."

It is the means for entering emptiness (*śūnyatā*); emptiness is realized through this means. When the subject and object are discussed together, it is called the contemplation of the two truths (*dvayasatya-vipaśyanā*).

Furthermore, it is not merely realizing emptiness, but also recognizing the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). The conventional is manifested by the ultimate (*paramārtha*); thus it is named the contemplation of the two truths.

Moreover, the conventional is that which is to be refuted, while the ultimate is that which is employed. When refutation and employment are discussed together, it is called the contemplation of the two truths. Entering the conventional from emptiness is termed "equality."
Regarding "contemplation": if one says that upon entering emptiness there is not even emptiness to be found, how could there be anything further to enter?
One should know that this contemplation is for the sake of transforming sentient beings; it is to know that the true is not [merely] true, and through skillful means to emerge from the conventional.

Therefore, it is said that by discerning the medicine and the illness from within emptiness, there is no error; thus, it is called "entering the conventional. The preceding contemplation destroyed the illness of the conventional and did not employ conventional dharmas, but employed only the true.

The Dharma has not yet reached equality. This contemplation breaks the illness of emptiness by employing the medicine of the conventional; since both the breaking [of the illness] and the application [of the medicine] are balanced, it is called the Contemplation of Equality.

As for the Contemplation of the Middle Way, the Supreme Truth: the former contemplation—conventional emptiness—is the emptiness of saṃsāra; the latter contemplation—emptiness of emptiness—is the emptiness of nirvāṇa.
To be free from both extremes is termed the Contemplation of the Two Emptinesses, which serves as the path of skillful means. One thereby attains...
In the midst of the assembly, it is said: "Therefore, one speaks of the mind and mind being quiescently extinguished, flowing into the ocean of *sarvajñā*.

Furthermore, first one contemplates the function of emptiness, and next one contemplates the function of the provisional; this constitutes the skillful means of maintaining both simultaneously. When entering the Middle Way, one is able to simultaneously illumine the two truths.
The Sūtra says: "If the mind is in meditative concentration (samādhi), one can know the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of worldly phenomena.

The purpose of the preceding two contemplations as skillful means lies herein. Someone may ask: "The Mahāyāna Sūtras state that if there is an excess of concentration or an excess of wisdom, one does not perceive the Buddha-nature. Why is this so?"
Answer: Regarding the third contemplation, the practitioners of the Two Vehicles and the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching possess the first stage of contemplation;
this belongs to those in whom concentration (*samādhi*) predominates and wisdom (*prajñā*) is deficient. The Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching possess the second stage of contemplation;

this belongs to those in whom wisdom predominates and concentration is deficient. Because these two are unequal, neither perceives the nature (*dharmatā*). However, if one takes these two contemplations as skillful means to enter the third, then one will be able to perceive it. Furthermore—
Question: A sutra states that bodhisattvas of the ten stages see [the nature] indistinctly due to their wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), yet it is not that they do not see at all.

Now, the first contemplation already belongs to the stage of the wisdom-eye, and the second belongs to the stage of the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*). Why, then, do you say that both eyes fail to see the nature? Answer:
If the eyes were sequential—such that one is fixed solely on concentration (*samādhi*) and the other solely on wisdom—the Buddha would have rebuked this. Therefore, one cannot speak in such a manner.
As for what is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*), it refers to the wisdom of simultaneous, non-sequential contemplation.

At the stage of the Ten Abodes where ignorance is shattered, the three contemplations manifest before one and the three truths are perfectly illumined; therefore, it is named "wisdom. The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "May I become like the World-Honored One."
The wisdom-eye is the foremost purity; it is not comparable to the minor wisdom of the two vehicles. It is impossible for minor wisdom to perceive the nature [of reality].

These three contemplations (samādhi) share names that appear similar with those explained in other contexts, yet their underlying principles are distinct; they may be understood by applying one's own reasoning to these categories.

This section follows the Mahāyāna in elucidating the characteristics of the three cessations (śamatha) and three contemplations (vipaśyanā), according to their meanings as they correspond to their respective forms. Itemized:

However, these are each distinct. If one discusses the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), there are provisional and ultimate, as well as shallow and deep aspects. If one discusses the three knowledges (*trividya*), there are distinctions of superiority and inferiority, and priority and posteriority.

If one discusses the three types of persons, there are gradations of rank and levels of small and great capacity. These are all teachings concerning gradual progression and do not represent the characteristics of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
As for the characteristics of the Perfect and Sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā*: when employing *śamatha* to take the Truths as its object, a single Truth is simultaneously the three Truths.
When one brings the mind to rest through the truths, then a single cessation is three cessations. This is like the three characteristics existing within a single moment of mind;

though it is but a single mind, it possesses the three characteristics. It is the same with cessation and the truths: the phenomena that are ceased are one yet three, and the mind that ceases them is three yet one.
When one contemplates the object through contemplation, then a single object is three objects, for it is through the object that contemplation is aroused.
Thus, in a single contemplation there are three contemplations. It is like Maheśvara, who has one face and three eyes; the contemplation of the object is likewise.

Contemplating the three is immediately the one, and giving rise to the one is immediately the three. They are neither provisional nor real, neither superior nor inferior, neither prior nor posterior, neither unified nor distinct, neither large nor small.
Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* proclaims them as "emptiness, the conventional, and the middle" (*śūnyatā*, *upāya*, *madhyama*). If one perceives this...

The essential meaning is precisely the characteristic of perfect contemplation. What is this characteristic? To illuminate the delusions of ignorance as being the reality of the true aspect is called "True Cessation" (zhēnzhǐ) in terms of essence and substance.
When this true aspect pervades all places, remaining unmoved while following conditions and traversing objects, it is called "Convenient Cessation according to Conditions" (suíyuán fāngbiàn zhǐ).
When both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are brought to rest, it is called "Cessation of the Two Extremes" (xī èrbiān).
Cease. To realize that all phenomena are conventionally empty is emptiness, which is the true mark (*dharmatā*); this is called entering the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

When this contemplation merges with the Middle Way, one is able to know the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of worldly phenomena as they truly are; this is called entering the contemplation of the conventional (*saṃvṛti-vipaśyanā*).

To realize that these are the ultimate reality, non-dual and undifferentiated, is called the contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-vipaśyanā*). Such meanings are all contained within a single thought-moment, without wavering.

Within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), there are various distinctions. As the Sūtra says: "One who is well able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena does not waver from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This is called the essence of the Perfect and Sudden Calm Abiding and Insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*). Second, clarifying the one with the eye of wisdom:
Now, the essence of the Dharma is perfectly quiescent; it is neither known nor seen. It is difficult even to speak of it, let alone to demonstrate it to others. Although it cannot be known...
One sees. Through the wisdom of the eye (*cakṣur-jñāna*), it can both be known and seen. Although it is not itself cause and effect, it must rely upon cause and effect to be manifested.

Cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) serve as the cause, and the wisdom of the eye serves as the fruit. Now, first I shall clarify the sequential order of the wisdom of the eye. If one abides in true cessation (*tattva-śamatha*), delusive afflictions do not arise.
Based on cessation, concentration (*samādhi*) is produced; from concentration, untainted (*anāsrava*) wisdom arises. Because the eye of wisdom opens, one sees the first [truth].
The Samādhi of the True Meaning of the One Reality is accomplished; thus, cessation (*śamatha*) can perfect the eye, and the eye can perceive the essence, thereby attaining the true essence.

If one practices cessation in accordance with conditions, one merges with the truth and emerges into the provisional, abiding securely in conventional principles. Because of this cessation, the Dharma-eye opens wide.
One destroys the obscuration of ignorance. By not viewing the various Buddha-lands through dualistic characteristics, the samādhi of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is perfected.

Thus, *śamatha* (calm abiding) can give rise to the eye; the eye can attain the essence—that is, the essence of the conventional. If one brings to rest the two extremes, then both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, emptiness and existence, are simultaneously stilled.
Based on this *śamatha*, the concentration of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) arises, and the Buddha-eye opens wide, such that there is nothing it does not perceive.
When illumination occurs, the Samādhi of the Middle Way is accomplished; thus, cessation can obtain the eye, and the eye can obtain the essence—the essence of the Middle Way.

If one enters emptiness from the conventional, and the wisdom of emptiness is brought into correspondence, one is then able to destroy the delusions of views and thoughts and accomplish all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*).

Wisdom is able to attain the essence; it attains the true essence. If one proceeds from emptiness into the provisional, distinguishing between medicine and illness, one then shatters ignorance and accomplishes the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā).

Wisdom is able to attain the essence; it attains the conventional essence. If one simultaneously negates both extremes as a skillful means for entering the Middle Way, one can shatter ignorance and accomplish the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā). Wisdom is able to attain the essence; it attains the middle essence.
This constitutes the three cessations and three contemplations, which together accomplish the three eyes and three wisdoms, each attaining its own threefold essence.

Someone may ask: "The eye sees and wisdom knows; are knowing and seeing different? The answer is: this should be analyzed by means of four propositions (catuṣkoṭi). There is that which is knowing but not seeing;

that which is seeing but not knowing; that which is both knowing and seeing; and that which is neither knowing nor seeing. This is because ordinary persons have not heard the Dharma and have not realized the principle.
There is neither knowledge nor vision. Because the followers of the Two Vehicles have realized [the truth], they also see; because they have heard [the teachings], they also know.

For Pratyekabuddhas, it is seeing because they have realized it, but it is not knowing because they have not heard [the teachings]. On the path of expedient means, it is knowing because they have heard it, but it is not seeing as long as they have not yet realized it.

Since the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) is thus, the remaining two types of wisdom and two types of eyes may be understood accordingly. Next, the non-sequential relationship between the eyes and wisdoms is clarified: cessation and contemplation are one.
In essence, vision and wisdom are not distinct; knowing is itself seeing, and seeing is itself knowing. The Buddha-eye encompasses the five eyes, and the Buddha-wisdom encompasses the three wisdoms.
The King Samādhi contains within it all samādhis, and the Śūraṅgama Samādhi subsumes all concentrations. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"If one wishes to attain the wisdom of the path, the wisdom of the aspects of the path, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and the wisdom of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), one should..."
Regarding the study of Prajñāpāramitā, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) up to the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*).

Although the eyes are but one, they are able to illuminate five objects. That which illuminates coarse forms, as seen by ordinary people, yet surpasses what ordinary people see, is called the fleshly eye.
That which illuminates subtle forms, as seen by devas, yet surpasses what devas see, is called the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*). These two penetrate both coarse and subtle forms.

Emptiness as perceived by the followers of the Two Vehicles is called the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*). Thoroughly penetrating conventional phenomena without error, as perceived by Bodhisattvas, is called the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*).

Perceiving the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) within all phenomena is called the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*). Furthermore, the Buddha’s wisdom illuminating emptiness as known by the followers of the Two Vehicles is called the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*).
Illuminating the conventional as known by Bodhisattvas is called the knowledge of the paths and their varieties (*mārgākārajñatā*). [Illuminating] emptiness...
Within both the provisional and the middle, one perceives the true reality; this is called the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Thus, the three types of cessation within a single mind constitute the three eyes, which perceive the inconceivable three truths. The three types of contemplation within a single mind constitute the three knowledges, which cognize the inconceivable three objects.
As for these objects and truths, and these perceptions and cognitions, though they differ as "left" and "right," they are in truth but a single inconceivable dharma. By employing this one...
The wisdom of the Dharma-eye is the realization of the essence of perfect and sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Regarding the realm of the three insights (*trividyā*):

if one has attained understanding through the wisdom of the eye, there is no need to rely on the discourse of the realms of the [Four] Truths. However, for those who are deluded and have not yet awakened to this, it shall be further clarified.
First, the intent of the realm is explained: the Sūtra states, "To open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision for all sentient beings. If there were no middle realm, what would there be to know or see?
One should know that there must be an objective realm for the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*). Furthermore, a sutra states: "In this world, who possesses the true divine eye (*divyacakṣus*)?

It is one who does not perceive the various Buddha-lands through dualistic characteristics (*dvaya-lakṣaṇa*). If there were no mundane objects, what would there be to see? One should know that there is an objective realm for the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*).
Again, a sutra states: "The wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*) perceives the truth. One should know that there is an objective realm for the wisdom-eye. These three truths are not... [incomplete].

It can be explained. If it is explained by way of conditions, there are three intentions: namely, explaining according to [the listener's] feelings, which is speech that accords with the intentions of others;

explaining according to feeling and wisdom, which is speech that accords with the intentions of both self and others; and explaining according to wisdom, which is speech that accords with one’s own intention.

Regarding "teaching according to [the listeners'] dispositions": it is like a blind man asking what milk resembles. He is told that it is like a conch shell, like fine powder, like snow, or like a crane.
The blind man does not understand; each clings to what he has heard and gives rise to four disputes. Ordinary people do not recognize the Three Truths.

Through the skillful means of great compassion, [the Buddha] makes distinctions for them: sometimes in terms of existence, sometimes in terms of emptiness, sometimes as both existent and empty, or sometimes as...

It is neither empty nor existent; each [school] clarifies the three truths. Although they hear the teachings of the four gates, in the end they cannot see [the truth], as they engage in mutual disputes of right and wrong.
In recent times, there have been twenty-three schools of interpretation regarding the two truths, each citing sūtras and śāstras, yet it remains unknown which is correct.

If these types of practitioners, according to their dispositions, hear various teachings on the three truths, they immediately understand that the Tathāgata, in condescension to the manifold dispositions of sentient beings, speaks of the three truths through speech that accords with the intentions of others.
Regarding "speaking according to disposition and wisdom": from the perspective of disposition, two [truths] are taught;

from the perspective of wisdom, one is taught. Why is this? Speaking from the standpoint of ordinary dispositions, all are expedient means; therefore, the three truths are subsumed into emptiness and the conventional.
Speaking from the perspective of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), all are realized as reality; therefore, the three truths are subsumed within the Middle Way.

When comparing ordinary beings with the noble ones, one speaks of the three truths through the intentional discourse regarding oneself and others. As for teaching according to wisdom: the three truths are profound and subtle, illuminated only by wisdom;
they cannot be shown and cannot be conceived, being exhaustively realized only by the Buddha. They are like the true color of milk, which can only be seen once the eyes are opened.
This is called the discourse on the three truths according to one's own intention. Furthermore, each [truth] is explained individually as possessing the four *siddhānta* intentions.
Regarding the four intentions that follow worldly sentiment: the principle of truth (*tattva*) is ultimately ineffable; yet when it must be expressed, it necessarily relies upon words.

Some take pleasure in hearing about the ultimate (*paramārtha*), some take pleasure in hearing about the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), and some take pleasure in hearing about the Middle Way (*madhyamā*). This application of the world-siddhānta (*loka-siddhānta*) according to sentiment is precisely this. Now, as for the multitude...

The inclinations of sentient beings differ. Some hear teachings on non-existence and thereby increase their precepts and wisdom; some hear teachings on existence and thereby increase their precepts and wisdom;
and some hear teachings on the Middle Way and thereby increase their precepts and wisdom. This is the *puruṣasāntāna* (teaching for individuals) employed according to their dispositions.

Furthermore, practitioners differ in how they destroy evil: some do so regarding existence and non-existence, while others do so regarding the Middle Way; they are able to destroy such states as dullness, distraction, doubt, and regret.
This is the application of the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic remedies) according to individual dispositions. Moreover, practitioners differ in how they realize the principle.

Some awaken to existence, some awaken to non-existence, and some awaken to the Middle; each attains realization and entry. This is the application of the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate truth) according to individual dispositions.

(The names and meanings of the four *siddhāntas* originate from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. It is said that through great compassion, these four methods are universally applied to enable sentient beings to obtain benefit.)
According to [the capacities of] sentiment and wisdom, and according to wisdom, the three truths are taught. Each employs the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) in this manner;

thus, there are twelve distinct ways of teaching the three truths through the combination of three and four. How can one use ordinary sentiments and limited measures to judge the sages, clinging to disputes and thereby destroying oneself?

Next, we discuss whether the object and wisdom are separate or unified. According to the various sutras that explain the truths, they may be one, two, three, or four, with differences in their separation or unification.

The Tripiṭaka is a teaching of expedient means that clarifies only the two truths. Bodhisattvas first take the ultimate truth as their object, next illuminate the conventional truth, and finally, having severed all afflictions of views and thought, they attain the wisdom-eye to illuminate the ultimate truth; only then do they become Buddhas.

Bodhisattvas illuminate only the conventional truth, while those of the Two Vehicles illuminate only the ultimate truth; the Buddha can encompass both, further adding the Middle Way of the Supreme Truth. Thus, there are either three or two [truths].

Both are skillful means (*upāya*). Separated, they constitute two; combined, they constitute three. This is called the characteristic of the separation and combination of the two truths and three truths within the Tripitaka teachings.

Next, regarding the fact that the three vehicles equally employ the path beyond words to sever afflictions: if one discusses the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), they are the same; if one discusses the ultimate (*paramārtha*), they differ.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There are two kinds of emptiness: first, mere emptiness (*tāvat-śūnyatā*); second, not-mere-emptiness (*na-tāvat-śūnyatā*). Thus it is said in the Sūtra.
It is said: Those of the Two Vehicles perceive only emptiness and do not perceive non-emptiness. The Wise One, however, perceives not only emptiness but is also able to perceive non-emptiness;
this non-emptiness is precisely Great Nirvāṇa. The wisdom of the Two Vehicles is like a firefly, while that of the Bodhisattva is like the sun.

Since their wisdoms differ regarding emptiness, there was previously a distinction between the Two Truths; now, they are unified as the Single Reality. For the Two Vehicles, there is only emptiness and no...

Regarding the function of transforming others: when a Bodhisattva enters into both "emptiness-only" (*śūnyatāmātra*) and "not-emptiness-only," they destroy ignorance and perceive the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), thereby transforming and delivering sentient beings.
This is fundamentally distinct from the previous [stage]. When emptiness-only and not-emptiness-only are united, they constitute the Single Truth; when separated, they form two truths.
Furthermore, the third truth is also called the Truth (*satya*) and is also called the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*); it possesses a distinct essence.

The Separate Teaching (Biezhì) differs from the Tripiṭaka Teaching. This constitutes the characteristics of the convergence and divergence of the two truths and three truths within the Shared Teaching.

Next, the two truths of the Separate Teaching are forever different from the former. In the previous teachings, the true and the conventional are combined; however, in the Separate Teaching, the "conventional" is defined such that for ordinary beings it is called conventional, while for the Two Vehicles it is called true.
