Although they differ regarding existence and non-existence, here they are collectively termed "conventional. As the Śrīmālā-sūtra states: "The two..."

The vehicle is emptiness. For sentient beings with distracted minds, the Great Sūtra states: "What I and Maitreya discuss as conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), the śrāvakas call ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).

If one discusses two truths, then conventional truth is not further differentiated. If one discusses three truths, then the conditioned is opened as conventional truth and the unconditioned is opened as ultimate truth;
this is contrasted with 'not merely empty' as the primary truth. This constitutes the differentiation and integration of the Separate Teaching (prthaktva-naya).

This is the characteristic [of the teachings]. Next, the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) clarifies only the single Truth of Reality (yishidi). The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra states: "In reality there is but one truth; it is through expedient means that two are spoken of.
By this analogy, it is also through expedient means that three are spoken of. The Lotus Sūtra says: "Furthermore, by means of diverse expedient means, I assist in manifesting the primary meaning.

This, then, is the characteristic of separation and integration within the Perfect Teaching. As for the meaning of the separation and integration of the four kinds of Four Noble Truths, it may be understood...

This is the explanation of the meaning. Next, the treatise discusses the combination and separation of the knowledges (*jñāna*). In the sūtras, there may be one knowledge, two, three, four, or even up to eleven knowledges.
The "one knowledge" refers to the Tathāgata’s knowledge; it is one yet threefold. The "two knowledges" refer to the provisional (*upāya*) and the real (*tattva*):

provisional knowledge contemplates existence and non-existence, while real knowledge contemplates the Middle Way. The "three knowledges" contemplate the Three Truths, which is easily understood. From four onwards...
Up to the eleventh [section], although the names and teachings differ, they essentially do not depart from the meaning of the three wisdoms and the three truths.

Those who have attained realization should discern this with refined attention. Regarding the fourth point, the clarification of loss and gain: "loss" refers to that which is conceivable (*saciṃtya*), and "gain" refers to that which is inconceivable (*acintya*).

If one claims that wisdom arises from the mind and can naturally illuminate objects, then whether it illuminates or does not illuminate, the object remains inherently as it is by nature. As it is said:
In this case, the two do not depend upon one another. If it is claimed that cognition is not cognition in itself, but cognition exists by virtue of the object;
and that the object is not the object in itself, but the object exists by virtue of cognition—such that they exist in mutual dependence—then they are co-arising through reciprocal causation.

If it is claimed that the object is not the object in itself, nor does the object exist because of cognition, but rather that the object and cognition are mutually conditioned, and the same applies to the meaning of cognition and object—this constitutes a name formed by their conjunction. If...
This means that these three types [of causes] do not exist; rather, things occur spontaneously. This would imply they are causeless, which—as with the four previous explanations—is a fallacy.
Why? Because where there are the four graspings (*upādāna*), there is dependence; where there is dependence, there is right and wrong;

where there is right and wrong, there arise conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*); and from contention, various karmas arise. One should know that the four graspings are the root of birth and death; therefore, Nāgārjuna cuts them down.
By means of the four modes—neither self, nor other, nor common, nor apart—one destroys these four natures, whereby all fetters and afflictions are eliminated.
For this reason, the wisdom regarding its own object and the suffering of the origin [of suffering] do not arise; this is what is called "the ineffable arising of arising.

Even up to the point where there is no cause and thus no arising, this is what is called "the ineffable non-arising of non-arising. Here, the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases. Body...
The disciple remained silent; Vimalakīrti closed his mouth. It was for this reason. If there were specific causes and conditions, any of the four modes of teaching would be appropriate.
Why? Because names have no inherent nature; these words neither abide nor do they not abide. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* calls this the realm of inconceivable wisdom.
That the inconceivable wisdom shines forth is precisely this meaning. One should know that the four negations constitute the reality.
The four [aspects] are said to be the provisional. Thus, regarding these provisional and ultimate objects and wisdoms, ordinary beings lose both;
those of the Two Vehicles gain one and lose one; and Bodhisattvas gain both. Why is this? Ordinary beings have four faults: they fail both in their own practice and in transforming others.

Those of the Two Vehicles eliminate these four faults but do not transform others. Only Bodhisattvas possess both. Furthermore, ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles alike remain within the realm of discursive thought.

The Bodhisattva’s attainment of both is inconceivable. Furthermore, in the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), the attainment of both is entirely conceivable; in the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), the attainment of both is inconceivable.

Moreover, in the Path of Instruction (Jiaodao) of the Distinct Teaching, which involves expedient means, the attainment of both is entirely conceivable; only in the Path of Realization (Zhengdao) is the attainment of both termed inconceivable.
As for the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the attainment of both the Path of Instruction and the Path of Realization is entirely inconceivable. Why is this? It reaches...

In principle, there is nothing to be said. Because it is conditioned by the four [truths], its teaching exists only as a provisional name (*prajñapti-nāman*). Since the name of a provisional name is itself unborn, both the teaching and its realization are inconceivable.
Because they are without thought or recollection, they are free from dependence, conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and the karma of fetters.

Being without karma, there is no birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). This is called attaining through one's own practice; it is the attainment of the ultimate reality (*tattva-vastu*). Thus, one is able to [realize] that which is ineffable.

It is said that by transforming and guiding sentient beings, one causes them to transcend birth and death and attain the true essence. When both self and others attain this essence, it is called the manifestation of the essence of śamatha and vipaśyanā through the realization of gain and loss.
Section Four: Comprehending the Dharmas.
Now, the names "calm abiding" (śamatha) and "insight" (vipaśyanā) encompass all dharmas. If the power of faith is not firm, doubt and confusion will inevitably arise.
Therefore, the dharmas they encompass are distinguished and explained herein. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, those who wish to study all dharmas should study the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
If *prajñā* is simply the wisdom of contemplation, and *śamatha* is the sovereign samādhi into which all samādhis enter, then by extending this principle broadly, there are six meanings:

namely, it encompasses all principles, encompasses all afflictions, encompasses all wisdoms, encompasses all practices, encompasses all stages, and encompasses all teachings. "Principles" refers precisely to the dharmas of the truths (*satya*).
Regarding that which is elucidated by the partial and the perfect: apart from the provisional and the real, there is no other principle. To say that there is would be a falsehood.

Since these are subsumed within *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, what principle could remain unexhausted? Furthermore, delusion regarding the principle gives rise to afflictions; this delusion is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*).
If one is deluded regarding the provisional principle, there arise the ignorance associated with the realms and the independent ignorance, as well as the views and afflictions (*kleśa*).
The conjunction of the various proclivities (*anuśaya*) is termed "associated" (*saṃprayukta*). That which is not associated is termed "independent" (*svatantra*).

From ignorance (*avidyā*) through old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), these twelve links of the wheel act as mutual causes and effects: afflictions (*kleśa*) pervade karma, karma pervades suffering (*duḥkha*), and suffering in turn gives rise to afflictions.
This is called the three paths of bondage that are inexhaustible. The separation between the three periods of time is called "segmented birth and death" (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*).

To speak of this illness is to know its medicine; the medicine consists of the *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* that enter from the conventional into emptiness. Therefore, this delusion is subsumed under the contemplation of entering emptiness.
If one is confused regarding the ultimate principle, then there are delusions outside the realms. Why? Because although the characteristics within the realms have been severed...
It should exist as a discrete entity, yet its habitual tendencies (vāsanā) still persist. The *Ratnagotravibhāga* states:

"Although those of the two vehicles possess the antidotes of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, selflessness, and so forth, they still maintain a perversion regarding the Buddha’s dharmakāya. This perversion is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*)."

The activity of solitary untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) constitutes the formations (*saṃskāra*). The three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) consist of: "mind" being consciousness (*vijñāna*);

"body" being name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*); the non-termination of ignorance (*avidyā*) being craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*); and the non-termination of defilement being existence (*bhava*).
That which arises immediately is "birth"; that the fruit of birth undergoes transformation is "old age and death. These constitute the three paths outside the realms (*dhātu*). Why is this?
From those below the Buddha, all possess ignorance (*avidyā*) which obstructs the true principle. It is precisely due to this delusion;

this delusion is what is remedied by the two contemplations of entering the conventional and entering the middle. This delusion is also called the "obstruction to knowledge" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), because it obstructs the higher-stage wisdom. Only...
The Buddha is without ignorance; being without ignorance, afflictions are exhausted. When afflictions are exhausted, karma is exhausted. When karma is exhausted, suffering is exhausted.

Therefore, one should know that the Middle Way encompasses the delusions beyond the [three] realms. Furthermore, the three contemplations encompass all-encompassing wisdom, which may be understood by analogy.
Moreover, they encompass all formations (*saṃskāra*). There are two kinds of formations: namely, the formation of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*) and the formation of practice (*caryā-caryā*).

The practice of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*) is the primary practice (*mūla-caryā*); the practice of conduct (*caryā-caryā*) is the auxiliary practice (*upakāra-caryā*). These two practices—primary and auxiliary—proceed in accordance with wisdom.

In the Tripiṭaka [Teaching], the analytical contemplation of impermanence is the practice of wisdom; the contemplations of impurity and loving-kindness are the practice of conduct. In the Shared Teaching, realizing that all phenomena are like illusions is the practice of wisdom;
practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* by traversing all phenomena and focusing on specific objects is the practice of conduct. These two teachings proceed accordingly...

In the two wisdoms of analytical and essential nature, both enter into emptiness. If, for the sake of transforming others, one cultivates the path of the knowledge of the modes (*jñānamārgajñatā*), taking conventional principles as its object, it is called the practice of wisdom (*prajñācaryā*);

taking conventional phenomena as its object, it belongs to the practice of conduct (*caryācaryā*). This practice follows wisdom in entering the provisional. If it takes the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its object, it is the practice of wisdom;
traversing various dharma-gates is the practice of conduct. This practice follows the middle wisdom in entering the true mark, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Furthermore, the various sutras state extensively that all practices of wisdom and all practices of cultivation are without exception subsumed within *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Next, regarding the subsumption of the various stages: if one says that the first stage is identical to the second stage, and the second stage is identical to the third stage, then within the midst of quiescent extinction (*śānti*), what sequential stages could there be?
If one speaks of stages according to their formal arrangement, it is as discussed in the *Abhidharma*: the seven types of noble seekers (*śaikṣa*) and the seven types of noble ones (*arhat*).

The four fruits of śrāmaṇya, as discussed in the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, and the twenty-seven distinct stages of the noble ones (*ārya*) are all subsumed under the analytical contemplation of emptiness (*prabheda-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), as discussed in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

These constitute the common stages for the three vehicles; from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vidyā*) up to the eighth ground, they are entirely subsumed under the contemplation of entering emptiness through the essence of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*).
If one enters the provisional (*saṃvṛti*) from emptiness and cultivates successive practices but does not attain the intended realization, one completes the thirty [stages].

The stage of subduing delusions within the mind is encompassed by both the Contemplation of Emptiness and the Contemplation of the Provisional. If one attains the essential meaning, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are accomplished;
this is encompassed by the Third Contemplation. If it is the Perfect and Real [Teaching], then reality is the Middle within phenomena.

From the Stage of Cultivation (*ābhisamskāra-mārga*) one enters the Stage of Similarity (*pratirūpaka-bhūmi*), proceeds to shatter ignorance (*avidyā*), and opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. These forty-two stages are all encompassed by the Middle Contemplation. Or it is said: "Of the Mahāyāna..."
If the stages [of practice] are not clarified within this, then what do *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* encompass? Answer: Within the Mahāyāna, there is no place and no stage.
If one fears the stages and enters a state of no-stage, one will not escape being unbound. Since the nature of words is detached, it is itself liberation.
Although stages are established, they are themselves no-stages, for the meaning of "no-phrase" is the meaning of a bodhisattva's phrase. It cannot be...
It is because of existence and non-existence that disputes arise. Next, regarding the subsumption of all teachings: teachings arise from the mind.

If one observes that the mind is deviant and follows the flow of ignorance, then there are all the worldly teachings of good and evil. If they emerge from the [enlightened] mind, they are the supramundane named teachings.
The *Ratnagotravibhāga* states: "There is a great thousand-fold world-system scripture within a single atom; when one person extracts it,"
The world is thus a skillful means for breaking through [delusion] and bringing forth this sutra to benefit others. The *Bodhicittavivaraṇa* states:
"For example, suppose there were a person who, seeing the Buddha-dharma perishing, inscribed the twelvefold scriptures upon the sky. No one knew of it.
Later, another person traveling through the sky happened to copy them down and showed them to sentient beings. These two treatises [demonstrate that] both emptiness and existence [are required].

This serves as an analogy. If one contemplates that the mind arises and ceases through causes and conditions and is impermanent, and practices the Eightfold Noble Path, this is equivalent to transcribing the sutras of the Tripiṭaka.
If one contemplates that the mind is itself emptiness, this is equivalent to transcribing the various sutras of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).

If one contemplates the mind by discerning immeasurable dharmas as seen by the Dharma-eye, this is equivalent to transcribing the various sutras of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao). If one contemplates that the mind is itself Buddha-nature, this is equivalent to transcribing the [Middle]...
Regarding the "Sutra of the Way," the observation that the mind is simultaneously provisional and middle encompasses the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

If one observes the mind as arising and ceasing through causes and conditions, it encompasses the *Tripiṭaka* Āgama sūtras. If one observes the mind as empty, it encompasses the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras shared with other vehicles.
If one contemplates the mind as possessing the three aspects of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle through causes and conditions, this subsumes the Vaipulya sutras.
If one contemplates only that which is "immediately empty," "immediately provisional," and "immediately middle," this subsumes the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and other Prajñā sutras.

If one employs only the contemplation of the mind as "immediately middle," this subsumes the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the sutra that reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and abandons expedient means. If one employs the mutual identity of the four phrases, this subsumes the *Nirvāṇa*.
Regarding this final sutra: furthermore, the mind encompasses all teachings. Briefly stated, there are two meanings. First, all sentient beings possess within their own minds all dharma-gates;
the Tathāgata, through clear and thorough discernment, illuminates these mental dharmas and, in accordance with those minds, expounds immeasurable teachings.
Thus, the dharmas emerge from the mind. Second, in the past, the Tathāgata practiced both gradual and sudden contemplations of the mind.

The partial and the perfect are fully present. Relying on this contemplation of the mind, one preaches for the sake of sentient beings and instructs disciples, causing them to learn how to break through the dust and reveal the scroll [of the Dharma] as the Tathāgata did.

Therefore, all scriptural teachings are entirely subsumed within *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). The sequence for subsuming the Dharma through the six intentions is as follows. To state it in brief:
if one simply directly cites a single dharma, there is nothing that is not encompassed; the principle is naturally so.
Indeed. Chapter Five:
On the Partial and the Perfect.

Now, since there is no dharma not encompassed by śamatha and vipaśyanā, and because the dharmas so encompassed are numerous, they become intermingled and difficult to distinguish. We shall now clarify them by means of five dharmas.
This is manifested as the Small and the Great; as the Half and the Full; as the Partial and the Perfect; as the Gradual and the Sudden; and as the Provisional and the Real.

To begin with, the ultimate principle is neither small nor great, even to the point of being neither provisional nor real. Yet, by means of skillful expedients and conditions, it was taught as "Small" for the sake of the five bhikṣus, and as "Great" for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
"Small" refers to the Hīnayāna; because their power of wisdom is thin, they practice only the analytical method (*vibhajya-dharma*).
Regarding *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*: the term "analysis" (*prabheda*) originally derives from non-Buddhist schools, carrying the sense of analyzing matter down to its subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites this view and refutes it, saying: "Are these atoms existent or non-existent? If there is such a thing as an atom of form, it must possess spatial divisions in the ten directions;

if there is no such atom of form, then there are no spatial divisions. If the analysis is not exhaustive, one falls into the view of eternalism; if the analysis is exhaustive, one falls into the view of nihilism."
The analysis of the mind is likewise. Thus we know that whether the analysis performed by non-Buddhists is exhaustive or incomplete, it all ultimately leads to heterodox teachings.

The treatise further clarifies the analytical contemplation (*vibhāvanā*) of the Tripiṭaka, stating: "Whether form is coarse or subtle, when observed as a whole, it is impermanent and without self. Why? Because form arises from ignorance; its essence is inherently impermanent.
Furthermore, the arising of even a momentary thought necessarily relies upon the sense faculties and their objects."* *Note: The original text appears to be truncated at this point.*
There is one dharma that does not arise from conditions. That which arises from conditions is entirely impermanent;

being impermanent, it has no master. The afflictions are fundamentally destroyed; there is neither karma nor suffering. Because birth and death have ceased, it is called nirvana. This is termed the contemplation of the analysis of dharmas (*vibhajya-dharma-vipaśyanā*).
In essence, by refuting and analyzing what is false, one clarifies the correct analysis. This applies not only to external heterodoxies;

even if a disciple of the Buddha clings to existence or non-existence and gives rise to views and attachments, these too must be analyzed. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "To refute [the misconception of] nirvāṇa does not mean to refute the nirvāṇa attained by the sages.
It is merely to use the skillful means of analyzing phenomena to refute those students who have not yet attained it but claim to have attained it. Therefore...
Knowing that the analytical contemplation (*vibhaṅga-vipaśyanā*) based on the Tripiṭaka is definitively of the Hīnayāna, whereas the Mahāyāna is characterized by profound and sharp wisdom;

it is the practice of great beings who cultivate the contemplation of the essence of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and is thus called the "Great Vehicle" (*Mahāyāna*). As the Treatise states: "Those who wish to attain the state of a Śrāvaka should study Prajñā.

Because the Dharma of Prajñā is great, and because the Great can encompass the Small, it includes the Śrāvakas as its ancillary aspect. Thus, although there is the Hīnayāna within it, it is ultimately termed 'Great'."
In those [teachings of] the Tripiṭaka, names are provisional while dharmas are real; one analyzes the real to render it empty, like breaking a pillar to make it empty.

Now, the essential meaning of the Mahāyāna is that both names and reality are provisional, their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are empty, and they are originally void and quiescent, like a pillar within a mirror.
Fundamentally, it is not a pillar; the reflection of the pillar is itself empty, unlike a real pillar. Since its origin is non-arising, it is without cessation. This is called...

The contemplation of the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is also called the contemplation that accords with principle (*yoniśo-manasikāra*). It is like seeking the illusionist through the illusion, or seeking the illusory phenomena through the illusionist;

it is like seeking sleep through the dream, seeking the mind through sleep, and seeking ignorance (*avidyā*) through the perception of form (*rūpa*). To realize the essence of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*);

one should know that this contemplation of the essence of phenomena is definitively named the Mahāyāna. Next, the distinction between the "half" and the "full" is clarified; some say that *nirvāṇa* is eternal.
The *Vihāra* [Abiding] stage is "full," while all others are "half. Bodhiruci states that the Tripiṭaka is "half" and everything from the *Prajñāpāramitā* onwards is "full.

Now, I maintain that "half" and "full" share the same meaning as "Small" (Hīnayāna) and "Great" (Mahāyāna). To analyze them is "half"; to take their essence is "full. Next, I shall clarify "partial" (*prādeśika*) and "perfect" (*paripūrṇa*).

"Partial" carries the sense of being biased or deviant; "perfect" carries the sense of being complete or fulfilled. The two names "Half" and "Small" both result in a state of deficiency and brevity; thus, they are "partial."
The meaning is not so. From the analysis of dharmas in the Tripiṭaka up to the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao), where one has not yet entered the Middle Way, all are termed "partial" (pian).

As the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra says: "Prior to this, we were all called people of false views. Only the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao), with its single mind and three truths, alone deserves the designation "perfect.
Next, the gradual and sudden are explained: the śamatha and vipaśyanā of the first three teachings are all gradual; [the śamatha and vipaśyanā] of the Perfect Teaching...

Contemplating this is sudden. Furthermore, because the first two teachings merely accord with partial truth (*ekāṃśatattva*), they are gradual. The Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*) is sudden because it takes the extremes as the center and practices the great direct path.
The Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*) is both gradual and sudden because those at the initial stage know the center yet still engage in expedient means (*upāya*).
Moreover, in the first two contemplations, there are teachings, practices, and realizations within the cause; at the level of the fruit, however, there are only teachings.
Furthermore, there is no practice or realization [in the cause]. Why? Because those at the stage of the cause are extinguished like ashes and sink into emptiness;

they cannot attain the fruit of a Buddha on the level of fruition. This is merely a teaching of skillful means; thus, while there is the teaching, there is no person [who realizes it]. In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), there is the teaching, there is practice, and there is realization within the cause;
yet even at the level of fruition, there is the teaching but no person. Why? Because if one shatters ignorance, that is precisely the first stage (prathama-bhūmi) of the Perfect Teaching.

It is not that the first stage (*bhūmi*) is something separate; if even the first stage is thus, how much more so the subsequent stages? Therefore, one knows there is no person who attains a fruit [separately];
only in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), from beginning to end, is there nothing that is not true reality.

Furthermore, regarding those who practice the teachings and conduct of the preceding three [teachings] of cessation-and-contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), if they have not yet harmonized them with the true Dharma, they do not yet know the Perfect [Teaching], let alone enter it. If the Buddha were to harmonize the schools and open [this teaching],...
To gradually reveal the sudden means that all [practitioners] may enter it. Although this is not the immediate sudden, it is the "gradual-sudden.

The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The path you practice is the Bodhisattva path; you have definitively realized the Śrāvaka Dharma. This is the King of all sūtras, and this is what is meant by "opening the gradual to reveal the sudden.
Furthermore, regarding the four kinds of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, entry into the Perfect [Teaching] does not necessarily depend on the completion of practice, nor is it necessarily...

Waiting for the gradual to open and then revealing the sudden is called "indeterminate. Furthermore, regarding the four types of śamatha and vipaśyanā, each of their respective teachings contains a gradual meaning;
yet the ultimate point indicated by each is the meaning of the Perfect (yuan). One should know that the Perfect is not a gradual perfection, and the gradual is not a gradual perfection.

However, while it is possible for the gradual to gradually become the perfect (en), the gradual-perfect cannot become the perfect-perfect. Why? Because the *Lotus Sūtra* provides definitive resolution;

thus, the gradual can gradually attain the status of the perfect-gradual. Since the meaning of the "gradual-perfect" was originally established as a provisional device (*upāya*), how could the fruit of the Tripitaka possibly constitute the wondrous enlightenment of the perfect?
Applying this principle, one should also say: that which is "small-small" is not "large-small," yet it can be made to become so.
The small and the large: the small and the large are not "large-large"; thus, "large-large" cannot be established. Expediency and expediency: expediency is not real expediency;

thus, real expediency can be established. Expediency and reality: expediency and reality are not real reality; thus, real reality cannot be established. The categories of meaning may be seen from this. Next, to clarify expediency and reality:
as for expediency, it is a provisional assumption used temporarily and then discarded. As for reality, it is true and constant, abiding forever without shifting. Now...

There are three meanings for establishing the provisional (*upāya*). First, the application of the provisional for the sake of the real. Second, the opening of the provisional to reveal the real. Third, the abandonment of the provisional to return to the real.
Now, the Buddha appears in the world for one great matter; the three provisional means he applies serve only for the sake of the one reality.

The provisional is not his fundamental intent, yet that fundamental intent does not lie outside the provisional. If one opens the provisional to reveal the real, then the provisional is itself the real; there is no [real] apart from it.

One may discuss this through the lens of skillful means (*upāya*). Thus, while the provisional is set aside, the real remains. It is precisely for this purpose that the three analogies of the lotus are intended. Someone may raise an objection:

"For what reason are these provisional and real [teachings] employed? The answer is: The Buddha knows the various dispositions of sentient beings and seeks to bring them to fulfillment through the four *siddhāntas*.

If a person wishes to hear about the correct causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), he is taught the contemplation of the Tripitaka. If he wishes to hear about immediate emptiness (*śūnyatā*), he is taught...

For those who wish to hear of universal contemplation (*sāmānyālambana*), one explains individual contemplation (*pratyekālambana*); for those who wish to hear of the immediate middle way, one explains perfect contemplation (*pariniṣpanna-ālambana*).

This is called the *loka-prasiddha-siddhānta* (the standpoint established according to worldly convention). It is the teaching of provisional means for the sake of the ultimate; it is the teaching of provisional and ultimate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

To refute false causes and conditions, one teaches the contemplation of the Tripitaka; to refute clumsy expedients, one teaches universal contemplation; and to refute common dharmas, one teaches individual contemplation.

Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). To break through [delusions] that still involve expedient means, one speaks of "perfect contemplation" (*yuan-guan*); this is called the teaching of provisional and real *śamatha-vipaśyanā* according to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*.

Furthermore, it is taught that the *Hīnayāna* (*zang*) constitutes the "goodness of phenomena" (*shi-shan*) that assists and supports the arising of the Truth, while the "Shared" (*tong*) constitutes the "goodness of principle" (*li-shan*) that assists and supports the arising of the Truth;

the same applies to the "Distinct" (*bie*) and "Perfect" (*yuan*) as they support the Middle Way. This is called the teaching of provisional and real *śamatha-vipaśyanā* according to the *pudgala-anusara-siddhānta*. For...
For those of dull faculties who enter the true reality through deliberate and clumsy means, the Contemplation of the Tripitaka is taught.

For those of sharp faculties who enter the true reality through non-deliberate and skillful means, the Contemplation of Penetration is taught. For those of dull faculties who enter the stage of seeing through non-deliberate and clumsy means, the Contemplation of Distinction is taught.
For those of sharp faculties who enter the stage of seeing through non-deliberate and skillful means, the Perfect Contemplation is taught.

Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). This is called "one reality established through three expedients" (*upāya*). When expedient means and reality are contrasted, there are four types of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

The arising and ceasing of these expedients and reality can be understood through reflection. If one definitively realizes that the Śrāvaka teachings manifest the true aspect of reality, then all four types are real.
If they cannot be said to be manifested yet there is speaking and manifesting, then all four types are expedient. Expedient means is itself reality; reality is...

This is precisely the provisional (upāya). It is also neither real nor provisional; that the nature of reality (dharmatā) is eternally quiescent, being neither real nor provisional, is called "stopping" (śamatha).

That which is quiescent yet eternally illuminating, being both provisional and real, is called "contemplation" (vipaśyanā). Being non-dual, non-distinct, non-unified, and non-dispersed is itself inconceivable stopping and contemplation (acintya-śamatha-vipaśyanā).
The sixth [topic], skillful means (*upāya*).

"Skillful" (*kauśalya*) is its meaning. It refers to skillful practice, whereby one accomplishes immeasurable conduct and realization through even a slight amount of wholesome dharmas and enters the stage of a bodhisattva.
As the *Mahā-śāstra* states: "One can, by means of even a small amount of giving and a small amount of precept-keeping, transcend the two vehicles. Furthermore...

"Expedient means" (upāya) has the sense of the harmonious convergence of various conditions. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The body of the Tathāgata does not arise from a single cause and condition, but is produced from immeasurable merits.
Regarding the discussion of expedient means, in the Perfect Teaching (Ekanaya), there are distant and proximate expedients.
The twenty-five dharmas constitute the distant expedient, while the ten types of objects constitute the proximate expedient. As for what are called the twenty-five dharmas:
This means possessing five conditions: censuring the five desires, abandoning the five hindrances, regulating the five matters, and practicing the five dharmas.
Now, the Way does not operate in isolation; its propagation depends on people. For people to propagate the sublime Dharma and advance along the Path, they must rely on conditions.

It is like a potter who first selects a fine location where water and grass are abundant and convenient, then establishes his workshop; next, he ceases other activities to apply himself to his craft. Furthermore, although he has ceased external distractions, internally—
If illness does not depart, one cannot engage in work. Even if the body is healthy and strong, if the tools and implements are not functional, one still cannot produce things.
Even if these various conditions are complete, if one lacks diligence, there will be no accomplishment. Mundane matters do not come together without their requisite conditions;
how much more so is this true for the supramundane path? Now, having traversed these twenty-five factors, one should examine them by practicing contemplation based on these specific matters.
To disperse [distractions] and bring about stillness—this is the skillful means (*upāya*). Regarding the five conditions:

they are purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*), sufficiency of food and clothing, dwelling in a secluded and quiet place, ceasing all worldly affairs, and obtaining virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). As for upholding the precepts: first, the names of the precepts are enumerated;

next, the nature of their observance and violation, as well as the methods of repentance (*pratyāpatti*), are clarified. According to the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*), there are ten kinds of precepts, namely: that which is not deficient, not broken, not pierced, and so forth.
It is unadulterated, follows the Path, is unattached, praised by the wise, sovereign, conforms to meditative concentration, and is complete. It takes the universal nature-precepts as its foundation.
The *Mahā-śāstra* states: "Nature-precepts are *śīla*. Regardless of whether they have been formally received or not, violating them constitutes an offense, while upholding them constitutes virtue.
If the nature-precepts are pure, they are the foundation of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) and the primary cause for liberation."

Therefore, from these natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*), there arises the unmanifested (*avijñapti*) precept acquired through formal undertaking. Furthermore, these ten types encompass all precepts without deficiency;
that is to say, one maintains the natural precepts up to the four grave offenses (*catur-guru-dharma*), guarding them with purity as if protecting a precious pearl.
If one violates them, it is like a vessel that has been broken. One who does not break them firmly maintains the thirteen [precepts] without any impairment. If one violates...

One who commits an offense is like a vessel that has broken; one who does not pierce [the precepts] refers to one who maintains the *pāyattika* and other such rules. If one violates them, it is like a vessel that is leaking.

One who is "unmixed" refers to one who maintains the precepts associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-samvara*); although they maintain the discipline, they still entertain thoughts of breaking the precepts.

It is called "mixed concentration. Constantly maintaining the mind is called "unmixed. "Conforming to the Path" means to accord with the principle of the Truths (satya), thereby being able to destroy the delusions of views (dṛṣṭi-kleśa).
"Unattached Precepts" refers to seeing the Truth; one is not stained by or attached to the delusions of thought (bhāvanā-kleśa).

These two pertain to maintaining the precepts in relation to the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya). As for "Precepts Praised by Wisdom" and "Mastery Precepts," these refer to the Bodhisattva’s transformation of others.
"Praised by the Buddha" and "attaining mastery within the world"—these two refer to the observance of precepts according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

"Conforming to the perfection of meditative concentration" means conforming to the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*. Without arising from the samādhi of cessation, one manifests various dignified demeanors and displays the forms of the ten realms to guide and benefit sentient beings;
therefore, it is called "conforming to concentration. Since the precepts of the Middle Way lack no precept that is not complete, [it is so named].

This is called "perfection. This refers to the observance of the precepts from the perspective of the Middle Way and the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Furthermore, the first three types of precepts are called the "precepts of restraint" (*saṃvara-śīla*);

they involve upholding the good and preventing evil, and even ordinary beings with distracted minds can maintain them. Regarding "unmixed": this refers to maintaining the mind through meditative states (*samādhi-dharma*), so that the mind does not wander;

ordinary beings can maintain these when they enter meditative concentration. Regarding "conforming to the Path": this refers to the realization of the First Fruit (*prathamaphala*) through insight (*darśana*).
Only the noble ones (*ārya*) are able to uphold it. As for those who are unattached (*asaṅga*), only those who have attained the three fruits [of the śrāvaka path] are able to uphold it.

Regarding the praise of wisdom and mastery, only Bodhisattvas whose primary concern is to provide lateral aid are able to uphold it. Furthermore, as for the perfection of meditative concentration (*samādhi-sampad*), this is not something upheld by Bodhisattvas of the general teaching through the six perfections;

rather, only those of great faculties on the supreme vehicle (*agrayāna*) are able to uphold it. This is discussed in terms of the relative heights of individuals and in terms of the precepts (*śīla*).

The degrees of depth and shallowness follow this pattern. If one contemplates the mind according to principle, then from the very first moment of the initial mind, one is fully capable of upholding these ten precepts.
The first four precepts are all phenomena produced by causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*); they collectively constitute the objects of contemplation.

The next two precepts involve contemplating the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of these causally conditioned phenomena; these are the precepts of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Furthermore, the final two precepts involve contemplating the conventional designation (*prajñapti*) of causally conditioned phenomena; these are the precepts of the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*).
Furthermore, regarding the next two precepts within the contemplation of the dharma of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*), this is the Middle Way contemplation of the precepts.

That which is called "contemplating the mind as a dharma produced by causes and conditions" means observing how a single thought arises from evil conditions and is thus able to destroy the root [of goodness].

Even if it does not mix with the precepts, it is contrary to wholesome states. Now, using a mind that accords with the wholesome to prevent the evil mind—prevention is precisely *śamatha* (calm abiding), and accordance is precisely...
Contemplation. This is called contemplating dependent origination to uphold the preceding four precepts. Next, regarding the contemplation that the causes and conditions of good and evil are empty:

the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states, "If one perceives dharmas as having characteristics or as being without characteristics, both constitute attachment to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span."

One does not perceive the characteristics of dharmas, nor does one perceive the characteristics of non-dharmas. As with the parable of the raft, even dharmas should be relinquished, let alone non-dharmas.

One should know that both dharma and non-dharma are equally empty and quiescent. By virtue of this contemplation, one is able to accord with the untainted (*anāsrava*), preventing and restraining the sixty-two views of existence and non-existence;
therefore, it is called "conforming to the Path" (*anuloma-mārga*). When this contemplation becomes fully matured, all forms and sounds—

All are immediately empty; this is called non-attachment. To prevent the afflictions of thought and to skillfully accord with the True Truth—this is called observing that causes and conditions are immediately empty while upholding the two kinds of precepts.
Next, one observes that causes and conditions are immediately provisional, realizing that the mind is not the mind and that phenomena are not phenomena.

Yet one does not remain forever stagnant in that which is neither mind nor dharma. By means of the skillful means of the *dharmamukhas*, one establishes the mind and establishes dharmas within the state of non-existence.
One uproots all mental factors (*caitta-dharmas*), guides and benefits sentient beings, and is praised by the Buddhas.
Not giving rise to attachment amidst immeasurable dharmas is called "mastery. Such provisional contemplation prevents ignorance and accords well with conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). That is...

This is the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*) which upholds the two kinds of precepts. Next, regarding "the contemplation of causes and conditions as the Middle": one contemplates that the nature of the mind is quiescent cessation;
it is neither empty nor provisional. Because it is not provisional, it is not of the mundane world; because it is not empty, it is not supramundane. It is neither an ordinary person nor a sage.
When both extremes are stilled, it is called the "nature of the mind. To be able to contemplate in this way is called the "supreme concentration" (*adhyāna*). That is...
The Śūraṅgama Samādhi simultaneously illuminates both truths and manifests all dignified demeanors. In accordance with such concentration, there is nothing that is not fully perfected.
It ceases the faults of the two extremes and accords with the principle of the Middle Way; this is called "maintaining the two kinds of precepts while abiding in the Middle."
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "Precepts are called the Mahāyāna; they are called the Light of the Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha-prabhā*).

Such precepts as these were recited by our Original Teacher, and I likewise recite them. One should know that the Middle Way’s wondrous contemplation is the true essence of the precepts. The *Ten Stages Sūtra* (*Daśabhūmika*) explains at length:

"If there is neither self nor what belongs to the self, if one is far removed from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and if nothing whatsoever exists, this is called the supreme *śīla* (morality)."
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Sin does not exist within, without, or in between. As it is with the mind, so it is with the defilements of sin.

One who can understand this is called one who understands well; such a person is called one who upholds the Vinaya. This is precisely the intended meaning. Regarding what is called "violating the precepts": [it refers to this very point].
Indeed, the destruction of the pure precepts arises from no other than these two factors: delusion and craving, and inverted views. A great sutra states:
"It is like a person wearing a life-preserving float to cross the great ocean. In the midst of the sea, a rākṣasa comes to beg for the float; at first, he begs for it in its entirety."

One does not give even so much as a mote of dust; the practitioner is likewise. If one gives rise to defilement because of craving, and gives rise to karma because of defilement, the skin-sack will burst, water will enter, and one will drown in the ocean and die.
This is called violating the *pratimokṣa* precepts due to craving. Clinging to and surveying the five desires violates the *samādhi-sahaja* precepts.
Being deeply attached to the various realms of existence violates the precept of immediate emptiness. Not ceasing worldly censure and failing to protect others [violates the bodhisattva precepts].
[This] mind violates the provisional precepts. Not believing that these precepts encompass all dharmas violates the precepts of the Middle Way.

Furthermore, a practitioner may, through the cultivation of vigor, perceive the mind as sharp and fierce, thereby giving rise to various faults and evils regarding the dharmas they have conceptualized;

or, having attained a small degree of dhyāna through cultivation, they become attached to it themselves. During the Buddha's lifetime, there was a bhikṣu who attained the four dhyānas and claimed them to be [the fourth...].
As a result, when he was near death, his vital signs (āśraya) arose, and he slandered the Buddha, saying, "Arhats are not reborn; how could one be born now?
The Buddha said, "This person has already fallen into hell. The *Ākāśagarbha Sūtra* states: "If one gives rise to such evil views, it is called the third pārājika offense."

What is meant by "evil views"? It refers to those who, having attained a conceptual understanding of emptiness and developed a modicum of wisdom, follow their own minds and establish their own positions, claiming to have realized the non-arising of phenomena.
Because their views are so rigid, they believe they can dismantle all dharmas, asserting that there is neither Buddha nor sentient beings. They ask: "What constitutes a transgression? What does not?
Yet, such discrimination is itself an obstruction; obstruction is not the truth. As the poison of these views intensifies, they give rise to all manner of evils. It is because of this...
Because of [wrong] views, the life-preserving bag is completely lost; this means that due to views, one breaks the *vinaya* and the precepts of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle way.

One should know that deviating toward emptiness is a great affliction for the Dharma. As the treatise says: "The Great Sage taught the Dharma of emptiness fundamentally to remedy attachment to existence;

yet if one becomes attached to emptiness, even all Buddhas cannot transform such a person. Such is the general meaning regarding upholding and violating [the precepts]. Furthermore, in terms of principle, it is called a vehicle (*yāna*).

In terms of its substance, it is called "precept" (*śīla*); in terms of its function, "vehicle" (*yāna*) takes movement and transcendence as its meaning, while "precept" takes prevention and restraint as its efficacy.

There should be a fourfold classification: namely, those for whom both vehicle and precept are urgent; those for whom the vehicle is urgent and the precepts lax; those for whom the precepts are urgent and the vehicle lax; and those for whom both vehicle and precepts are lax.
Because their cultivation differs, their karmic fruits likewise differ: some may realize the Path in a single lifetime, while others [may fall] into the three evil realms.

Some attain deliverance; others are deluded regarding the Dharma among humans and devas, or sink into perpetual stagnation. As their conditions vary and differ, they ought to be precisely distinguished. Regarding what is called the method of repentance (*chánfǎ*):
now, both transgressions of fact and principle obstruct *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. There are many paths for repenting transgressions of fact, which cannot be cited in their entirety.

The *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna-sūtra* (Puxian guan) says: "Sitting upright and contemplating the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)—this is called the foremost repentance. This refers to the Samādhi of Sublime Victory (*miao sheng ding*).
It is said: Regarding the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes, there is nothing capable of saving one except for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

If one wishes to repent of these two types of heavy obstacles from past lives, one must first investigate their fundamental root. From beginningless time, through false conceptualization of self and others, the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) arises.

Because of this view of a self-body, there is perversion; because of perversion, greed, hatred, and delusion arise, leading to the extensive creation of various karmas. Thus, one undergoes birth and death. At that point, one should...
If one looks back at the nature of this deluded craving, it is entirely a gate of tranquility. When greed or hatred arises, from where does it arise?
One should know that it arises from false conceptualization; false conceptualization dwells in perversion; perversion dwells in the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);

and the view of a self-body dwells in the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). Yet, the view of a self has no place of abiding; even if one searches thoroughly throughout the ten directions, a self cannot be found. My mind—
It is empty of self. Since sin and merit have no master, and the root of delusion is already empty, one can then extinguish all transgressions.
If one does not understand this mind, even if one enters the place of practice, it will be in vain as a mere asceticism, yielding no great benefit in the end. A Great Sūtra says:

"If one claims that diligently practicing asceticism is the proximate cause for Great Nirvāṇa, such a thing is impossible. Furthermore, by contemplating the view of the body, one causes consciousness to be non-existent.

This clarifies the origin of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya*). For example, Udraka Rāmaputra attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); the people of the world revered him as if he were a Buddha, yet when his retribution ended, he fell back down.

How much more so for one who does not even equal Rāmaputra—would this not be a great perversion? Such a person is attached to the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*) and does not understand these matters;

this is called ignorance (*avidyā*). Based on views, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) arise; when views and formations depend upon form (*rūpa*), they constitute name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Thus one is deluded.
From the arising of craving for form, there is becoming; from becoming, there is future birth-and-death. This cyclic turning of birth-and-death—how could it be quiescence?

To take what is not the Path as the Path, and to reckon what is not the cause as the cause, is called the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); this constitutes the theft of the cause. To point to the fruit of future suffering as *nirvāṇa* is called the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*);
this constitutes the theft of the fruit. Such a mind of views is entirely the accumulation of suffering (*duḥkhasamudaya*), not cessation (*nirodha*) or the Path (*mārga*).
Furthermore, this is not even the Path and Cessation of the Tripitaka; how much less could it be the Path and Cessation of the Mahāyāna?

If one can know the causes and effects of the mundane world as well as the causes and effects of the supramundane, then one knows what is the Path and what is not the Path. This constitutes knowing and seeing the suffering and its accumulation within the mind.

Moreover, "profound" means not only knowing the causes and effects of the Tripitaka, but also knowing that causes and conditions are simultaneously empty, simultaneously provisional, and simultaneously the Middle Way.

This is the fruit. Thus, by means of a single insight into the mind, one knows all causes and effects. Having known causes and effects, one then knows that all inverted views are fundamentally empty and quiescent;
yet I failed to understand this and falsely gave rise to various views, like a person with a feverish illness who sees various dragons, ghosts, and other such things.
Now, observing them as being like illusions and transformations, both sin and merit are entirely empty. Furthermore, apply this with earnest and profound respect.
The mind does not begrudge even body or life; this is called the dual repentance of phenomena and principle (*dharma* and *tattva*).

Because the precepts of phenomena are pure, the fundamental samādhi manifests before one, and mundane knowledge (*loka-jñāna*) and the knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*) are developed. Because the precepts of non-arising (*anutpāda*) are pure, the samādhi of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) manifests before one, and all-knowledge (*sarvajña-jñāna*) is developed.

Because the precepts of the provisional (*prajñapti*) are pure, the samādhi of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) manifests before one, and the knowledge of the paths and their varieties (*mārga-jñatā-jñāna*) is developed.
Because the purity of the intermediate precepts is thus established, the King Samādhi manifests before one, and the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) is developed.
Since one attains this Samādhi of the Three Truths, it is called the King Samādhi; all other samādhis enter into it.

One should know that the purity of maintaining the precepts serves as the primary condition for śamatha and vipaśyanā. Furthermore, regarding the provision of food and clothing: food and clothing are necessary to ward off hunger and cold.
Only then does the body stand firm; once the body stands firm, the Way can be cultivated. A sutra says: "The Tathāgata attained Bodhi immediately after eating.
Although this is a minor circumstance, it is capable of accomplishing a great matter. Regarding food and clothing as objects of contemplation, a Mahāyāna sūtra states:
"Though a bhikṣu wears the kāṣāya, his mind is not yet dyed with the dharma-garment of the Mahāyāna. The Lotus Sūtra says: "Wearing the robe of the Tathāgata..."
That which comes as clothing is the mind of gentleness and patience. A great sutra further states:
"Although you practice begging for food, you have not yet obtained the food of the Mahāyāna Dharma. This 'food of the Dharma' is the food of the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna.

The Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "Those who are equal regarding food are also equal regarding the Dharma; like one who has drunk milk-rice and requires nothing more, this is true liberation. True liberation...
The one who is liberated is the Tathāgata. Next, regarding "dwelling in a secluded and quiet place": if one follows one's own whims, there is no place that is not peaceful;
however, if one practices the three samādhis, it is essential to be in a quiet location—whether in deep mountains and remote valleys, or in a secluded and tranquil dwelling.

Once one no longer perceives objects of desire, it becomes easy to maintain contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). If one contemplates while residing in a dwelling, it is the principle of the Middle Way Truth (*madhyamā-satya*) that serves as the basis.

As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* says: "The ultimate house is emptiness and stillness. Next, one should cease from worldly affairs (*ālambana-karma*). Worldly affairs obstruct meditation (*dhyāna*), a fact that has been so for a long time.
Briefly, there are three types: social obligations, artistic skills, and academic learning. Now, to leave one's kin and depart from one's teacher is fundamentally...

One seeks the essential Way. If human affairs do not cease—where congratulations and condolences follow one after another—it is like drilling for fire while seeking ice; it is not what is appropriate.

Furthermore, regarding medical prescriptions, divination, writing, calculation, incantations, debates on victory and defeat, and the exhaustion of recitation and chanting: when the water is turbid and the pearl is obscured, how is there leisure to cultivate contemplation?
Therefore, all such activities must be brought to rest; the intent of this contemplation is thus evident. Next, as for the "good friend" (kalyāṇamitra), he is...
This is a great cause and condition, namely, to transform and guide others so that they may attain the vision of the Buddha. The *Dhyāna-sūtra* states:

"Although all conditions may be fully present, the guidance depends upon a good teacher. Regarding the observer as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are the good spiritual friends."

The reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* states: "The factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are the spiritual friends;
through them, one achieves perfect awakening. Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka* speaks of the demon of the spiritual friend, the demon of samādhi, and the demon of the bodhicitta.

These demons can cause people to abandon the good and follow evil, and they can also lead people to fall into the stages of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha). An arhat merely attains the truth of emptiness (śūnyatā-satya), and so forth...

In the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), because the Middle Way has not yet been realized, both [the practitioner and the objects] are termed "Māra. As the Sūtra says: "Except for the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, everything else is the work of Māra.

Furthermore, regarding the censure of the five desires—namely, the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch: these are fundamentally not desire-phenomena themselves;

rather, it is because the practitioner gives rise to a mind of craving toward them that they are designated by the name "desire. As for "form" (*rūpa*): it refers to anything possessing physical substance.

Regarding the category of what is lovely and delightful, as taught in various sūtras, the harm caused by form (*rūpa*) is particularly profound. A sūtra states: "Sentient beings are greedy and predatory toward forms;
because of them, they fail to attain the Way. If one knows the affliction of form, one will not be deceived by it. Furthermore, regarding sound for the ear:
Fragrance to the nose, flavor to the mouth, and touch to the body—these are all where great desire resides; their movement constitutes affliction.

To obtain them without satiety causes evil to blaze ever more fiercely, like adding fuel to a fire. Worldly phenomena rob and harm one another; if one knows their origin, one should utterly revile and abandon them.
Furthermore, regarding the observation of the mind that reviles form: because of form, views, craving, and afflictions arise. One should...

Contemplating this, one sees that vision depends upon ignorance (*avidyā*). Ignorance is impermanent; arising and ceasing without abiding, one should not give rise to wholesome or unwholesome karma regarding form (*rūpa*).
When karma passes away, its fruit ceases; when the fruit ceases, there is liberation. This is called the "reproach of form" according to the Tripiṭaka.
If one realizes that all views are themselves ignorance, and that ignorance is emptiness, then all views are also empty.

Therefore, the *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) is said to have "entered the stream," yet in reality there is nothing entered; they do not enter into form, sound, or dharmas. This is called the True Truth that reviles form.
If one were merely to enter the emptiness of form, one would be unable to discern the various characteristics of all forms. Sentient beings give rise to all [delusions] regarding form.

Regarding the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudaya*), I do not know how to transform and deliver beings. Therefore, one knows that emptiness is not [mere] emptiness; from emptiness arises the provisional (*prajñapti*).

Although there is still conceptual differentiation, it exists only as a name. Since the name is itself empty, it is called "provisional. This is what is meant by the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) refuting form (*rūpa*).
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: "Within form there is no characteristic of flavor; ordinary persons should not be attached to it. Within form there is no detachment."

Characteristics. The two vehicles should not be detached from them. If there were definitely a "taste" (attachment), there should be no detachment; if there were definitely detachment, there should be no taste.
Because taste is not fixed, it is not taste; because detachment is not fixed, it is not detachment. That which is neither detachment nor taste is the Middle Way within form.
This is called the Middle Way’s censure of form. The Commentary states: For the sake of dhyāna, the two vehicles censure form; this is not [the ultimate] name.
Pāramitā. When a bodhisattva thoroughly reviles form (*rūpa*), they perceive the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of form and also perceive the true mark of dhyāna.
Because they reach the other shore (*pāra*) regarding form, it is named a pāramitā. To revile form deeply serves as the skillful means (*upāya*) for śamatha and vipaśyanā;

the remaining four sense objects (*viṣaya*) are to be understood accordingly. Furthermore, one abandons the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). The first five desires are the five faculties (*indriya*) responding to the five present sense objects (*viṣaya*), which give rise to—

Regarding the five consciousnesses: these five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) are now the five consciousnesses as they transition into the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), becoming great obstacles within the mind.

They are: sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. "Hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*) means to cover or veil, preventing concentration and wisdom from arising. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

One leaves behind desire and unwholesome states. Unwholesome states refer to the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*). What are their characteristics? When the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) arises, one recollects the five objects of desire experienced in the past;
this acts as an adversary to the five faculties, and through such mental preoccupation, delusion is produced and right mindfulness is lost.
The hindrance of ill-will arises when one recalls that a person has previously harmed oneself; the mind becomes fierce and the spirit surges, with anger continuing in succession.
As for the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor, the mental faculty is clouded and darkened, becoming dazed and devoid of awareness; if one is fond of sleep, then sleep increases further.

The *Śāstra* states that torpor (*middha*) is a great darkness. As for restlessness and remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*), these arise as a mixture of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), taking all phenomena as their objects;

they rise and subside repeatedly, burning without ceasing. The body wanders in delusion and the mouth engages in idle chatter. If there is restlessness without remorse, it does not constitute a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*);

however, when the mind is heavily burdened by remorse, it becomes an obstacle to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). As for doubt (*vicikitsā*), one may either doubt whether oneself is a fit vessel for the Path, or [doubt] while practicing it...

What benefit is there? One may doubt that the teacher is merely an ordinary person and that he could possess no profound Dharma; or one may doubt whether the Dharma received is necessarily consistent with reason.
When these three doubts dwell in the mind, meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) does not arise. Such are the characteristics of the afflictions of the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).

For those in whom a particular affliction predominates, it should be treated first: impurity (*aśubha*) treats lustful desire; loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*) treat ill-will; and vigor (*vīrya*) dispels lethargy and sleep.
Counting the breath remedies distraction; deep faith suppresses doubt. If one treats the stronger [defilement], the weaker will naturally depart.

Common people say that the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) are dull fetters (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*) that merely obstruct the first dhyāna. Now it is said that the five hindrances are sharp fetters (*tīkṣṇa-bandhana*) capable of obstructing the True Dharma (*satya*).
What is this? Grasping at views is craving; other false speech is anger; ignorance is torpor; conceptual proliferation is restlessness and remorse;
and being overcome by delusion is doubt. If these hindrances are removed, one attains the first fruit [of the path]. Furthermore, grasping at the real is called "attachment."

The abandonment of volition is called anger (*dveṣa*). When the afflictions of volition are not yet exhausted, it is called torpor (*middha*). Erroneous thought is called agitation and regret (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*).

Not having yet attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is called doubt (*vicikitsā*). If these hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are removed, one realizes arhatship. The manifestation of the samādhi of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is called omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

Furthermore, based on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), hindrances arise that obstruct conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Why is this? To sink into emptiness and grasp at realization is greed; to loathe and detest birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is aversion.
To abandon [the objects] and fail to contemplate them is anger. To have no illumination regarding the provisional function of unconditioned emptiness and quiescence is sleep.

For sentient beings whose minds are distracted by emptiness, this is agitation and regret. When provisional wisdom is not clear, this is doubt. If these hindrances are discarded, then the samādhi of the conventional truth manifests before one, and the knowledge of the aspects of the path is accomplished.
Furthermore, based on the Middle Way, hindrances arise that obstruct the true reality (*tathatā*). Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva, in regard to—
To give rise to attachment toward the profound Dharma is greed. To take no pleasure in the Two Vehicles is anger.

For ignorance not yet exhausted to be "sleep" means that although the three karmas are without fault, they are still considered "outflows" (āsrava) when compared to the Buddha; this constitutes restlessness and regret.

That the principle is perfect from beginning to end, yet the wisdom of the initial mind does not reach that of the subsequent [stages], is doubt. If these hindrances are removed, one opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and accomplishes all things.
The Wisdom of All Modes. If the characteristics of these hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) were fully detailed, they would be exceedingly vast; how could they be limited to the desire realm alone?

The practitioner deeply contemplates that the nature of the hindrances is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. In a single thought-moment, they are perfectly eliminated, and one perceives the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the hindrances. One who grasps this meaning can, even at the initial stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), completely abandon all hindrances.
Furthermore, there are five matters to be regulated: namely, regulating food, regulating sleep, regulating the body, [regulating the mind, and regulating the breath].
Regulating the breath, regulating the mind, and regulating food: these are the means for curing illness and settling the body, and are what one ought to consume.

Furthermore, one should observe moderation between hunger and satiety. Regulating sleep: sleep should not be excessively restricted, nor should it be indulged in. Rather, by avoiding both restriction and indulgence, one regulates the body so that it is neither too relaxed nor too tense;
one regulates the breath so that it is neither too sparse nor too frequent; and one regulates the mind so that it does not sink into dullness.
It does not float. These three matters must be harmonized. If one can harmonize these three matters of an ordinary person, they become the three dharmas of a sage.

Form (*rūpa*) is the source from which precepts arise; breath (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*) is the gate through which concentration (*samādhi*) enters; and mind (*citta*) is the cause for the birth of wisdom (*prajñā*).

From beginning to end, there are only these three dharmas, never separated from one another. The five matters for contemplating the mind can be understood through reflection. Furthermore, as for practice...
There are five factors: namely, desire, diligence, mindfulness, skillful wisdom, and one-pointedness of mind. Indeed, if a task is not pursued with single-minded focus, it will not reach completion.

Although the preceding twenty factors may be fully present, if there is no yearning or aspiration, and if one lacks the application of mindfulness and skillful means with a body and mind free from indolence, and does not resolutely fix the mind upon a single object, then śamatha and vipaśyanā will ultimately never manifest before one. One should know that these five factors collectively constitute the great [foundation].
To provide a skillful means for those of lesser capacity, the *Abhidharma* employs these [terms] to distinguish between the general and specific aspects of the four dhyānas;

the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* differ in their selection and rejection [of these terms], but neither represents the primary intent here. What is meant by "desire" (chanda) now is the desire to enter nirvāṇa from saṃsāra.
"Vigor" (vīrya) is that which is unmixed and untainted, never regressing. "Mindfulness" (smṛti) is mindfulness of nothing but nirvāṇa.
Not thinking of other matters; "skillful wisdom" means discerning the dharmas of what is right and wrong, and what is true and false.

"Single-mindedness" means resolutely practicing the Eightfold Noble Path, proceeding straight on without turning back; this is the skillful means for entering the truth. Furthermore, "desire" means wishing to extensively deliver sentient beings and accomplish the Buddha-dharma.
"Diligence" means that although sentient beings are infinite, one vows to deliver them all without regret. "Mindfulness" means...
Regarding them as one’s own children is the "thought. Skillful wisdom is the clear application of the medicine of the Dharma. Single-mindedness is the direct pursuit of transformative merit.

This constitutes the skillful means of entering the provisional. Furthermore, "desire" is like Sadāprarudita in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, who desired to hear the *Prajñāpāramitā* and did not spare his body or life.
"Vigor" refers to weeping for seven days and constantly practicing for seven years for the sake of hearing the *Prajñāpāramitā*. "Mindfulness" [is likewise].
"Constant mindfulness" means always thinking, "When shall I hear [the Dharma]? "Skillful wisdom" means that Māra cannot obscure it; one transforms demonic activities into Buddha-activities.

"Single-mindedness" means that the resolve is firm and unshakable. These constitute the skillful means for entering the Middle Way. Furthermore, "desire" means desiring to enter the Middle Way from one side;
being unmixed with the two extremes constitutes "purity. Flowing spontaneously constitutes "progress. Binding the object of focus to the Dharma...

Taking the *dhātus* as mindfulness; skillfulness in the practice of the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*) as expedient means (*upāya*); and the pure, ever-unified ability to perceive *prajñā* as one-pointedness of mind (*ekacitta*).
These twenty-five expedient means, when analyzed in detail, become immeasurable expedient means that can be understood through the mind.
Now, these are used as external expedients for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. By means of them, one trains until the principle is suddenly perceived.

At the moment of perceiving the principle, who would discuss "internal" or "external"? The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "This wisdom is not attained through internal contemplation, nor through external contemplation, nor through both internal and external contemplation;
yet it is not apart from internal and external contemplation. Nor is this wisdom attained through the absence of contemplation. If one understands this purport, [one will realize the truth].
Thus, whether far or near, internal or external, there is nothing that is not a skillful means (*upāya*). If one does not grasp the essential intent (*tattva*), then none of them are skillful means.
(End of Volume Two, Original Edition)
*Śānding Zhiguan*, Volume One;
*Śānding Zhiguan*, Volume Two.
By the Liang Dynasty [Master].

The seventh section, "Correct Contemplation," consists of six chapters from the "General Meaning" to the "Expedient Means. Based upon the sūtras, one opens up sublime understanding; now, based upon that sublime understanding, one establishes correct practice.
Indeed, oil and light depend on one another, and the eyes and feet mutually assist each other. When both practice and understanding are diligent, then obstacles will arise.

There is the affliction of Māra that destroys cultivation; whether it be dullness or distraction, it obscures and disturbs the clarity of samādhi. One must not follow it, for if one follows it, one goes away and cannot return.
One must not fear it, for if one fears it, one loses what one guards. One should observe dullness with observation (*vipaśyanā*);

then, within dullness, there is clarity. One should settle distraction with settling (*śamatha*); then, within distraction, there is stillness. As for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, when they are sublime, they are sublime; when they are base...
The inferior are base and lowly. If one is not such a person, the Way will not manifest in vain. One should extensively discern their objects so that they may be clearly and easily perceived.
The objects of contemplation are opened up into ten categories: first, the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; second, afflictions; third, illnesses; and fourth, the characteristics of karma.

1. The five demonic activities (*māra-karman*); 2. The six dhyānas; 3. The various views (*dṛṣṭi*); 4. Arrogance (*adhimāna*); 5. The two vehicles (*yāna*); 6. Bodhisattvas. Regarding the fact that the aggregates (*skandha*) are placed first:

the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that while Śrāvakas practice the path by relying on the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), Bodhisattvas first contemplate form (*rūpa*) up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Furthermore, since practitioners possess bodies, what among them is not comprised within the aggregates and sense-bases (*āyatana*)? As these great objects stand before one, they should be taken as the starting point.

First, regarding contemplation: since one has already contemplated the fruits of the aggregates (*skandha*), the causes of their accumulation are thereby activated; therefore, the afflictions (*kleśa*) are discussed next.

The four great elements and the three poisons constitute the maladies of body and mind, yet ordinary people remain unaware of them. If one contemplates the objects of perception with discernment, the power of contemplation arises, and consequently, these afflictions are also brought forth.
Furthermore, immeasurable karmas are beyond calculation; though the wholesome roots of scattered practice are weak and unable to move them, now—
Because the signs of karma manifest through the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), the discussion of karma follows next after the discussion of illness.

Karma is either wholesome or unwholesome; when the wholesome manifests, the wholesome arises, and when the unwholesome moves, the unwholesome ceases. When the application of the Path is about to prevail, Māras emerge as obstacles; therefore, the discussion of Māras follows next after the discussion of karma.

If one transcends the realm of Māra, meritorious qualities arise and various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) compete to manifest—whether they be characterized by attachment to flavor (*āsvādana*) or by purity (*śuddha*). Therefore, next...

The Māra-discourse on dhyāna: Dhyāna possesses factors of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), which give rise to false wisdom and cause perverse views to arise. Therefore, following the discourse on dhyāna, there is the discourse on views.
If these perversions are stilled, both greed and hatred—whether sharp or dull—will not arise; those without wisdom claim this is the realization of *nirvāṇa*.

In the Hīnayāna as well, there are those who recklessly calculate the four dhyānas to be the four fruits; in the Mahāyāna too, there are those to whom Māras come to bestow predictions of enlightenment.
These are all people of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) who have not attained what they claim to have attained. Therefore, after the discussion on views, pride is addressed.
