The thought "I understand, but he does not" gives rise to pride (*māna*). Not recognizing the suffering and its origin within existence (*bhava*) constitutes delusion (*moha*).

The inability to resolve these afflictions constitutes doubt (*vicikitsā*). These ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) pervade the three realms; according to their presence or reduction, they total eighty.

There are eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). The same applies to the remaining three views, and so on through all sixty-two views; each individual view possesses eighty-eight underlying tendencies.

Furthermore, just as when the eye perceives beautiful forms, ugly forms, or neutral forms, each contains its own *skandha* (aggregate) and its own *samudaya* (origination), so it is for the mind when it takes dharmas as its object.
Within one faculty there are three [types of objects]; within those three there are six; and with the six faculties complete, they constitute the three [realms].

Sixteen [factors] across the three periods of time constitute one hundred and eight. Passing through the sixty-two views, each of the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) likewise possesses one hundred and eight.
One should know that when the mind is raised and a thought moves, it is vast and boundless; yet due to the cause of ignorance and blindness, one perceives nothing at all.
Regarding the fourfold views: they are "existence," "non-existence," "both existence and non-existence," and "neither existence nor non-existence."
"Neither existence nor non-existence, neither non-existence nor existence"—this constitutes a double view.

Within each of these views, there are again eighty-eight latent proclivities (*anuśaya*), one hundred and eight, and so forth, as previously described. Regarding the possession of four views: the view of existence possesses four, namely:

existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence. The view of non-existence likewise possesses four, namely: non-existence, [existence],... [text fragmentary].

There is no [existence]. There is neither existence nor non-existence. There is neither non-existence nor that which is neither existent nor non-existent. Next, regarding the four views comprised by "both existence and non-existence," they are:
existence that is both existent and non-existent; non-existence that is both existent and non-existent; that which is both existent and non-existent and also both existent and non-existent;

and that which is both existent and non-existent and neither existent nor non-existent. Next, regarding the four views comprised by "neither existent nor non-existent," they are: neither existent nor...
"Neither existence nor non-existence; neither existence nor non-existence, yet both existence and non-existence;

neither existence nor non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence—this is called being fully endowed with the four views. Each phrase is fully endowed with the eighty-eight *anuśayas* (latent tendencies).

Passing through the sixty-two views, each is individually endowed with the eighty-eight *anuśayas*, the one hundred and eight [defilements], and so forth, as previously described. Regarding those who see beyond words: whether single or combined, they are fully endowed."
Beyond these, each possesses a "view beyond words. Each of these views, moreover, is endowed with all the underlying propensities (*anuśaya*) as previously described.
Thus, one should understand how views arise in relation to non-Buddhists. Furthermore, four views arise based on the Buddha-dharma.

Within each of the four gates—from the Tripiṭaka and Shared Teachings up to the Distinct and Perfect Teachings—four views respectively arise. Moreover, each of these likewise possesses a "view beyond words," and each of these, in turn, is endowed with [all the aforementioned factors].

The eighty-eight afflictions (*anuśaya*) and the one hundred and eight, etc., are as previously explained. Generally speaking, regarding the delusions of view (*darśana-heya*), names are established not only according to their specific interpretations, but they are also designated by their essential nature as "provisional" (*prajñapti*).
"Provisional" signifies that which is false, illusory, and inverted. Furthermore, there should be single, compound, complete, and ineffable forms of the provisional.

Moreover, within each individual form of the provisional, there are again three types of provisionality: namely, the provisional of causal formation (*hetu-siddha-prajñapti*), the provisional of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-*)... [text fragment] ...the provisional of designation (*upādāya-prajñapti*).

Continuity-conditionality (*santati-pratītyasamutpāda*), conditionality-by-dependence (*apekṣā-pratītyasamutpāda*). The simultaneous arising of the internal faculties, external objects, and a single moment of mind is called "arising through causes" (*hetu-siddha*).

The uninterrupted succession of preceding and succeeding moments is called "continuity. Waiting for other states of non-consciousness to know that one possesses consciousness is called "conditionality-by-dependence.
If we speak in terms of form (*rūpa*), the karmic actions of previous lives are the cause of this body; this is "arising through causes. From childhood...
That which continues without interruption is called "continuity" (*saṃtati*). That which exists by depending on what is not itself is called "mutual dependence" (*apekṣā*).

Both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna share this principle. In the Mahāyāna, the three types of provisional designations (*tri-prajñapti*) arise in dependence upon ignorance (*avidyā*), being like illusions or transformations;

they cannot be found in reality. If even the four subtle elements (*catvāri-aṇu*) within a mirror are empty, how much more so an illusory pillar? If the substance of the pillar is already empty, how much more so its existence?

Continuity and mutual dependence are termed "conceptual existence" (*prajñaptisat*). This differs in meaning from the "substantial existence" (*vastusat*) of the Hīnayāna. Furthermore, the *Śāstra* clarifies the three types of existence:

relative existence (*apekṣāsadbhāva*), nominal existence (*prajñaptisadbhāva*), and substantial existence (*dharmasadbhāva*). For example, long depends on short; far depends on near; east depends on west;
that depends on this. These names do not correspond to reality; this is relative existence. It is like the color, fragrance, taste, and touch of curd, which exist as causes.
Because of the conjunction of conditions, it is conventionally designated as "curd. Furthermore, because of the colors, odors, tastes, and tangibles of atoms, there is hair;

because of hair, there is wool; because of wool, there is felt; because of felt, there is cloth. This is what is meant by conventional existence (*prajñaptisat*). Moreover, when various dharmas combine, they exist;

this is what is meant by dharma-existence (*dharmasat*), which is identical in meaning to the three types of conventional designations. The *Yingluo jing* (Adornment Sūtra) also contains this teaching on the three types of conventional designations.

One should know that each of the four teachings and four gates possesses the three provisional designations (*trividha-prajñapti*), extending even to the eighty-eight afflictions (*anuśaya*) and so forth.

When the Tathāgata reveals to people the Dharma-gate of non-contention (*araṇa-dharmaparyāya*), for those who can assimilate it, it becomes nectar (*amṛta*); for those who cannot assimilate it, it becomes poison. As the *Śāstra* says:

"The Prajñāpāramitā cannot be grasped from its four sides"—this is precisely its meaning. Next, the explanation of the contemplation that shatters the provisional (*prajñapti-bhaṅga-vipaśyanā*) is divided into four parts.
First, refute the single; next, refute the double; next, refute the complete; next, refute the wordless. Regarding the refutation of the single:

if a single thought-moment arises within the four single views, it must be that one view is itself the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*) and so forth; its very substance is emptiness. This is called cessation (*śamatha*).
Furthermore, contemplate that ignorance is itself the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*); they are neither two nor different, neither arising nor ceasing, ultimately pure.

This is called the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional. For those of dull faculties, not only do they fail to awaken through hearing and reflection, but they may even increase their faults;

therefore, it is necessary to extensively refute all views. One should universally employ Nāgārjuna’s fourfold negations—neither self-caused, nor caused by another, nor both, nor without cause—to refute them until they are completely purified.
If a single thought arises, it is already endowed with the three types of conventionalities; one should contemplate this.
A single thought-moment arises: does it arise from the mind itself, in response to an object, through the co-arising of sense organ and object, or apart from both sense organ and object?
If it arises from the mind itself, then the preceding thought-moment would be the sense organ and the succeeding thought-moment would be the consciousness. One asks:

regarding this self-arising, does it proceed from the organ or from the consciousness? If the organ can produce consciousness, does it produce consciousness because the organ possesses consciousness, or because the organ lacks consciousness?

[If you say] consciousness is produced: if there is consciousness, then the sense organ and the consciousness would exist simultaneously; furthermore, there would be no producer and produced. If there is no consciousness, why can all insentient things not produce it?
Furthermore, if you say that although the sense organ lacks consciousness, it produces consciousness because it possesses the nature of consciousness (*vijñānatva*), we ask:
does this nature of consciousness exist or not? If it exists, then consciousness already co-exists with the organ; how [could it be otherwise]?

This is called "nature. If it were non-existent, then being without nature, how could it give rise to consciousness? Furthermore, is the nature of consciousness identical to consciousness, or is it different?
If they were identical, there would be neither subject nor object. If they were different, it would still be produced from something else.

By investigating in this manner, one ultimately realizes that the mind does not arise from itself. If one says that the mind arises from objects, we now investigate these objects and find that they are, in fact, the mind.
Arising occurs because it is not the mind. If the object were the mind, it would not be called an "object";

it would not exist externally, it would be identical to self-arising, and there would be no distinction between subject and object. If the object is not the mind, how can that which is not the mind cause arising?
If you claim that because there is a nature of arising within the object, it is able to produce arising, then does this nature exist or not? If it exists, it must coexist with the object.
Furthermore, there is neither subject nor object. If these do not exist, they cannot give rise to the mind. Through such investigation, one knows that the mind ultimately does not arise from objects.
If the mind were to arise because of the union of the sense organs and their objects, then the organs and objects would each possess a mind such that their union could produce it.
Since they lack individual substance, how could they possibly unite? It is like a mirror’s surface: because each possesses its own image, they can unite.

Regarding the production of an image: since each [the mirror and the face] individually lacks an image, they must combine to produce the image. If each possessed its own image, there would necessarily be two images.
If each individually lacks an image, how could their combination produce one? If you claim that the image is produced when the mirror and the face combine into one, in reality they do not combine;

if they were combined, there would be no image. If you claim that the image is produced when the mirror and the face are separated, then as they occupy different locations, the image [would likewise be split].
They should appear [as such], yet now none do so. The same applies to the meeting and parting of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).

By investigating in this manner, one knows that the mind ultimately does not arise from their conjunction. If it is further claimed that the mind arises because the nature of the sense faculty and the nature of the object each exist and these natures conjoin, then one must likewise investigate as before whether this nature exists or does not exist.
Since it cannot be found, one should further know that [the mind] does not arise from such a nature.
They arise through conjunction. If they were to arise while the sense faculties and their objects were each separate, this would be arising without causes or conditions.
One should examine whether this separation exists or does not exist. If it exists, then existence itself is a condition; how then can it be called "separation"? If it does not exist...
Once this has ceased, nothing remains; and what that which does not exist could produce? If one claims that it exists apart from its nature, that principle is even less tenable.
By investigating in this manner, one knows that the mind is not produced from separation. To observe in this way is the intent of Nāgārjuna’s *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.

If one investigates by means of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) to seek the arising [of phenomena] through their causes, it cannot be found; thus, attachment to their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) becomes thin.

There is only a name, which is designated as "arising. This name does not exist within, without, or in between; nor does it exist eternally of itself. This designation neither abides nor does it not abide.

This designation is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). If one investigates the nature through the four propositions and does not perceive that nature, this is the refutation of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Nature is also called the emptiness of nature. If one investigates names through the four propositions and does not perceive the name, this is the ultimate truth that subverts the conventional; it is also called the emptiness of marks.
This constitutes the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional. If one examines the sense bases and does not find the mind, this is internal emptiness.

Examining the objects of the senses with no mind is the emptiness of the external. Examining the union of the faculties and their objects and finding them unobtainable is the emptiness of the internal and external.

Examining and finding them unobtainable when separated from that union is the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). Examining the four natures and finding them unobtainable is the emptiness of nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Examining the four propositions and finding them unobtainable is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).

Examining the sensory objects, one finds no divisions of the ten directions; this is the emptiness of great space (*mahā-śūnyatā*). Seeking the Supreme Vehicle, one does not find it; this is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

Not finding [anything] through the causes and conditions of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), this is the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*). Since neither existence nor non-existence can be found, this is the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).

Seeking the origin of the mind through the four propositions, one does not find it; this is the emptiness of that which has no beginning (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*). Seeking the cessation of the mind through the four propositions...
One cannot find the dispersion of emptiness itself. Seeking the mind through the four propositions—whether it arises and ceases, or neither arises nor ceases—it is entirely unobtainable;

this is ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). There are no separate dharmas within the three realms; they are all produced by this single mind. Now, since the mind cannot be found when sought, everything is empty.

Contemplating emptiness and finding no emptiness is the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*). Contemplating existence and seeing that the three types of conventional designations (*tri-prajñapti*) are unobtainable is...

There is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). When the three provisional designations (*tri-prajñapti*) cannot be found through the view of non-existence, this is the emptiness of non-phenomena (*adharma-śūnyatā*).
When the three provisional designations cannot be found through the view of both existence and non-existence, this is the emptiness of non-phenomena and phenomena (*adharmadharma-śūnyatā*).

To contemplate in this manner is the eighteenfold contemplation of entering emptiness from the provisional (*prajñapti*) as found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. If one pursues these causes in this way and yet fails to attain awakening, one then enters the provisional designation of continuity (*santati-prajñapti*).
This is refuted. Why? Although four types of refutation are established based on [the premise], the arising of the mind cannot be established.
Yet, we currently observe that the mind arises and ceases in every moment in a continuous succession. How can it be said that it does not arise?

Does this momentary [mind] arise after the preceding moment has ceased, or does it arise without the preceding moment having ceased, or does it arise while both ceasing and not ceasing, or does it arise neither ceasing nor not ceasing? After which of these does the subsequent moment arise?

When one contemplates their arising, thus tracing this continuity sentence by sentence, it is entirely unfindable. Grasping at the mind then thins away; there is only the continuity of names, which lacks intrinsic nature.

This is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) where breaking down intrinsic nature results in the emptiness of nature. When continuity is nameless, this is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) where breaking down the provisional results in the emptiness of characteristics.
This continues up to the eighteen kinds of emptiness; this is called "entering emptiness from the provisional. Furthermore, [one] does not find...
As for "entering": it is like calculating that there is a mind that awaits a non-mind; thus, through mutual dependence, delusion arises. One should examine this mind:
does the mind arise by depending on the non-arising of phenomena? Does it arise by depending on their arising? Does it arise by depending on both arising and non-arising?
Or does it arise by depending on neither arising nor non-arising? If it arises by depending on non-arising...
Furthermore, let us ask: does this "non-arising" exist or not? If there were an arising to be awaited, then it would be awaiting existence;
how could it be awaiting non-existence? If there is existence, then mutual dependence constitutes self-arising. If this non-arising does not exist, what is there for it to depend upon?

If the mind were produced in dependence upon non-existence and non-production, then all instances of non-existence and non-production would likewise have production. To expect existence from non-existence is itself "other-production.
If the mind were produced in dependence upon both production and non-production, one would fall into two faults: if each exists, then two productions would occur simultaneously;
if each is absent, then logically it is entirely impossible. If the mind were produced in dependence upon that which is neither production nor non-production...
That which arises from causes and conditions cannot even be found; how much less so that which is without causes and conditions?
Thus, by investigating dependent designation, one fails to find the mind. What was grasped becomes attenuated. The arising of names is not truly arising; their nature cannot be apprehended.

When the nature of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is thus deconstructed, this is the emptiness of nature. When names cannot be apprehended, conventional designations are deconstructed; this is... [the emptiness of designation].

The emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) means that when one seeks within the nature and characteristics [of phenomena], the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) cannot be found;

this is the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*). When one seeks within the nature and characteristics for a self (*ātman*) or a person (*pudgala*), they cannot be found; this is the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*). This extends up to the eighteen kinds of emptiness. This is called "entering emptiness from the conventional" (*saṃvṛti*).

By attaining this, one opens the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*) and perceives the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). It is not merely that the delusions regarding the three types of conventionalities are eliminated upon seeing them; rather, all views are [extinguished].
There is no delusion that is not purified; this is called the gate of non-arising, which penetrates both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

If one does not awaken to this, then faith in the Dharma turns back and becomes the path of skillful means (*upāyamārga*), wherein one suppresses the view of existence (*bhavadarśana*). If one further falls into the calculations of the view of non-existence (*abhavadarśana*), it will be refuted as explained later.

When the practitioner employs *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to destroy the three types of provisional constructs (*trividha-prajñapti*), they enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in a state of total dissolution, perceiving nothing and hearing nothing.
When all things are entirely pure, one then claims that one’s own mind is the correct contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda-samyag-darśana*) and gives rise to views and attachments.

To take the dust of emptiness (*śūnyatā-rajas*) that is thus produced as being *nirvāṇa*—since there is already a subject that contemplates—it constitutes the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).

Because of this view of a self-identity, there are faults such as the eighty-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), which arise from the dust of emptiness. The *Śāstra* calls this "clinging to the contemplation of emptiness," which is [the error of] outsiders.

Regarding the Way and its Dharma, there is that which the Buddha did not transform. When a disciple of the Buddha contemplates non-arising, he knows that this empty mind is itself ignorance (*avidyā*), possessing the delusions of the three provisional designations (*trividha-prajñapti*).
One should then investigate whether this non-arisen mind arises from the sense organ (*indriya*), from the mental faculty (*manas*), or from the sense object (*viṣaya*);
whether it arises through their conjunction or their separation. If one says it arises from the organ, does the organ possess consciousness or lack consciousness? Thus one proceeds by extension...
Turning the observation, one sees that objects (*dharmas*) are likewise; even to the point of being neither separate nor inseparable, this non-arising cannot be found when sought.
This is precisely entering emptiness from the perspective of "non-view" and attaining right wisdom. For those who have not yet entered, they skillfully subdue this "non-view.
If they should cross over into the view of "both existence and non-existence," it shall be refuted as follows. Next, the view of "both existence and non-existence" is refuted.

Regarding those who perceive the three provisional designations: when the practitioner should subdue the time of non-perception, yet non-perception does not arise, or when concentration and wisdom slightly emerge and correspond to both existence and non-existence, they immediately say: "If there were no mind, who would know non-arising?
Non-arising is non-existence; the presence of knowing is existence. Once this mind has arisen, they grasp at and stubbornly cling to this view of both existence and non-existence.
It is not abandoned. Since this aggregate of sensation exists, the other four aggregates are likewise fully present. These aggregates are themselves suffering.

Furthermore, because there is that which can know and that which can act, the view of self arises. Once the view of self has arisen, there is the view of extremes. If one negates cause and effect, it becomes false view.
To reckon this [view] as the path constitutes the grasping of rules and rituals; to reckon it as nirvana constitutes the grasping of views. This opposes aversion and accords with joy.
My understanding is that pride [arises] from others' failure to recognize suffering and its origin, which constitutes delusion; later, one will experience great doubt.

As one traverses the three realms, the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) are fully present, all arising within a mind characterized by the view of both existence and non-existence. This immediately entails the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*).

One then proceeds to refute each of these using the aforementioned four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). If one then enters into the view of neither existence nor non-existence, it is refuted as follows. Next, [the following] is refuted:

Regarding the view that "neither exists nor does not exist": previously, when one was subduing the views of both existence and non-existence, one suddenly claimed to have transcended the mind of existence and non-existence.
Why? Because if the mind were definitively existent, it could not be made non-existent; if the mind were definitively non-existent, it could not be made existent.
How can it be said that it both exists and does not exist? If it is not determinately existent, it is not existence; if it is not determinately non-existent, it is not non-existence.
That which is not existence does not arise; that which is not non-existence does not cease. To conceive of this non-arising and non-ceasing as the Middle Way gives rise to immeasurable faults.
Why is this? If you claim that this mind is real, then it should possess permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

Purity. Now, since this mind undergoes arising and ceasing, how can it be considered permanent? Where there is sensation, there is no pleasure. How can that which lacks self-mastery be called a "self"?

That which possesses defilement and impurity—how can it be termed pure? To possess the notion of a self is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). To not yet be free from [the extremes of] existence and non-existence is the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
To take what is incorrect as correct and to subvert all causes and effects is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). It is said to be... [non-existent].

To hold that which is neither conditioned nor unconditioned as the Middle Way is called the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). To falsely conceptualize *nirvāṇa* is called the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

Following attachment, opposing aversion, there is delusion, pride, and subsequently great doubt. If one seeks to destroy these views, one should again employ the previous four propositions to pursue and refute them.
If they do not enter [the path], one should rely on faith in the Dharma, employ skillful means to turn back [the mind], and subdue the views to establish the path of skillful means.

If one further enters into the state beyond verbal expression, it shall be refuted as follows later. Next, the view of a "person" (pudgala) who holds the position that there is nothing expressible is refuted:
The practitioner, having previously subdued the afflictions through concentration and wisdom, experiences a sudden opening of insight and again gives rise to this understanding:

"All four positions—existence, non-existence, and so forth—are empty, false, and unreal. The very moment this 'existence' arises, it is precisely ignorance. One should know that the ultimate principle lies beyond words."
Beyond these four phrases lies that which is non-arising. To claim that one has "severed" them is merely a self-deception; in reality, there is nothing to sever.
Indeed, when the net of views is dense and thick, it is difficult to escape from it. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Ghosts and sprites are found everywhere.

One likewise uses the aforementioned four phrases to shatter this view of ineffable silence. Furthermore, beyond the categories of single, multiple, and complete, each possesses its own principle of ineffable silence.
Hypothetical. Having attained the breaking of the four simple views through silence, one immediately enters the complex. Breaking the complex, one enters the complete.
To remain silent externally is like avoiding empty space; how could it be like evading the principle? One should know that this silence is the root of birth and death.
From the preceding sections, each has been broken horizontally across various views; now, furthermore, they are broken vertically, so that gain and loss may be observed. This which is clung to—
The mind exists. Existence is precisely birth. What kind of birth is it? Is it the birth of the five *smṛtyupasthānas* up to the *laukikāgradharma*?
Or is it the birth of the true illumination of *duḥkhakṣānti*? Or is it the birth of the various stages (*bhūmis*) of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*)?

Or is it the birth of the stages of abiding and so forth in the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*) and the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*)? If one reckons this mind as non-existent, then non-existence is non-birth. Furthermore, what kind of thing would that be?
It is non-arising. Is it because views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) do not arise? Or is it because the *pāṃśu-rajas* [afflictions] and ignorance (*avidyā*) do not arise?
Use such arising and non-arising to examine your grasping mind; there is not even the slightest portion of it. How can you call that which is not a delusion of views "non-arising"?
Even calculations of both arising and non-arising, or neither arising nor non-arising, are all overturned by this principle. Furthermore, it is utterly beyond words.
Much. Your inquiry concerns the various categories—singular, dual, and plural—and each of these is ultimately beyond words. The Brahmin’s acceptance of the "dumb" dharma is also beyond words;
so too is the Long-nailed One’s refusal to accept any dharma. The Vātsīputrīya says, "In conventional truth there is a self;
this self exists within the 'ineffable storehouse' (avaktavya-kośa)," which is likewise beyond words. Thus, the realization of truth through the three baskets and four gates is entirely identical.

It is ineffable. In the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), afflictions are severed through the absence of verbal expression. In the Distinct and Perfect Teachings (*pratyekabuddha-yāna* and *vaipulya-yāna*), both realization and expression are ineffable;
thus, the Tathāgata remained silent and Vimalakīrti closed his mouth—both were instances of transcending words.

What kind of "ineffability" is yours? You do not even equal the Vātsīputrīyas, let alone the Tripiṭaka masters. Why? Because the Vātsīputrīyas designate the "ineffable" as conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). You...

This is what is called nirvāṇa; one should know that the distance between them is extremely vast. Furthermore, regarding the description of being "beyond words" and "outside the four propositions" (*catuṣkoṭi*):

there are two kinds of four propositions. The first is the four propositions of fixed positions, wherein the meanings of the propositions are definitively established and their assertions differ—this refers to the propositions of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
If one takes non-propositions as propositions, this refers to the propositions of the sages (*ārya*). Moreover, for ordinary beings, existence is a proposition.
The Two Vehicles are the phrase of "non-existence. Bodhisattvas are the phrase of "both existence and non-existence. The Buddha is the phrase of "neither existence nor non-existence.

These two [categories] constitute the four phrases of the provisional and the real. Regarding the four-phrase gate of all dharmas: the three and four phrases are the provisional; the one four-phrase is the real.
If one opens up all four-phrase gates, they all enter into the single real four-phrase gate; this is called "opening the provisional."
The phrases that reveal reality are each and every one ineffable. When you say they exist "outside," outside of which phrase do they exist? Thus, one should know that this is beyond words;
it is the exhaustion of the bonds of suffering and its origin through the perfection of the three provisional designations. One should diligently apply *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to dismantle them.

If one attains entry into emptiness, then one sees that the net of views is entirely destroyed. Someone may ask: "Regarding the gains and losses of various views through the application of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, how should one answer?
One should respond by employing a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*). First: the old delusions are not eliminated, and new delusions arise again, like taking medicine [that fails to cure the illness].

Therefore, the old afflictions are not eliminated, and the medicine itself becomes an affliction. Second, the old afflictions are eliminated, but new afflictions arise again, like a disease being cured while the medicine itself subsequently causes illness.
Third, the old afflictions are not eliminated, yet new afflictions do not arise, like a disease that, though not cured, does not worsen.
The medicine does no harm. For four reasons, past delusions are eliminated and new delusions do not arise. It is like when a disease has been cured, the efficacy of the medicine also ceases.
First, although one originally used *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to treat delusions, greed and desire increase;

because of this practice, views of inversion further arise, whereby one destroys causes and effects and commits every kind of transgression. Second, while practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, all dull afflictions (*kleśa*) subside.
They are able to endure bitter suffering and are able to renounce wealth and treasures, yet their attachment to views becomes increasingly severe; this is truly terrifying.

These two types of practitioners of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are identical to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Third, those among the followers of the Buddha who practice *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* deeply understand the maladies of views and craving.

One employs the three provisional designations and the four propositions to gradually dismantle and eliminate [clinging]. Although greed and hatred are not yet exhausted, attachment is gradually abandoned; such a person is one who practices through skillful means.

Fourth, if both nature and characteristics are empty, one gives rise to true vision and realizes the principle; this constitutes entering the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*) and becoming a noble one (*ārya*).
Furthermore, regarding the discussion of destroying views: according to the Tripiṭaka masters, destroying views establishes the stage of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).

In the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), the destruction of views constitutes the stage of the Eight Persons (*aṣṭamaka*). In the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), the destruction of views constitutes the Ten Abidings (*daśa-vihāra*).

In the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*), the destruction of views constitutes the stage of the Six Faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Although the names of what is destroyed are the same, the contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) differs; thus, one must not conflate the meanings based on the names alone. Someone may ask:

"Why not directly clarify the stages of the Perfect Teaching, rather than proceeding through those of the *Hīnayāna* (Treasury) and Shared Teachings? The answer is: This is because [the author] intends to...
This merely demonstrates the shallow and deep stages of the Dharma positions. Furthermore, it seeks to clarify the positions of the "half" and "full" teachings.

Generally speaking, all entry into emptiness via the half-letters (*ardhākṣara*) serves as an expedient means (*upāya*) to assist the fulfillment of the full teaching. Moreover, how could there be a reality that exists apart from expedient means? The half is itself the full.
Therefore, it is said that whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to the two vehicles is all the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

As for the meaning of "the substance is provisional and enters emptiness," which establishes the principle of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*: the cessation of the wheel of various views and the non-retrogression of a single reception is called *śamatha*.

The realization of this nature-emptiness and characteristic-emptiness is called *vipaśyanā*. This is precisely the meaning of the gate of non-arising as it penetrates both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and it is also [itself] *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

This establishes the meaning of the gate of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Having completed the refutation of the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) by entering emptiness from the conventional, [the first volume ends here] (End of Volume Three, Original Text).
Next, regarding the essence of contemplating the conventional to enter emptiness and the universal refutation of phenomena (*dharmas*): "Contemplation" refers to greed, hatred, ignorance, and pride;

these are called the dull afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*). They pervade the three realms across nine stages (*bhūmi*). Each stage has nine grades, totaling eighty-one grades. All of these are capable of moistening karma so that one undergoes birth within the three realms.

Regarding "birth": the term "affliction of thought" (*sī-fǎn*) is established based on understanding. Initially, when contemplating the Truth, one is still hindered by objective phenomena; later, through repeated reflection on the Truth, these delusions are eliminated.
Therefore, it is called the "affliction of thought. As for this body of craving and desire, those who enter emptiness provisionally must deal with the nine grades of the affliction of desire.

Each and every category arises as being endowed with the three types of provisional existence (*prajñapti*). When a woman desires to approach a man, she defiles his sense faculties; the greedy mind arises within, and the signs of greed manifest without.

Even those who have attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) are not yet able to sever this, let alone ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). When the dust of sensory objects agitates the mental faculty (*manas*), it constitutes the "provisional existence by way of cause" (*hetu-prajñapti*).

As thoughts arise in succession, this desire is thereby established; this is the "provisional existence by way of continuity" (*santati-prajñapti*). Where there is desire in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), there is no absence of desire.

Regarding dependent designation (*upādāya-prajñapti*): one should first examine this desirous mind—does it arise from the sense organ (*indriya*), from the object (*viṣaya*), from both together, or independently?

If it arises from the sense organ, then the organ should produce it spontaneously even before encountering the object. If it arises from the object, since the object belongs to another, what concern is it to me?
If it arises from both together, two minds should arise simultaneously. If it were without cause, that would be even more illogical.

This is not so. When one uses the fourfold analysis to investigate desire as ultimately empty and quiescent, a person of sharp faculties observes that a single grade of the provisional is shattered and a portion of the real is revealed.

Even if they have not yet attained entry, by means of the four *siddhāntas* they believe in the Dharma, turn back [from delusion], and skillfully harmonize *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, whereby they will immediately attain correspondence with reality.
If, however, a person of dull faculties does not remove even the first grade while observing within the "accomplishment of causes," [they remain obstructed].

One should then observe within the continuum: does [the subsequent thought] arise after the preceding thought has ceased? Does it arise without having ceased? Does it arise both having ceased and not having ceased?
Or does it arise neither having ceased nor not having ceased? When one seeks it within these four alternatives, it cannot be found; furthermore, these four alternatives themselves do not exist.
When observing in this manner, one shall likewise attain entry [into the truth]. If one still does not enter, one should further observe within the context of mutual dependence (*apekṣā*).

The preceding examples may be understood accordingly. As it is with the first category, so it is with the subsequent eight categories. As it is with the refutation of greed, so it is with the nine categories of hatred, delusion, and pride.
When the nine categories of reality are revealed, this is the non-arising of principle. When the nine categories of affliction are exhausted, this is the non-arising of causes.

When [afflictions] do not arise in the desire realm, this is the non-arising of results. Because they do not arise, they do not cease; this is the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Next, regarding the destruction of the nine grades of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*): when a practitioner uses mundane wisdom (*laukika-jñāna*) to destroy the obstacles of nature and gives rise to the first dhyāna, eight tactile sensations touch the body, and the five factors (*pañcāṅga*) of merit arise therein.
Craving for these flavors is called "greed" (*lobha*). Being unable to attain lightness is called "pride" (*māna*).

Not knowing the suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*) within the dhyāna is called "delusion" (*moha*). Such are the nine grades; in each grade, there are furthermore three types of false conceptions (*prajñapti*) concerning form.
The Dharma consists of eight types of contact (*sparśa*). Contact with the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) in the desire realm is called "accomplished through causes" (*hetu-siddha*).

The uninterrupted continuity of discernment is called "succession" (*saṃtati*). The arousal of this dhyāna, as distinct from its non-arousal, is called "relative" (*apekṣā*). If one does not dismantle these conventional designations (*prajñapti*), one will be reborn according to the dhyāna attained.

What is meant by "non-birth"? Now, one practices the skillful means of śamatha and vipaśyanā through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). The severance of the afflictions of a single category is called the "path of non-obstruction" (*ānantarya-mārga*). [This is] the realization.

The state free from delusion is called the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). This is precisely the non-arising of cause and effect and so forth; this is termed "entering emptiness through the conventional establishment based on causes.
The same applies to the functions of continuity and mutual dependence. It is likewise for the remaining eight categories. It is likewise for ignorance, pride, and the rest.
Whether it be the destruction of the first dhyāna up to the second, third, or fourth dhyānas, each is treated with the wisdom of the fourfold logical analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*).

One follows this and breaks it down. Each of the nine grades [of the form realm], including the three types of conventional designations (*prajñapti*), is treated in this same manner. Next, regarding the breaking down of the nine grades of the formless realm:

if one eliminates the three kinds of form, such as "resistance" (*sapratigha*), one breaks through the barrier of intrinsic nature and enters the concentration of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*).

This state likewise possesses craving (*tṛṣṇā*), pride (*māna*), and delusion (*moha*). One again employs the fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) to contemplate the non-arising of phenomena according to both principle and fact. If [the afflictions] do not depart, one further cultivates their characteristics.

Continuing with the discussion on mutual dependence and so forth: this applies equally to the eight grades of delusion, conceit, and the rest. First, one takes emptiness as the object; if emptiness becomes excessive, the mind scatters.

Abandoning emptiness and taking consciousness as the object, one achieves the concentration of the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*). Furthermore, abandoning the excessive consciousness and taking nothingness as the object, one achieves the concentration of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*).

The previous sphere of consciousness is like an abscess, while the sphere of nothingness is like a sore; there is yet another superior stage called the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
It is neither perception nor non-perception. Previously, perception was eliminated within the sphere of nothingness; now, moreover, non-perception is eliminated.

Having relinquished both perception and non-perception, it is therefore called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception. One should know that each of these meditative attainments possesses the three provisional designations (prajñapti) and the nine grades.
Now, using exclusively untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna), one refutes them through the four propositions; this is called the refutation of the nine grades of the provisional designation of thought.

When the eighty-one grades of delusion are exhausted, it constitutes the universal destruction of the dharmas that constitute the body [of affliction]. The preceding section clarified the method for destroying the afflictions of the realm of thought;

this section clarifies the stages for destroying those afflictions of thought. There are four types: first, the Tripitaka Teaching; second, the Shared Teaching; third, the Distinct Teaching; and fourth, the Perfect Teaching.

First, regarding the *piṭaka* that refutes the stage of contemplation (*cintāmayī bhūmi*): from the abandonment of one grade of desire-defilements (*kāma-kleśa*) up to the sequential exhaustion of the fifth grade, all are termed "candidates for the fruit of once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka*).

If one abandons them by leaping over [the intervening grades] up to the fifth grade, this is termed "one who goes from family to family" (*kulānkula*). Next, when the sixth grade is exhausted, it is termed the "fruit of once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*).

If one abandons them by leaping over [the intervening grades] up to the sixth grade, this is termed "one who returns only once" (*ekavīcika*). Next, from the abandonment of the seventh grade... up to the [eighth grade]... [text continues].
The eighth grade is called the candidate for the fruit of *anāgāmin*. Having transcended and severed up to the eighth grade, one is called a "single-seeded" (*ekabījī*).
Next, having severed the ninth grade entirely, one attains the fruit of *anāgāmin* and will never again return to the desire realm.

Subsequently, from the first grade of the first dhyāna up to the eighth grade of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there are seventy-one grades in total; these are all called the candidate for the fruit of *arhat*. [Having severed...]

The ninth stage of the realm of non-perception is called the fruit of Arhatship. If one discusses the Pratyekabuddha, the distinction lies in further eradicating and severing the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*).
This refers to the stage of analyzing the provisional and severing discursive thought. Second, regarding the commonality of the essence of contemplation in the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*):

from the Stage of Dry Wisdom up to the sixth stage, one shares with the Śrāvaka; from the seventh stage, one shares with the Pratyekabuddha; and from the eighth and ninth stages, one shares with [the Bodhisattva].

The Bodhisattva, upon transitioning from the Bodhisattva stages into the tenth stage, is named a Buddha-stage. These three types of persons equally sever the active outflows (*āsrava*) and equally enter both the *sopadhiśeṣa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa* nirvāṇas;
therefore, they are said to be "common. Among them, the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) refers to the positions of the three virtuous ones and the external ordinary beings.

The Stage of Nature (*gotra-bhūmi*) is the stage of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) within the four roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*). These two stages involve the suppression of the afflictions of the view (*darśana-heya*).

The third is the Stage of the Eight Persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*), which enters the samādhi of non-interruption (*ānantarya-samādhi*). The fourth is the Stage of Seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*), which is the stage of abandoning the afflictions of the views of the three realms.

The fifth is named the Thin Stage (*tanu-bhūmi*); this is the stage of removing the afflictions of the desire realm that are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). The sixth is named the Stage of Freedom from Desire (*vītarāga-bhūmi*); this is the stage where the afflictions of the desire realm abandoned through cultivation are exhausted. The seventh...

This is called the Stage of Having Accomplished [the Goal]. Excluding the stage where the volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) of the form and formless realms are exhausted, the eighth is called the Stage of the Pratyekabuddha;

this is the stage of eradicating the residual tendencies (*vāsanā*). The ninth is called the Stage of the Bodhisattva; here one severs the ignorance of residual tendencies and attains the Path of the Dharma-eye, which is the stage of contemplating the dual flow.
The eleventh, the "Thought in Accordance," is the supreme stage of the Buddha. This constitutes the realization of the severance of the essence according to the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-śāsana*).

This refers to the stage of contemplation (*cintā*). However, a detailed analysis of these successive stages is not the primary intent of this treatise on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; it is mentioned briefly only for the purpose of clarifying the delusions to be eliminated.

If one follows the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna*) regarding the destruction of the provisional, first the views are destroyed upon entering the first *vihāra*, and by the second *vihāra* up to the seventh *vihāra*, the provisional nature of the delusions of contemplation (*cintā*) is destroyed.
From the eighth to the tenth *vihāra*, the stage of habituation (*vāsanā*) is severed. The ten practices (*daśapratipatti*) constitute the stage of emerging from the provisional. If...
Regarding the stages of destroying the provisional according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*): first, destroying the provisional of views is precisely the stage of the First Faith (*shixin*).

From the Second Faith through the Seventh Faith is the destruction of the provisional of thought. From the Eighth Faith to the Tenth Faith, the residual habits (*xi*) are completely severed. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"At the moment of first generating the mind, both the active afflictions (*zheng*) and the residual habits are exhausted; there remain no further realms of active afflictions or residual habits outside. Now, as for the term "exhausted" (*jin*), it refers to...

It is simply that within the realm [of the threefold world], one exhausts the practice of cultivation. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, one has already surpassed the Muni.

This refers precisely to this meaning. Nevertheless, while traversing these various stages, the destruction of conventional designations is the same; however, there is a difference in the application of wisdom when taking the principle as its object.

The two vehicles of the Tripiṭaka and Shared Teachings destroy conventional worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), yet at the time of death, they no longer possess the function of emerging from conventionality. The Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching destroy...

Regarding the provisional conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*): at the time of death, one is still able to emerge from the provisional and take birth with mastery. When the conditions for transformation are exhausted, one dissolves the body to realize emptiness.

In the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), the conventional truth is established to manifest the Middle Way; thus, although one dies, one ultimately does not abide in emptiness. In the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*), one breaks through [delusions] to see the Truth (*tattva*);

this is precisely entering the Other [Realm], which is precisely entering the Middle. One suppresses ignorance (*avidyā*) perfectly—this is what constitutes the difference. Furthermore, let us distinguish them according to their sequence.

There are the aforementioned numerical sequences; however, practitioners do not necessarily enter them in successive order. One should know that there is the principle of "transcending the fruits. As for clarifying "perfect transcendence":

it is like the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* clarifying the sudden enlightenment of the Tathāgata, or the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* stating that one attains perfect awakening in a single kṣaṇa—this is the meaning of transcendence.
Alternatively, due to the original vow of compassion, one may vow not to become a Buddha; this is the meaning of non-transcendence. [Pure...]
It is called "Cloud. Although he has attained the Buddha-way, he practices the bodhisattva path to deliver sentient beings. This is thus both transcending and not transcending.

Within the principle of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), there is neither transcending nor non-transcending. According to capacities, he moves everywhere; according to principle, he is eternally quiescent.

The essential meaning is thus evident. Furthermore, one may employ four gates to clarify this principle of refuting the provisional. Regarding the two delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*saṃjñā*), there is no gate through which they do not pass.
The *Abhidharma* clarifies that the self (*ātman*), persons (*pudgala*), and sentient beings (*sattva*) are as unobtainable upon investigation as the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit;

there exist only real dharmas (*bhūta-dharma*). One becomes deluded regarding these real dharmas and gives rise to views and thoughts in a distorted manner. These views and thoughts are impermanent in their conceptualization.

Mindfulness does not abide; real dharmas shift and move, arising and ceasing moment by moment. To observe and break through them in this way is called the intention of the "Gate of Existence" (*yu-men*) within the Tripiṭaka for breaking dharmas.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If one attains the skillful means (*upāya*) of Prajñā and enters the Abhidharma, one does not fall into existence.

The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* states: "Those who hold the view of permanence say that different moments of thought are severed [from one another]; this is precisely the meaning of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) breaking the fetters."

Is this not the Gate of Existence (yǒumén) that refutes the provisional? Furthermore, the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* clarifies that the self and persons are fundamentally non-existent; although real dharmas exist, they are floating and empty, and thus not truly existent.
If one is deluded by these floating and empty things, one will perversely give rise to views and afflictions, transmigrating through birth and death.

To contemplate that both the provisional and the real are non-existent is called "equality-emptiness" (*pingděngkōng*). To break [delusion] through such contemplation is what is meant by the intention behind the refutation of dharmas in the Emptiness Gate of the Tripiṭaka. Therefore...

That treatise states: "I shall now clarify the true meaning within the Tripitaka. The true meaning is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The *Āgama* Sūtra says: 'This is old age and death; who ages and dies? Both [positions] are false views.
'This is old age and death' refers to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); 'Who ages and dies' refers to the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
It further states: 'The Buddha's Dharma-body is itself emptiness. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: 'If one does not obtain the skillful means of Prajñā...'"
Entering emptiness leads to falling into non-existence. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "Those with the view of annihilationism say that [existence] is severed in a single thought-moment.
Is this not the meaning of the equality of emptiness? For example, Kātyāyanīputra composed the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, clarifying that real dharmas both exist and do not exist;

by contemplating this existence and non-existence, one destroys the provisional. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "If one attains the skillful means of Prajñā and enters the gate of the *Vibhāṣā*, one does not fall [into extremes]."

"Existence is also within non-existence," as explained in the *Śāstra*. The Buddha taught this to Chandaka in the *Nandaka-Kātyāyana Sūtra*, stating that one attains the Way by departing from both existence and non-existence.
By observing this, one breaks through the provisional to enter emptiness; thus, the meaning of the Tripiṭaka’s "neither existence nor non-existence" is the breaking of the provisional.
It is like a city with four gates, where their convergence is no different [in purpose]. If one were to say that the gate of existence is coarse, [then] emptiness...
The gates are considered inferior. When viewed in this light, all three gates are equally deficient, not just one alone.

Why is this? This is the provisional teaching of the initial instruction; *Nirvāṇa* refers to it as "half-syllables"; the *Lotus Sūtra* names it "constantly making [them] remove filth for twenty years";
the *Śāstra* calls it a "clumsy physician"; the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* titles it "the dharma favored by the poor"; and Vasubandhu refers to it as...
The "inferior vehicles" all refer to these four gates; they are not what is employed here. Next, regarding the four gates of the Shared Teaching for the refutation of the provisional:

if one holds that all provisional and real phenomena arise from ignorance, and since ignorance is like an illusion, then all things are like illusions—existing though empty—this is the contemplation of illusion.
Therefore, it is said that while all dharmas are unarisen, Prajñā arises. By means of this, the provisional is refuted.

This is the meaning of the Gate of Existence (*yǒumén*). If one maintains that all things are like illusions, such that the nature of both the subject who contemplates and the object contemplated is quiescent—being true within the very midst of illusion—this is the meaning of the Gate of Refuting the False as Emptiness (*kōngmén*).

If one maintains that all phenomena are like images in a mirror, being non-existent yet existent, and existent yet non-existent, this is the meaning of the Gate of Refuting the False as Both Existent and Empty (*yòuyǒu yìkōngmén*). If one maintains that since...
To speak of illusory transformations, how could they truly exist? Since they do not exist, they cannot be said to exist; since they are not non-existent, they cannot be said to be non-existent.
Thus, this refutes the provisional and establishes the meaning of being neither empty nor existent. The Treatise says: "The Prajñāpāramitā..."
It is like a great fire; one cannot grasp it from any of its four sides. It is further said that there are four aspects of *prajñā*, and that one enters the cool pond through four gates.
One should know that those who do not grasp or cling can enter through them, whereas those who grasp or cling will be burned by it.

The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states that the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is attained in common by three types of persons; in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, this is called "shared *prajñā*."
Nirvana is likened to three animals crossing a river; this applies to all four gates of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), yet it is not what is employed here.

Next is the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), which has four gates. These involve contemplating the distinct principle to sever distinct delusions; thus they do not coincide with the former [Shared Teaching]. They involve gradual cultivation and realization;

thus they do not coincide with the latter [Perfect Teaching]. Therefore, it is called "Distinct. As for the four gates: one contemplates the illusory transformations of view-delusions and thought-delusions, and the emptying of false form. This is the Distinct [Teaching].
There is a sublime form called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "That which is 'empty of emptiness' is the view of the non-Buddhists;
liberation is that which is not empty. This is the true, wholesome, and sublime form, the secret treasury (*tathāgatagarbha*) of the Tathāgata, which must exist and cannot be absent.
Furthermore, "the self" is the Tathāgatagarbha, and the Tathāgatagarbha is Buddha-nature. As stated in the *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*, it is like [gold] wrapped in tattered rags.
The analogies of gold and so forth represent the meaning of the "existent gate" (yu-men). The Mahāyāna Sūtra states: "Kapilavastu is empty; the Tathāgata is empty;
the Great Parinirvāṇa is empty. It further states: "It causes all sentient beings to attain formless nirvāṇa," and "Nirvāṇa is not existent."
It is named "nirvāṇa" due to worldly convention; it is neither form nor sound. How, then, can it be seen or heard? This is precisely the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, it is said: "The wise perceive both emptiness and non-emptiness. If one speaks of emptiness, then there is no permanence, bliss, self, or purity.
If one speaks of non-emptiness, who then would receive this permanence, bliss, self, and purity? It is like water, wine, curd, or a jar, which cannot be described as either empty or [otherwise].

"Both non-empty and empty" is the gate of both existence and emptiness (*yō-u-ya-kū-mon*). Furthermore, it is said that "neither eternal nor annihilated, and ineffable," is called the Middle Way (*chūdō*);
this is the meaning of the gate of neither emptiness nor existence (*hi-kū-hi-u-mon*). If one grasps this intent, one enters the true reality (*shissō*) through universal penetration;
if one does not grasp this intent, one forms a sequence of skillful means (*hōben*) to suppress delusions. Nirvāṇa designates this as the Bodhisattva.

The "Noble Practice" (ārya-caryā) is referred to in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* as the "Unshared Prajñā. This constitutes the four gates of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*), which is likewise not what is employed here.

Next are the four gates of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-śāsana*). Its wondrous principle is taught instantaneously, differing from the *āgama* and *śrāvaka* teachings; its perfect interfusion without obstruction also differs from the sequential and distinct [teachings]. As for the four gates:
one contemplates that these very views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are themselves the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), fully endowed with all dharmas. Furthermore, all...
Dharmas are themselves the causes and conditions of the dharma-nature; even the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is likewise a cause and condition. As the Great Sūtra says:
"By extinguishing ignorance, one immediately attains the blazing lamp of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). This is called the gate of existence (*bhāva-mukha*).
If one contemplates this view and thought, as well as all dharmas, they do not reside in causes nor belong to conditions. Both the self and *nirvāṇa* are empty; there remains only...
Emptiness is illness; emptiness itself is also empty. This is called the gate of emptiness.

If one considers that within illusory transformations there are immeasurable marks of views and thoughts, and is well able to discern them—just as a single mote of dust contains a great thousand-fold scripture—then one speaks of provisional names and marks within that which is devoid of names and marks.

This is precisely the gate of both existence and non-existence. If one contemplates these delusions of perception and thought (*dṛṣṭi-saṃskāra*) as being the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they are not mundane and thus not existent;
they are not supramundane and thus not non-existent. Every single form and every single fragrance is the Middle Way. Within the One, all are the Middle.
Since Vairocana pervades all places, how could perception and thought not be the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*)? This is precisely...
It is neither the gate of emptiness nor the gate of existence. Furthermore, one gate is itself three gates. Why? Contemplating phenomena produced through causes and conditions is the first gate;
thus, all things are the first gate. The first gate is emptiness: when one is empty, all are empty—this is the second gate. This first gate is also the provisional:
when one is provisional, all are provisional—this is the third gate. This first gate...
This is precisely the Middle Way. Within one, all are included within the Middle. This is the fourth gate: one is three, and three is one.

Thus, for those who destroy the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) by relying on the gate of non-arising (*anutpāda*), this is the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). One gate encompasses all gates; it is not limited to non-arising alone.
One destruction encompasses all destructions; it does not merely stop at destroying views and afflictions. It is the entry from the conventional into emptiness.
When one is empty, all are empty; it is not merely that birth and death are empty. These four gates are precisely what is employed here now. In reality, they are a single dharma.
Because ordinary people are dull-witted and ignorant, it was not explained [to them] so they would not know. First, three types were shown to them. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"Though various paths are taught, in truth they are for the sake of the One Vehicle. And as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Furthermore, there is one practice which is..."

The practice of the Tathāgata is explained in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* solely as the Unsurpassed Way (*anuttara-mārga*). In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it is termed the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) which knows all phenomena (*dharma*).
In the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, it is illustrated by the metaphor of entering a campaka grove and not smelling any other fragrance.

In the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, it is designated as the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). These are the meanings of these four gates. This gate of non-arising (*anutpāda*) is the gate of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*), not a gate of expedient means (*upāya*). Therefore—
This is called the "Pervasive Refutation of Dharmas. △ Second, regarding the pervasive refutation of dharmas from emptiness into the provisional:

first, clarify the intent of entering the provisional; second, clarify the causes and conditions; third, clarify the contemplation of entering the provisional; fourth, clarify the stages of entering the provisional. First, clarify the intent of entering the provisional.
Some enter the provisional from emptiness alone; some know that emptiness is not [ultimate] emptiness and break through emptiness to enter the provisional.

Now, while the followers of the Two Vehicles also realize the principle of emptiness, they are not called Bodhisattvas because they lack great compassion. Bodhisattvas enter emptiness from the provisional; by breaking their own fetters and attachments, they differ from ordinary beings.
By entering the provisional from emptiness, they are able to break the fetters of others, differing thus from the followers of the Two Vehicles. Thus they abide in existence.
Unstained by emptiness, one does not abide therein. With the Dharma-eye as medicine and compassion as the probe, one treats the ailments of sentient beings.

Through universal love and impartial salvation, the mind functions with sovereign mastery, like planting a tree in the sky; this is the entry into the provisional meaning. There are briefly five causes and conditions for entering the provisional.
First, the gravity of the compassionate mind; second, the recollection of original great vows; third, the sharpness and acuity of wisdom;
fourth, skillful means; and fifth, the power of great diligence. By virtue of these five factors, there arises the function of emerging from the provisional and the merit of vast salvation.
Pure Fame (Viśuddhakīrti) explains three kinds of consolation: first, contemplating the impermanence of the body is the consolation of entering emptiness (*śūnyatā*);

finally, stating that one should become a King of Physicians is the consolation of entering the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*); and the intermediate section is the consolation of entering the provisional (*prajñapti*).

This accords with the principles of those five conditions. Next, the contemplation of the provisional is explained in three parts: first, knowing the illness; second, identifying the medicine; and third, administering the medicine.

The method: To know the illnesses means to recognize the two illnesses of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and afflictions (*kleśa*). One knows that the "self" (*ātman*) is the root of all views; from this delusion of self arise immeasurable views.
If the view of self is emptied, the branches and twigs will naturally fall away. Furthermore, one knows the causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) that give rise to these views.

These causes and conditions differ according to the faculties, natures, physical forms, dwellings, and desires of sentient beings, which vary individually and divergently in thousands of categories and ten thousand types.

Regarding categories: since the dependent and the primary [realms] differ, one knows that karma differs; since karma differs, the arising of views also differs. One should perceive the end-consciousness as the root, and perceive the external as internal.

Furthermore, one should know the duration—whether long or short—of the arising of views, as well as their frequency: whether they are heavy or light, single or repeated, complete or incomplete, and so forth, including the ineffable.

Each individual view further possesses the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*), the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*), the four *siddhāntas*, and the emptiness of both nature and characteristics (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*). Moreover, in terms of...
The sixty-two views, the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), and so forth—medicines and ailments are immeasurable; even boundless skill in calculation cannot enumerate them.
One must skillfully discern them without error; this is knowing the origin (*samudaya*). Knowing the origin is knowing suffering (*duḥkha*).

Recognizing oneself and recognizing others is like seeing various forms and images in a mirror. Next, one knows that the ailment of volitional thought (*saṃskāra*) has delusion (*moha*) as its root, category by category.
The number of categories is weighty; both that which can destroy and that which is destroyed are likewise immeasurable and boundless.

What is seen by the Dharma-eye is the knowledge of the disease. Next, one enters the provisional consciousness of medicinal remedies. Briefly stated, there are three: first, the worldly dharma-remedy;

second, the supramundane dharma-remedy; third, the supramundane-supreme dharma-remedy. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* refers to these as the three kinds of Dharma-giving. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "All worldly..."

The intervening scriptures are all spoken by the Buddha; they are not the teachings of external paths. Now, benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom, as well as all other wholesome dharmas, provide great benefit within the world.
However, these are merely worldly physicians. As a sutra says: "Though a worldly physician may cure [a patient], the illness will arise again.
The supramundane medicine of the Dharma is as described in various sutras: though the paths differ, they lead to the same destination; sometimes a single path serves as the medicine.
As with the *ekavyūha-samādhi*, there may be two paths as medicine, namely concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); three dharmas as medicine, namely the three gates of liberation;
and so on, up to the four foundations of mindfulness, the five powers, the six perfections, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the nine perceptions, and the ten knowledges.

Thus, the number increases until it reaches the infinite. Each individual dharma possesses various names and characteristics, as well as various functions, which emerge from the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
The Bodhisattva cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā through great compassion. The Dharma-eye is opened, such that there is nothing not fully known.
Furthermore, he brings forth the supreme, world-transcending medicinal elixir of the Dharma, taking the single dharma of śamatha-vipaśyanā as that medicine; this is the one true reality (ekasatyatā).
Ignorance and the dharmatā combine to form all illnesses; now, even the dharmatā cannot be apprehended—how much less ignorance and all other phenomena?
Alternatively, two dharmas serve as the medicine: namely, inconceivable and non-referential *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Three dharmas are the three *samādhis*.

This continues through four, five, six, and seven, up to *dharmamukhas* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, which increase or decrease according to the faculties and capacities of sentient beings.

Just as a great physician prescribes a formula where the dosage varies according to the illness, so too is it with the Bodhisattva: traversing all dharmas, they employ them all according to the four *siddhāntas*.

One should employ it with a mind of giving. That which is remedied by the Two Vehicles is sufficient through a single flavor; however, a Bodhisattva must know all suffering and its accumulation, as well as all paths and their cessation.
How could one maintain the status quo and obstruct this path of transformation? The *Śāstra* says: "Based on and following the teachings of the sūtras, names and meanings are extensively established;
this is the Dharma-giving of names and meanings. When a Bodhisattva cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā and attains clear awakening, within the entry into the conventional...
Thus, one attains mastery. Regarding what is called the method of administering medicine:
having understood both the symptoms of the illness and the potency of the medicine, if sentient beings lack the capacity for world-transcending [realization], one guides them through worldly dharmas.

If one administers world-transcending medicine, since the faculties and natures of sentient beings differ, the administration of the medicine also differs. That is to say, there are the lower, the middle, the upper, the higher-upper, and the supreme-upper. The lower...

One should administer the medicine of the Four Truths—the arising and ceasing of dependent origination—according to the faculties [of the recipient]. Regarding those of inferior faculties, there are four ways they delight in hearing the Dharma:

for those who delight in existence, one explains the Abhidharma; for those who delight in non-existence, one explains the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*; for those who delight in both existence and non-existence, one explains the *Kun-lê* (Samyukta) Śāstra;

and for those who delight in neither existence nor non-existence, one explains the Sūtras that transcend existence and non-existence, causing them to perceive the True Truth. This constitutes the four gates for entering the provisional.

It is medicine. For those of middling faculties whose wisdom gradually excels, one should administer the medicine of the Four Noble Truths as being empty, causeless, and unarisen by means of the four gates;

this likewise employs the four gates in its administration. For those of superior faculties whose wholesome wisdom is vast and open, one should administer the medicine of the immeasurable Four Noble Truths of provisional names to sever the delusions of the five abodes and gradually enter the Middle Way; this also employs the four gates in its administration. As for those of the highest of superior faculties...
To speak directly of the medicine of the true reality (*dharmatā*) is precisely the principle of the Four Noble Truths of Non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). These are also bestowed through four gates;
that is to say, if one hears these words directly, the illness is immediately cured. If one enters the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), there is not even a single dharma;

yet now, by means of the sixteen paths of cessation, one treats the sixteen aspects of suffering and its origin. This is truly the One Sound (*ekasvara*) that accords with the capacities of beings, enabling them to receive and practice it—just as in the parable of the single [remedy].
It is merely that the grasses and trees grow as the clouds rain upon them. Next, the stage of entering the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) is clarified.

Ordinary people first eliminate the conventional of views and subsequently break through the conventional of thought; yet even the fruit of entering emptiness remains far off, so how could it be within one's power to emerge from emptiness to transform sentient beings?
Consequently, they look upon the precipice and abandon their efforts. Now, we shall distinguish the differences between the stages and ranks. As for the Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka:
Initially, one uses emptiness to subdue delusions but does not sever the fetters; if the fetters were severed at this stage, there would be no merit from the six perfections.

This is the stage of the first asaṃkhyeya-kalpa. In the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, afflictions diminish and merits flourish. In the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, one correctly enters the provisional position.
This refers to those of inferior capacity. Those of middling capacity are able to transform sentient beings after two *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, and do not wait for three.

Those of superior capacity recognize the true principle (*tattva*) at the very moment they first resolve their minds; for the sake of delivering others, they do not seek personal cessation or realization. They enter the provisional immediately and do not proceed to the second stage.

Regarding the stages of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*), some say that one severs the fetters up to the seventh ground before practicing the emergence into the provisional; however, this is logically incorrect.
