However, the Buddha distinguished three capacities. Those of inferior capacity must exhaust their afflictions before they can emerge into the provisional (conventional) realm. Those of middling capacity can enter the provisional as soon as they sever the delusions of views.
Those of superior capacity realize that both views and thoughts are empty from the very first moment of the path;

having already become a place of reliance for sentient beings, how could they wait until the seventh stage to emerge into the provisional? This is illustrated by the analogy of the great bird falling and dying found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Upon investigation...

This can be taken as evidence. For those of inferior faculties in the Separate Teaching, they enter the provisional [truth] through cultivation after the ten abidings; it is only upon the merits of the ten practices that [the function] arises.

Those of middling faculties enter the provisional [truth] at the very first thought of the ten abidings; having once received it, they do not regress and are immediately able to manifest its application.

Those of superior faculties and initial resolve realize that all meritorious qualities are like illusions and transformations; they do not stagnate in names and thus immediately enter the provisional.

In the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), when the six sense organs are purified, one perceives and hears the phenomena of the ten realms, and the six organs function interchangeably.

One immediately enters the stage of the provisional (the conventional). Furthermore, when disciples of the five ranks correctly practice the six perfections, they immediately enter the stage of the provisional;
it is not necessary to wait until the stage of the six faculties. Moreover, for a beginner who contemplates the three truths in their totality, how could they not be entering the provisional?

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that upon first sitting at the site of enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening and turns the wheel of the Dharma—this is precisely the meaning of entering the provisional. How could this depend on the five ranks? Indeed.
The Bodhisattva originally does not long for emptiness; rather, they cultivate emptiness for the sake of sentient beings. Because they do not long for it, they do not abide in emptiness;

because they seek to deliver others, they must emerge from the provisional. Thus, there arises that which emerges from the true: responding to the Dharma-eye and responding to the capacities of beings.

Whether it be through the body of a Buddha or even through the bodies of devas, ghosts, or spirits, they manifest in accordance with what is appropriate, preaching the Dharma for them and bringing them to fulfillment.

"Purifying the Buddha-lands" refers to the vast benefit of the merit achieved through emerging into the provisional realm. The "emerging into the provisional" of the Tripiṭaka masters consists of tainted supernatural powers (*sāsrava-abhijñā*);

it is not the true arising of response [to beings], nor is it the discernment of worldly wisdom, nor is it the clarity of the Dharma-eye. Although it benefits sentient beings, it does not bring them to fulfillment;
although it performs the work of a Buddha, it is by no means the purification of a land. This is merely a partial teaching, and its benefit is exceedingly slight.

If one follows the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), one relies solely on the two truths to recognize the illness, yet does not deeply recognize the medicine nor extensively apply mental attention. Consequently, supernatural powers may suddenly appear only to vanish;
while providing temporary minor benefit, they do not constitute true accomplishment. By dissolving the body to enter emptiness, one does not reach a pure Buddha-land.

In the Separate Teaching (Biejiao), the ten practices (shixing) of entering the conventional share the same efficacy as the Shared Teaching. Upon ascending to the stages (bhūmi), one attains a single body that is immeasurable in extent, remaining profoundly serene.

One should respond to all beings, exhausting the very source of their illnesses and reaching the depths of the treasury of medicines. Responding spontaneously and perfectly, there is none who does not receive benefit;

thus, one establishes a pure Buddha-land. This is the case for those at the ten stages and the stage of Equal Enlightenment; even those at the first dwelling of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) are already capable of doing so.
If one grasps this principle, then by distinguishing the four types of persons who emerge into the provisional (chujia), the true and the false will naturally be discerned. Otherwise, it is not so.
Furthermore, Māra is also able to manifest a form free from outflows (*anāsrava*), transforming himself like a Buddha and preaching all dharmas;
even with the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and worldly wisdom, there is nothing he cannot do. How could one recognize him without this Seal of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*)?

Moreover, the methods of contemplation previously recorded are repetitive and cause many people to become confused; I shall now directly summarize them according to my own understanding. Prior to the emergence of true realization, in accordance with whatever...
Adherence to views—whether of hundreds, thousands, or tens of millions of kinds—is all termed "view. It is like a blind man asking about milk;
since he does not see the color of the milk, what does it matter to him whether it is a rope or a pestle? Such views are merely the products of delirious speech; a view is itself a mere convention.

Therefore, one must examine and dismantle them by traversing through their single, dual, and complete forms. To dismantle them until they are exhausted is called "universal dismantling" (*paryādāna*). Furthermore, this is how "universality" is discussed in terms of words and letters.
The mind, however, is not so. Generally speaking, seeing and thinking are themselves ignorance (*avidyā*); ignorance is itself the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).

When ignorance is shattered, one sees the dharma-nature and enters the emptiness of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*); only then is it called "universal shattering of dharmas. The same applies to the universal shattering from emptiness into the provisional (*prajñapti*).
Before the Dharma-eye has been awakened, although one may discern and perceive various aspects, this is not yet called "shattering" [ignorance].
When the six sense faculties are purified, one understands a single phrase and penetrates all phrases, receiving and upholding everything taught by all Buddhas at once;

this is called "shattering through semblance-ignorance. Only when subsequently illuminating both truths simultaneously is it called "universal shattering. To state the essentials: this is the sequential shattering.

If one were to do so, there would be things not universally encompassed. To refute [the opponent] without following a sequential order constitutes universal refutation. The two preceding contemplations clarify this refutation; it is exhausted here. Regarding the universal refutation of phenomena through the correct contemplation of the Middle Way, as explained below, there are four points:

first, the intent of practicing the Middle Way contemplation; second, the conditions for practicing the Middle Way contemplation; third, the actual practice of the Middle Way contemplation; and fourth, the result of the practice. △ Third, clarifying the universal refutation of phenomena through the correct contemplation of the Middle Way, there are four meanings.

First, the intent of practicing the Middle Way contemplation. Second, the conditions for practicing the Middle Way contemplation. Third, the actual practice of the Middle Way contemplation. [Fourth, the result of the practice. (The fourth point follows.)

Fourth, the stage of clarity. The Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka exclusively employ worldly wisdom to illuminate the conventional; the followers of the Two Vehicles employ the analysis of the provisional to enter the real; and for the Buddha, the two truths are fully perfected.
The third contemplation is merely a provisional hypothesis to depart from the two views of existence and non-existence; in reality, there is no Middle Way principle to be contemplated.

In the Shared Teaching, the followers of the Two Vehicles realize the provisional to enter the real, while the Bodhisattvas, out of compassion, enter the provisional; this applies only to the Buddha-way.

Regarding the contemplation of the two streams (*dvayadhārā*): although there is no distinct principle to be contemplated therein, it bears the name of the Middle Way—which is like an illusion or a transformation, neither arising nor ceasing.
By means of connecting the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*) to the Shared Teaching, it likewise possesses the significance of the Middle Way.

If the Distinct Teaching employs the Two Truths, it takes the Middle Way as the Truth (*satya*) and existence and non-existence as the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). If it employs the Three Truths, the meaning of the Middle is self-evident. However, regarding these two modes of contemplation...

This serves as the skillful means (*upāya*) for the Middle Way. It is not so in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*); from the very first moment of the mind, one cultivates the three contemplations (*sanguan*), and there is no sequence between what is destroyed and what is realized.
For this reason, it is necessary to clarify the third contemplation. Next, there are four causes and conditions for cultivating the Middle Contemplation (*zhongguan*):
first, unconditional compassion (*wuyuan cibei*). This compassion is of the same essence as true reality (*shixiang*); because it does not grasp at sentient beings, it is called "unconditional."

It is not a view of attachment; it does not grasp at nirvana, and therefore it is not empty stillness. That which is not empty stillness is not the compassion based on dharmas (*dharmālambana-maitrī*);

that which is not a view of attachment is not the compassion based on sentient beings (*sattvālambana-maitrī*). As the Great Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata’s compassion is called unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*)."
This is the great mass of compassion; this is true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata.
If one wishes to cultivate this compassion, how can it be attained if one abandons Madhyamaka? To fulfill the two [accumulations], one first makes the four vows, which are equal to space.

The contemplation of emptiness and conventionality involves knowing suffering, severing the origin, cultivating the path, and realizing cessation; yet, regarding the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it is not yet fully perfected.

If, however, it is the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*), then one knows all suffering, severs the origin within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), cultivates the unsurpassed path, and realizes ultimate cessation.
To fulfill this vow, one practices the third contemplation. Third is the seeking of the Buddha’s wisdom;
this is the knowledge of the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-encompassing wisdom) and the vision of the Buddha-eye. Such vision and wisdom cannot be accomplished without the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*).

Fourth is the study of great skillful means (*upāya*); this is the Tathāgata’s effortless expedient and boundless application. Abiding in the *śūraṅgama-samādhi*, there is no seed that is not [cultivated].

The *Sūtra* states: "Furthermore, by means of diverse skillful expedients (*upāya*), one assists in manifesting the primary meaning. In the cultivation of the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*), causes and conditions are not unitary;

I have merely cited four points as examples. Next is the actual cultivation of the Middle Way. This contemplation directly destroys ignorance (*avidyā*). Since ignorance is utterly severed, how can it be contemplated?

For instance, when first contemplating reality (*tattva*), reality has no spatial location; one simply contemplates the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the three types of provisional existence (*prajñapti*).
The delusion of these four propositions is skillfully resolved; when the outflow-free state (anāsrava) arises, it is called "seeing the truth.

Furthermore, observing that the wisdom of emptiness can render things non-empty gives rise to the Dharma-eye, which universally discerns the medicine and the disease; therefore, this is called "conventional observation" (parikalpita-vidarśana). Now, observing ignorance is likewise so.

The wisdom that contemplates the two [truths] is intended to destroy the two delusions; thus it is called "wisdom. However, when viewed from the perspective of the Middle Way, this wisdom is entirely delusion.

Because these delusions act as obstacles to Middle-Way wisdom, they are termed "obstructions to wisdom" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). To enter into these obstructions to wisdom is what is meant by being "within the obstructions to wisdom."
The obstruction of knowledge is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*). Now, one contemplates this ignorance in three ways: first, contemplating ignorance;
second, contemplating the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); and third, contemplating true conditions. Regarding what is called "contemplating ignorance":

when the two wisdoms of emptiness and the provisional correspond with the mind, one then contemplates whether these two wisdoms arise from the nature of phenomena, arise from ignorance, arise from their combination, or arise from their separation.
If [the self] were derived from the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), then the nature of phenomena is without arising. If it were derived from ignorance (*avidyā*), then ignorance is unreal.

Whether they are conjoined or separated, both principles are untenable. Thus it is extensively refuted, as explained above in the section on "Conditioned Arising through Causes" (*hetusamutpanna-prajñapti*). When one contemplates in this manner:
It is utterly pure and serene. Both the observer and the observed are like empty space; there is no clinging to the four propositions, and one is free from the faults of the two extremes.
Furthermore, there is neither that which ceases nor that which is ceased, reaching the fundamental source and abiding in great tranquility.

It is neither cessation nor non-cessation, neither contemplation nor non-contemplation. This is precisely contemplating ignorance while practicing the Middle Way within the Middle. Moreover, this wisdom...

The hindrances consist of three provisional [categories] and four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). These four propositions constitute the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*). One contemplates by means of this gate; through faith in the Dharma, one turns back [from delusion].

As previously stated regarding what is called "contemplating the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*): first, one employs the four-proposition contemplative wisdom to observe that hindrances are definitively unobtainable.

Alternatively, one may give rise to a certain kind of understanding and attain a certain kind of concentration. "Definitively" means that ignorance itself is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). As it is said:

This contemplation is not yet the awakening of the mind. One should immediately turn the observation to consider whether this nature arises from the cessation of ignorance, or arises from the non-cessation of ignorance, or arises from both cessation and non-cessation, or arises from neither cessation nor non-cessation.

Thus, regarding these four propositions, one should repeatedly reflect upon and investigate each one according to the Dharma. Although one has not yet attained awakening, one must nevertheless remain single-mindedly focused.
Cultivation. There is no other course. That which is called "contemplating true conditions" refers to contemplating this contemplative wisdom:

in dependence upon what does it receive its name? Is it wisdom, or is it non-wisdom? If one says that it attains great illumination by subsequently destroying delusion, then in relation to the present state, it is ignorance.

Regarding such illuminating wisdom, is it cultivation through conditions, is it true cultivation, or is it cultivation through the union of the true and the conditional? Or is it detached [cultivation]?

Cultivation by means of conditions (*pratyaya-bhāvanā*). If it is cultivation by means of conditions, since those conditions are impermanent, how could the permanent arise? If it is true cultivation (*tattva-bhāvanā*), what is there for the truth to cultivate?
Some say that cultivation by means of conditions reveals true cultivation; others say that when cultivation by means of conditions ceases, the truth manifests of itself.

If it manifests by itself, it belongs to self-arising; if it manifests through conditions, it belongs to other-arising; if both are combined, it is co-arising; and if they are separated, it is causeless.
These four [positions] together constitute obstacles. If one is free from attachment, all four can be understood. When meeting with specific capacities and conditions, all four may be taught;

thus the sūtras and śāstras differ according to the conditions they address. Sometimes it is said that the permanent arises from the impermanent, because this [impermanent] cause is itself impermanent...

The fruit is eternal. Furthermore, it is said that *eranda* produces sandalwood; or that one is born from the lineage of the Dharma King; or that by extinguishing ignorance, one attains the lamp of bodhi;
or that this wisdom is attained neither through internal nor external observation. These various divergent explanations ultimately converge upon a single truth.

Since ancient times, disputants have contended with one another, each creating their own obstructions. Using this interpretation, [the ice... The clouds of affliction melt away. Holding this Dharma-seal, what dharma would not be in accord? What is called "relying on the meaning and not on the words" refers precisely to this intent.
Someone may ask: "If ignorance is itself the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and the nature of phenomena is itself ignorance, then when ignorance is destroyed, is the nature of phenomena destroyed?
When the nature of phenomena is revealed, is ignorance revealed? The answer is: In truth, there is no name; it is only in contrast to ignorance [that the nature of phenomena is designated].
It is called "dharma-nature" (dharmatā). When dharma-nature manifests, ignorance is transformed into clarity; when ignorance is destroyed, there is no longer any ignorance.

Toward whom, then, could one further establish "dharma-nature"? Furthermore, it was asked: "If ignorance is itself dharma-nature, and there is no longer any ignorance, with what else could it be identical?
The answer was: "It is like someone who does not recognize ice; they point to water and call it ice. This is merely a name. How could there actually be two things?"

The mutual identity of phenomena is indeed profound. It is like a single jewel that produces water when facing the moon and fire when facing the sun; yet when not so directed, there is neither water nor fire.
Though it is a single entity without difference, there arises the distinction between water and fire. The wise should attain understanding through this analogy.

Next is the stage of cultivating Madhyamaka. The preceding two types of *śamatha* serve as the skillful means of the Middle Way’s non-duality of both negation and affirmation; the two types of *vipaśyanā* serve as the skillful means of the dual illumination.
By means of this negation and illumination, one enters the Middle Way, where they naturally flow together and naturally illuminate each other.

There are three distinct locations for the cultivation of this dual flow: if one connects the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) to the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), it is discussed as "cultivation" in the seventh stage and "realization" in the eighth stage within the *Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra*. The Separate [Teaching]...

Regarding the teachings, the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) discuss cultivation, while ascending the stages (*bhūmi*) discusses realization. For one who cultivates in this manner, there is no distinction at the initial stage.

Now, we shall directly discuss the beginning of the five grades of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*): an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is immediately able to perform the perfect contemplation of the three truths (*tisraḥ satyaḥ*), cultivating emptiness within the midst of form.
The Tathāgata’s seat is the cultivation of the patience of cessation; the Tathāgata’s robe is the cultivation of the Buddha’s concentration and wisdom;
the Tathāgata’s adornment is the cultivation of unconditioned compassion; and the Tathāgata’s chamber is likewise [the cultivation of great kindness].

Entering in this manner, one reaches the stage of the six sense organs being purified in semblance and advances into the first dwelling (*prathamavihāra*), where one shatters ignorance. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* describes the merit of the first dwelling, saying: "Ultimately free from falsehood..."

Delusion-free, unstained like space, the pure and wondrous Dharma-body is serenely responsive to all things. Both fundamental afflictions and habitual tendencies are exhausted, leaving nothing remaining;

this is what is meant by "surpassing the Śramaṇas from the very beginning. From the first stage (*ādikarmika*) up to the first abode (*prathamavihāra*), this can be cultivated and realized within a single lifetime.
How could it wait for the seventh ground of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇavyākhyāna*) before being cultivated? This refers to the beginning of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekavyākhyāna*).

If one asks whether this constitutes realization on the [first] stage (*bhūmi*), it should be understood that this is a teaching of skillful means (*upāya*). The cultivation and realization of the Perfect [Teaching] constitute the ultimate reality.
As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Now I shall explain for you the most ultimate truth. This is precisely that meaning.

Having previously completed the general refutation of the two preceding contemplations, we now proceed with the Middle Way contemplation, which contemplates ignorance (*avidyā*) and the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) without relying on the two extremes or the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
It is ultimately pure. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "I prostrate to the one who is like space, having no dependence. When this wisdom opens wide, all things are shattered;
therefore, it is called "universal shattering" (*pòbiàn*). Furthermore, regarding "one gate is all gates":

if one shatters [the truth] universally through a single gate, then one also attains its shattering through all gates. The eight gates of the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* refer to non-arising and non-ceasing.
Neither eternal nor annihilated; neither identical nor different; neither coming nor going.

In various sutras, they are described as neither existent nor empty, neither defiled nor pure, neither abiding nor attached, neither bound nor liberated. These are immeasurable in number, yet one can penetrate them all.
As previously discussed in the single gate of "non-arising," it should be understood that this already encompasses the meaning of all gates. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says: "Not..."
Arising is not different; non-extinction is not identical. Non-arising is not eternal; non-extinction is not discontinuous.
Non-arising is not coming; non-extinction is not going. Non-arising is not defiled; non-extinction is not pure.
Non-arising is not increasing; non-extinction is not decreasing. Non-arising is not bound; non-extinction is not liberated.
Arising is non-existent; non-extinction is non-non-existent. Therefore, profound contemplation of neither-arising-nor-extinction is the meaning of all the gates.
If one contemplates the non-arising of the ten objects, such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*), each gate is likewise so.

If one contemplates the non-arising of the mind, it is like a master painter who creates the five aggregates and so forth, achieving the inconceivable, and even proceeding to the arousal of the mind of enlightenment.

The same applies to the mind and so forth across all gates. If one grasps this principle, then in explaining various sūtras and śāstras, word by word and meaning by meaning, there will be nothing that does not accord with it.
Why is this? If one uses this principle to explain the *Acarasūtra*, then all dharmas enter the gate of non-action (*acarya*).
If one explains the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, then they all enter the gate of non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhita*). And so on, even to a single...
All the sutras became suddenly clear and unobstructed; matters and principles were vast and expansive.
To raise one and follow from it—were it not for one who surveys with transcendent distance and penetrates deeply into the characteristics of dharmas, who could possibly participate in this?

Furthermore, as explained above, by means of the horizontal and vertical, the deep and the broad, all false attachments are shattered, all sutras and treatises are expounded, all contemplative practices are cultivated, and all capacities and conditions are accommodated, turning [the wheel of Dharma].
It is inexhaustible; such verbose discourse is difficult to perceive. Now, I shall summarize the essential points to reveal their true meaning:

if there is no gate of non-arising, even if things are layered a thousand or ten thousand times over, they are merely phenomena produced by the causes and conditions of a single thought-moment of ignorance—immediately empty, immediately provisional, and immediately the Middle Way.

The three truths and three contemplations are merely the seeds of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). To explain this briefly: it is simply through a single thought-moment of ignorance that one cultivates these various dharmas.
Having already sequentially and comprehensively heard [the teachings on] the horizontal and vertical aspects, one now hears how dharmas arise from the single mind;
this immediately transcends all aforementioned dharmas produced by sequential causes and conditions, and one directly perceives the inconceivable arising of dharmas through causes and conditions.

Regarding the Dharma: previously, one heard of the various emptinesses (*śūnyatā*) in their sequential order; now, hearing that the single mind is empty, one transcends all the meanings of emptiness explained above.

One anticipatorily realizes the wondrous, inconceivable emptiness. Regarding the various provisional designations (*prajñapti*) clarified previously: now, hearing that the single mind is itself provisional, one transcends the provisional designations of the sequential stages mentioned above.
One anticipatorily realizes the provisional designations of the dual illumination of the two truths (*satyadvaya*). Now, hearing that it is neither empty...
The provisional. All the various emptinesses transcending the provisional are not empty; all the various provisionalities are not provisional.

Furthermore, within the views of the simple, the compound, and the complete as they are conceptually differentiated, there is neither existence nor non-existence. Within the Tripitaka, the Shared, and the Distinct [teachings], there is neither existence nor non-existence.

Now, hearing that there is neither existence nor non-existence, one realizes that everything transcending the provisional is neither existent nor non-existent. This is known by transcendence and is beyond thought.
The deliberation concludes that the Middle Way is neither existent nor non-existent. These three truths are understood within a single mind.

To speak in terms of ultimate reality, this single mind is itself emptiness, provisionality, and the middle. This applies equally to the three contemplations, the three wisdoms, the three cessations, and the three eyes. It is just like this.

One who contemplates in this manner is itself a sentient being who opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*). Contemplation is called the Buddha’s knowledge; cessation is called the Buddha’s vision.

When this contemplation is accomplished, it is called the first stage, the Stage of Rejoicing (*anumodanā-parivarta*). Reciting and upholding it so that this contemplation becomes increasingly clear constitutes the second stage.

Explaining it according to one's practice constitutes the third stage. Practicing it while concurrently performing the merit of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) so that the merit becomes increasingly profound constitutes the fourth stage.
Chapter: Having fully practiced the six perfections such that both principle and phenomena are without deficiency, one completes the fifth stage.

One then enters the purification of the six sense faculties and advances to break through the stages of the forty-two grounds of ignorance; this is called the retribution of purity. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* refers to this as the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

When the object accords with wisdom and wisdom accords with the object, from the perspective of the object it is the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*), and from the perspective of wisdom it is the Retribution Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). This is according to its function.

This refers to the *saṃbhogakāya*, which is endowed with permanence, bliss, self, and purity; all of this is stated in reference to the contemplation of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
The same applies to the remaining aggregates, bases, and elements. This concludes the universal method for breaking through phenomena by contemplating the aggregates, bases, and elements.
To discern what is permeable and what is obstructed is also called knowing gain and loss, and it is also called knowing the letter and the non-letter.

Since the various attachments have already been thoroughly refuted, one should immediately penetrate into the unborn (*anutpāda*). If one does not enter therein, then there is still something obstructing or adhering to one.

If one is like the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who are attached to the wisdom that contemplates emptiness, one should use the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) to universally refute both the refuter and the refuted, so as to cause all beings...
If one does not cling to the wisdom of emptiness, then one can destroy what is not as it appears, merely destroying obstructions while preserving passability.
If this is so, one is a great guide who well understands both obstructions and passability; leading the multitude, one is able to traverse five hundred yojanas.
Regarding the "five hundred *yojanas*": in terms of lands, the three realms of retribution constitute three hundred;

the land of skillful means with remainder and the land of true reward and non-obstruction together constitute five hundred. In terms of afflictions, the views and thoughts of the three realms constitute three hundred;
the afflictions of dust and sand constitute four hundred; and ignorance constitutes five hundred. In terms of contemplative wisdom, it is as follows:

The wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*) knows three hundred; the wisdom of the conventional (*prajñapti-jñāna*) knows four hundred; the middle wisdom (*madhya-jñāna*) knows five hundred. The explanations of various masters are confused and inconsistent, and thus none of them are accepted.

Now, regarding *yojana*s in this treatise, there are those that are horizontally obstructed or unobstructed, and those that are vertically obstructed or unobstructed. As for the horizontal, it is fully explained in terms of three dharmas:

suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) constitute obstruction; the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*) constitute passage. The twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) constitute obstruction; [the first link,] ignorance (*avidyā*), [is the point of entry].

The equal cessation [of afflictions] constitutes the passage. The six obscurations constitute the blockage. The six perfections constitute the passage. Regarding the vertical alignment of passages and blockages: the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and the birth-and-death of limited segments (*paricchinna-bhava*) constitute the blockage;
the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) constitutes the passage. The birth-and-death of ignorance regarding skillful means (*upāya*) constitutes the blockage;

the contemplation of entering the conventional from emptiness (*śūnyatā*) constitutes the passage. The birth-and-death caused by the conditions of ignorance (*avidyā-pratyaya*) and so forth constitute the blockage; the correct contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*) constitutes the passage.
Penetration. Now, one should observe penetration and obstruction by interweaving the horizontal and the vertical.

Just as entering emptiness destroys all views and afflictions (*kleśa*), so too must one not grasp or cling to the delusions of views and afflictions, which are fundamentally defiled and turbid. To claim "this is right" or "that is wrong" gives rise to various fetters and karmic actions.

Falling into the cycle of birth and death, one perceives only suffering and its origin, but does not perceive the path and its cessation. Not understanding these Four Noble Truths is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because ignorance is not extinguished, one clings firmly and cannot relinquish [these views]; thus, remaining only on this shore and failing to reach the other shore, it is called an obstruction.
If one knows that the mind has no intrinsic nature, then karma will not arise. Without karma, there is no fruit; this is called the Path. This is the Path.
Therefore, there is cessation. If ignorance ceases, then old age and death cease. One is able to relinquish all modes of existence (*bhava*) and reach the further shore.

Examining each and every moment of mind, and each instance of subject and object: if the three obstructions arise, shatter them so they become permeable; if the three permeabilities exist, nurture them until they are perfected. Thus one transcends the obstructions of views and afflictions.
Next, one again contemplates the permeability and obstruction of the contemplation that enters the provisional from emptiness.
This refers to all illnesses, all medicines, and the methods for administering medicine. One clearly recognizes and understands the conditions and the means (*upāya*) for each individual phenomenon.

Whenever there is an obstruction, one breaks it open to allow passage, thereby transcending the blockage of ignorance. Next, one further examines within this state whether there is penetration or obstruction regarding the Middle Way.

Regarding each phenomenon, such as the dharma-nature of ignorance, its true conditions, and so forth, one likewise employs the truths, conditions, and liberations to break through obstructions and allow for penetration;

thus, the obstruction of ignorance is broken, and one penetrates the five hundred *yojanas*. Furthermore, from the very first moment of the mind, it is already in correspondence with the three contemplations.
One is precisely three; to penetrate this with unimpeded clarity is for the initial mind to be able to traverse five hundred *yojanas*.

Yet, penetration exists only in contrast to obstruction; where there is no obstruction, there is no penetration. To penetrate that which is non-penetrating is true penetration. If one does not accord with this, [it is not so].
Conversely, when ignorance regarding the origin of suffering arises, one should carefully contemplate that which can destroy [ignorance] as being like that which is destroyed.

Regarding each dharma, each capacity, and each object, one realizes that each is simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle Way, fully possessing the truths, the conditions, and the perfections.
This is called "neither penetration nor obstruction, illuminating both penetration and obstruction. This is called "knowing letters and non-letters," and knowing gain and loss within the unarisen.
The opening and closing of the gates is thus; it is the same for the remaining gates.
Regarding the harmonization of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*): each and every one of the thirty-seven factors is itself a site of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

A single category, the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), pervades all the categories, and all the categories likewise pervade the foundations of mindfulness. Furthermore, by practicing the foundations of mindfulness, one can give rise to right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*). Right effort...

One develops the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). From the bases of psychic power arise the five faculties (*indriya*); from the five faculties arise the five powers (*bala*); from the five powers arise the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*);
and from the seven factors of enlightenment one enters the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). Such sequential arising is called "skillful adaptation.

Although the practitioner has previously fully recognized the points of penetration and obstruction within the horizontal and vertical dharmas, they have not yet encountered the ultimate truth; therefore, one must now employ the Path.
One cultivates these factors and brings them into harmony. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The thirty-seven factors are the dharmas for practicing the Path. Someone may ask:
"The factors of the Path (*mārga-aṅga*) are the Dharma of the Two Vehicles; how can they be the Path of a Bodhisattva? The answer is: Not so. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"The factors of the Path are spiritual friends; through them, one achieves perfect enlightenment. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* also says: "One who is able to contemplate the Eightfold Noble Path..."

One then perceives the Buddha-nature. Now, the Truth of the Path consists of four aspects; thus, these factors of the path (mārga-aṅga) may be with outflows (sāsrava), without outflows (anāsrava), or both with and without outflows.

The texts and meanings of the various teachings traversed differ; here, we clarify only the meaning of the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskāra) factors of the path as constituting the principle of the threefold contemplation within one mind.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "One who wishes to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness by means of all modes... is...
The Dharma-realm encompasses all phenomena and all destinies; yet these destinies do not transcend the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). As the *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"All kinds of characteristics and essential natures are, in their entirety, a single kind of characteristic and essential nature—namely, the characteristic and essential nature of the Buddha-seed.

Now, when a single thought-moment arises, the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) of the ten realms appear without mutual obstruction: one form is all forms, and all forms are one form.
A single form is neither one nor all; it simultaneously illuminates both the one and the all. The forms of the nine dharma-realms are likewise so.

This is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). This applies equally to sensation (*vedanā*), mind (*citta*), and phenomena (*dharma*). Such foundations of mindfulness encompass the meanings of both the Small and Great Vehicles.
Both [extremes] destroy the eight inversions; both manifest flourishing and decay; both negate flourishing and decay. Thus, one enters parinirvāṇa in the very midst [of these]. Why is this so?
Form is truly not pure, yet ordinary beings falsely reckon it to be pure. It is truly not impure, yet those of the Two Vehicles falsely reckon it to be impure.
Both are inversions. Now, observing that form is itself emptiness, within emptiness there is no purity; how then could one be stained?

This is the overturning of the delusions of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), whereby the "withered" stage of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is established. Furthermore, form (*rūpa*) is itself provisional; since provisional designations are infinite, how could one be obstructed by emptiness?

To dismiss it by calling it impure is the overturning of the delusions of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), whereby the "flourishing" stage of the foundations of mindfulness is established.

This is called the simultaneous overturning of the eight inversions, wherein both the withered and the flourishing are established together. It is not empty, therefore it is not withered; it is not provisional, therefore it is not flourishing. Boundless and without limit.
The middle is called the intermediate. Thus, *nirvāṇa* is called the secret treasury.

This applies even to feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, the mind that is neither permanent nor impermanent, and phenomena that are neither self nor non-self; both negation and affirmation are established, and the meaning is likewise in all such cases.
The wisdom that contemplates the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is called mindfulness (*smṛti*). The single truth and the three truths are called the locus (*sthāna*).

All things are emptiness; all delusions, flourishing, and decay are without exception empty. All things are provisional (*upāya*); the two extremes and the twin trees are without exception provisional.

All things are the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*); there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and there is nothing that is not real. From beginning to end, it is fully complete; there is no need to further cultivate other dharmas.
If one cannot enter [the practice] in this way, one should attach the names and meanings from other chapters to form a method of contemplation, using it to discipline and harmonize oneself.
One may infer the rest by analogy; they need not be detailed here again.

Regarding the remedies for the path: those practitioners whose obstacles are light and whose faculties are sharp enter the three gates of liberation within the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
However, for those of dull faculties whose afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are heavy, their contemplation of the mind is destroyed as soon as it is established;

such individuals must therefore discuss the application of remedies. When practicing samādhi, if stinginess and greed suddenly arise, one should employ the practice of giving (*dāna*) as the remedy. [Likewise,] regarding the breaking of precepts...
When the mind arises [with afflictions], one should use ethical discipline (*śīla*) as the remedy. When anger erupts, one should use patience (*kṣānti*) as the remedy.

When there is negligence and dissipation, one should use diligence (*vīrya*) as the remedy. When there is distraction and instability, or when delusion and darkness increase, one should use meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as the remedies.

According to the severity of the illness, whether by means of phenomena or principles, through direct confrontation or transformation, one should extensively apply these across various teaching gates.
These are accomplished through the skillful means of the six perfections and the *siddhānta*. The efficacy of their remedial function is limited by the entry into principle (*tattva*).

Furthermore, the profound contemplation of these auxiliary dharmas is itself inconceivable; they encompass all phenomena, even to the point where there is neither a remedy nor that which is to be remedied.
This meaning is evident.

Regarding the knowledge of successive stages: it has been cautioned since ancient times that those who have not yet attained realization claim to have attained it. How much more so now, when the Sage is far removed and there is no standard by which to judge?
To follow one's own mind and consider oneself correct, recklessly comparing oneself to the sages and saints, leads to self-delusion and the delusion of others;

the resulting faults and calamities are boundless. For the sake of such people, I shall again clarify the stages within the sequence of practice. "Stages" refers here to the three baskets (Tripitaka), as well as the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect [teachings], including the Middle Way.
The stage of "semblance" (*sāmantaka*) has already been briefly discussed within the previous refutation of the provisional; it need not be recorded here at length again.
As for "patience" (*kṣānti*): generally, that which is clear is difficult to obscure, and that which is eloquent is difficult to silence.

If one possesses internal wisdom and understanding yet externally conceals one's traces, practicing in secret, one can quickly enter this stage. Otherwise, praise will spread abroad and verbal proliferation will flourish.
This will cause one's own practice to decline and greatly increase obstacles to the Path. Therefore, one must remain settled and endure it;
one should vow to sever [external ties], dwell in solitary seclusion, and deeply cultivate samādhi. Furthermore, even if there are no external conditions, internal obstacles may arise spontaneously;

in such cases, one should employ the four modes of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* to regulate and protect [the mind]. Thus, there will be no danger of falling back or regressing. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Immeasurable people have resolved upon Bodhi..."
"Grasping at the mind" refers precisely to this: falling mostly into the stages of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
As for "those without craving for dharmas," it means that when a practitioner cultivates the nine superior dharmas and transcends internal and external obstacles, they ought to realize the truth;

yet, if they do not realize it, it is because they dwell in attachment due to craving for dharmas. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* calls this "falling from the summit. Now, if a person on the Path does not reach [the goal] even after ten thousand attempts...

This. Upon reaching this point, protection is successfully accomplished. Regarding "falling from the crown" (*mūrdha-pāta*): it refers to this stage where, due to the craving for the Dharma (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), one neither advances nor retreats.

If one transcends this, one enters the three gates of liberation and abides in the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which is also called the patience of cessation (*nirvāṇa-kṣānti*).
Through the *śūraṅgama* [samādhi] and the play of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-vikrīḍita*), only Buddhas with Buddhas can act in this way. Now, as for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*:
The skillful means are brought to a conclusion at this point. These ten kinds of dharmas are called the Mahāyāna contemplation. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"He gave each of his sons an equal great carriage. Those carriages were high and broad, adorned with various jewels, surrounded by railings, with bells suspended on all four sides.
Furthermore, canopies were spread above them, decorated with rare and miscellaneous treasures and precious cords."
Interlaced with hanging flower tassels, layered with fine mats and cushions, and provided with crimson pillows;
drawn by white oxen whose coats are pure and clean, whose forms are beautiful, who possess great strength, whose gait is level and upright, and who move as swiftly as the wind;
accompanied by many attendants and guards—so too is the Mahāyāna of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the Great Vehicle of the equality of true reality.
It penetrates the source of the three truths—this is its height. It encompasses the ten dharma realms—this is its breadth. The immeasurable factors of the path are its various jewels.

That which blocks obstructions and allows passage is its balustrade. The eloquent proclamation of the four analytical knowledges is its hanging bells. Great compassion covering all universally is its canopy.
The dharmas of the ten powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities are its ornaments. Sustained by great vows, it is its jeweled cords.

The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) that gladden beings are like flower garlands. The various dhyānas and samādhis are like layered carpets. The four gates through which one returns to the source, wherein all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) come to rest, are the place of repose.

The right wisdom of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) that eliminates dark delusions is the great white silk. The right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*) that increase the wholesome and extinguish the unwholesome are the sturdy, clean [clothing].
The mastery of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) is the exquisite beauty. The five faculties (*indriya*) are firm and solid, which is to say, the sinews. The five...

The "powers" (bala) accomplish [the goal]; this refers to power. The "seven factors of awakening" (saptabodhyaṅga) are the forward progress; they are the steps. The "eightfold path" (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga) is secure and peaceful; it is level and upright.

Through patience and detachment from craving, one can swiftly give rise to the truth; it is as rapid as the wind. The "factors conducive to enlightenment" (bodhipakṣadharma) extensively encompass all dharmas.
It has many attendants. Such a precious vehicle is the Supreme Vehicle; it is the Tathāgata Vehicle. All Bodhisattvas ride this Dharma to reach the stage of the Tathāgata;
therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna Contemplation. Indeed, all dharmas are entirely the One Vehicle.
Wherever there is a mind, this vehicle is fully present; this is called the Vehicle of Principle (*li-cheng*). Up to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), it is termed "Ultimate Reality."
The wondrous enlightenment is the ultimate. Having attained this meaning, one passes through all objects; there is nothing that is not the inconceivable realm of reality.

Furthermore, regarding the practice of contemplating the aggregates (*skandhas*) as one encounters conditions and confronts objects, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In relation to conditions, there arises the agent;
in relation to sensory objects (*viṣaya*), there arises the experiencer. "Agent" refers to the six agents; "experiencer" refers to the six experiences. Now, I shall explain this briefly.

As previously analyzed regarding the ten dharmas, one first contemplates them in relation to movement. By "movement," one may understand walking, standing, sitting, lying down, speaking, and remaining silent.

Now, this movement is a dharma of form (*rūpa*); form is set in motion by the mind. This mind that relies upon form is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). The experiencing of this movement is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*).
The conceiving of a self within this movement is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*). The performing of good or evil is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). [Movement...]

The mind within the center is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). When mental objects (*dharma*) correspond to the faculty of mind (*manas*), there are the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*).
This applies likewise to the eye, forms, mind, and mental objects. Thus, these aggregates, elements, and bases are all fully present in the space of a single raised footstep.

The aggregates are ignorance (*avidyā*); ignorance is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); the nature of phenomena is the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). All phenomena converge upon mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and there is no convergence beyond this.
It is one yet many, without mutual obstruction; this is called the inconceivable realm within practice. When one penetrates this realm, compassion and wisdom arise together.
One knows that all classes of living beings are none other than the One Vehicle, yet they are deluded by the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*).
I vow to shatter these delusions and become a refuge for all beings; thereafter, I shall settle my mind in samādhi and prajñā, using stillness to illuminate.

Furthermore, I shall universally shatter the obstacles of the three truths—view-delusion, thought-delusion, ignorance, and nescience. Moreover, I shall skillfully discern what is permeable and what is obstructed.

I shall understand how the factors of the path serve as antidotes and aids within practice, distinguish the stages and ranks of the sages and worthies within practice, and subdue [the afflictions] within practice.

Free from internal and external hindrances and without giving rise to attachment to dharmas, one enters the stage of the Copper Wheel (*tāmracakra*) by means of these ten dharmas and realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Whether lifting or lowering the feet, one proceeds from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and abides in the Buddha-dharma. Furthermore, regarding the contemplation based on the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*):

the eye and form arising in a single thought-moment are themselves the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle Way. To illumine emptiness is wisdom (*prajñā*).
The eye: illuminating the provisional is the Dharma-eye; illuminating the middle is the Buddha-eye. Thus, a single eye has two functions.

When the eye enters through the nose, it arises from the nose; when the nose enters through the eye, it arises from the eye. Though moving, it is quiescent; though quiescent, it moves. This is the inconceivable eye.

My eye and the eyes of sentient beings are, in principle, without distinction. By giving rise to compassion, one fulfills the virtue of this eye. When the ten vehicles are fully realized, [this is accomplished].
This is the realization of the true eye. It is the same for all sense faculties, objects, and sensations. Indeed, it is not difficult to know; the difficulty lies solely in practice.
If one knows but does not act, it is like a snake harboring a jewel: though it possesses brilliance, what benefit does it bring to the snake?
(End of Volume Four, Original Edition)
*Śānding Zhiguan* (Excerpts and Determinations on Stopping and Contemplation), Middle Volume; *Śānding Zhiguan*, Lower Volume.
By Master [Huisi] of the Liang Dynasty.
Part Two of Correct Contemplation (Contemplating the Objects Arising Therefrom).

Second, regarding the contemplation of the objects of affliction: if a practitioner contemplates the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*) without awakening, it will not be appropriate for them.
Yet, by observing without ceasing, they instead stir up afflictions. It is like iron that has not been joined with fire; it remains merely black. But if it were joined with fire...
When combined, they blaze forth with intense heat. It is also like a flow of water that is not particularly swift; yet, if one strikes it with a wooden pole, turbulent waves immediately arise.

One should observe that the movement produced by the power of contemplation within the realm of afflictions is likewise to be viewed in this way. This consists of four parts: first, a brief discernment of its characteristics;
second, clarifying the causes and conditions; third, reconciling apparent discrepancies; and fourth, the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Regarding what are called the "characteristics":

The dharma of delusion and affliction distresses and harms the mind and consciousness. If one distinguishes between the *darśana-heya* (to be abandoned by insight) and *bhāvanā-heya* (to be abandoned by cultivation), there is a distinction between the sharp and the dull faculties.

However, the five sharp afflictions (*pañca-akuśala-mūla*) are not necessarily restricted to the *darśana-heya*; they also encompass the *bhāvanā-heya*. Likewise, the five dull afflictions are not necessarily restricted to the *bhāvanā-heya*;

they also encompass the *darśana-heya*. Now, let us distinguish them according to their stages: if one has not yet developed meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), although one may possess worldly wisdom, the perceptions associated with the *darśana-heya* remain weak.

There are ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that belong to the dull category. If they arise from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the mind of view is intense and powerful; all such ten underlying tendencies belong to the sharp category.
What is being examined here refers only to those that arise when concentration has not yet been attained. Those arising from concentration will be explained further below.
However, if one were to expand upon these categories of sharp and dull, their number would be infinite; for now, they are collectively designated as four divisions.
The three poisons manifest predominantly as the three divisions. When they manifest equally, it is called "equal-part" (*samabhāga*).

If these are abandoned within the realm [of desire] by those who share the path with the Two Vehicles, they are called "universal afflictions" (*paryavasthāna*). If they are outside the realm, they are not abandoned by the Two Vehicles and are thus called "particular afflictions" (*pakṣika*).

If one establishes their mutual relationship, the particular afflictions are the root and the universal afflictions are the branches. One attains true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*) to sever the branches, and attains middle wisdom (*madhyamajñāna*) to sever the root. If...
If spoken of in terms of the inconceivable, there is no further distinction between the general and the specific. Next, the causes and conditions for the arising of afflictions are discussed;
there are three: first, the seeds of habitual causes; second, the impelling force of karma; and third, that which is fanned into being by Māra.

The activities of Māra are as explained elsewhere. One observes that which is moved by habitual tendencies; this is what is observed here. Next, the methods of treatment are discussed. In the Hīnayāna, there are five types of treatment:

counteractive (*pratipakṣa*), transformative (*parivarta*), non-transformative (*aparivarta*), combined (*miśra*), and complete (*sakala*). By applying these five types together with the wisdom of the Truths (*satyajñāna*), one enters the Real.
As for what is treated in the Mahāyāna, it is neither counteractive nor combined, and so forth; this is called the "treatment of the ultimate meaning" (*paramārtha-pratipakṣa*).
Just as the *agada* medicine can cure all illnesses, within emptiness and non-arising, who is afflicted and who is cured? What is combined with what, and what is transformed by what?

Next, regarding the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, there are likewise ten dharmas; furthermore, one must distinguish between the conceivable (*cintya*) and the inconceivable (*acintya*). As for the conceivable realm:
if one does not immediately restrain a single thought of desire, it will increase until it reaches the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes. This is called...
Afflictions lead to birth in the realm of hell because of the arising of desire; there, one no longer possesses propriety and ritual, nor does one know shame or modesty.

Birth in the realm of animals results from extreme stinginess and greed. Birth in the realm of hungry ghosts results from jealousy, envy, suspicion, and treachery. Birth in the realm of asuras results from seeking future desires while practicing present virtues.
Birth in the human realm results from the ten wholesome karmas and the aspiration for celestial desires. Birth in the heavenly realm results from contemplation.
Desire is the origin; the origin invites suffering. To weary of this accumulation of suffering and cultivate the Path to extinguish it constitutes the realm of the Śrāvaka.

Contemplating that desire and ignorance give rise to the twelve links of dependent origination, such that when ignorance ceases all conditions are stilled, constitutes the realm of the Pratyekabuddha.
Contemplating desire as an obscuration, one gives rise to various forms of compassion and practices the various perfections; this is the realm of the Six Perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā).

Contemplating desire as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wherein emptiness is itself *nirvāṇa*, constitutes the realm of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*). Contemplating these desires as the suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*) with their infinite characteristics, fully analyzed and complete, constitutes the realm of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*).
Such a sequence is termed the "realm of thought and deliberation. As for the "inconceivable" (*acintya*), it is the state of non-practice (*anabhisamskāra*).
The Sūtra says: "Lust is itself the Path; so too are hatred and delusion. Within these three dharmas, all the Buddha-dharmas are fully contained.
Although these four parts are indeed the Path, one must not follow them; for if one follows them, one will fall into the evil realms.
They are not to be severed; to sever them would constitute overweening pride (*adhimāna*). It is by not severing delusion and craving that one gives rise to various forms of clarity and liberation;
this is what is called the Way (*mārga*). Abiding in self-discipline is the way of the *śrāvaka*; abiding in lack of discipline is the way of the fool. The Bodhisattva is not like this:
they enter *nirvāṇa* without severing the afflictions (*kleśa*), purify the faculties without abandoning the five desires, and are born through non-arising. They do not...
Defiled by the phenomena of birth, they know emptiness yet do not realize it as empty; they are not realized through the dharma of emptiness.
This is what is meant by "not abiding in discipline and not abiding in non-discipline. The deluded and ignorant followers of the末法 (mofa / final age) fail to grasp this essential principle;

they openly practice what is unlawful while claiming to be unimpeded. As the Sūtra says: "One who is greedily attached to the dharma of non-obstruction is far from the Buddha, like the distance between heaven and earth."
In this way, it is called abiding in non-discipline; it is not that one does not abide [in discipline].

Furthermore, there are practitioners who, hearing of discipline and non-discipline, fear both extremes and seek only middle-way wisdom, waiting until these delusions are exhausted before they call it the Path. In this way, it is called abiding in discipline;
it is not that one does not abide [in discipline]. The World Teacher [the Buddha] is fully aware of these two errors, and being far removed from the principle, both are termed [delusions].
Obstruction. How could it have anything to do with non-obstruction? Thus, both being disciplined and not being disciplined are called "undisciplined. Why is this?
Because they are all merely ordinary sentiments and are not the conduct of the noble ones (ārya). Now, it is said that one does not abide in discipline, nor does one abide in non-discipline;
one does not abide in neither discipline nor non-discipline, nor does one abide in both discipline and non-discipline. Furthermore, one abides in discipline...
They abide in non-subjugation; they also abide in that which is neither subjugated nor unsubjugated; they also abide in both subjugation and non-subjugation. Why is this?
Because afflictions are themselves emptiness, they do not abide in non-subjugation. Because afflictions are themselves the conventional, [they abide in both].
One does not dwell in subduing, because afflictions are themselves the Middle Way. One does not dwell in both subduing and non-subduing, because one illuminates afflictions through their duality.
One does not dwell in neither subduing nor non-subduing. Furthermore, one dwells while not dwelling, and does not dwell while dwelling.
Why? Because one does not observe any single phrase in isolation; a single phrase is all phrases, and all dharmas converge therein.
Craving. Craving is that in which all phenomena reside. To realize its essence in this way is what is called "unimpeded.

That "all unimpeded people transcend birth and death via the single path"—this is precisely the meaning. If a single thought-moment of craving contains the hundred dharmas of the ten realms, though many, they do not exist as such;
though one, it is not non-existent. The many do not accumulate; the one does not disperse. The many are not different; the one is not identical. The many...

The one is precisely the many; the many are precisely the one. A sutra says: "In the darkness, the shadows of trees are not seen because of the darkness. When the divine eye sees them, this is 'light within darkness.
When the obstruction of ignorance is extremely blind and dark, this is 'darkness within light. It is also like a lamp and darkness coexisting;
thus, light and darkness do not obstruct each other, nor do they destroy each other. Why? Because there is a lamp in the room."
One does not know where the darkness goes; when the lamp is extinguished and darkness arises, one likewise does not know its point of origin. Seeking darkness, no darkness is found;

the light has nothing to destroy. Seeking light, no light is found; the darkness has nothing to cover. Although their substance cannot be apprehended, the destruction and covering are nonetheless manifest.
For this reason, it is called the inconceivable contemplation of the darkness of afflictions: that very darkness is the manifestation of great wisdom, the clarity of the Buddha’s Bodhi.
"Ti. When contemplating in this manner, one regrets one's own past transgressions and takes pity on sentient beings.

Why is this? In principle, there is neither light nor darkness; yet, due to delusion, the darkness of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) arises. Because the methods for liberation and treatment exist, there is the light of the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*). Taking this darkness as the basis, compassion (*karuṇā*) arises;
taking this light as the basis, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is born. Infinite great vows arise simultaneously with these objects. To fulfill these vows, one must necessarily [cultivate] the Great..."

Practice. Practice is precisely *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. If the eye of wisdom has not yet opened, one should thoroughly break through all points of stagnation so that all obstructions are cleared away.

Furthermore, employ the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) for harmonious adjustment, with the primary and auxiliary practices supporting one another. Use the successive stages to distinguish the true from the false, and use patient endurance (*kṣānti*) to dispel the web of hindrances.
Once the web of hindrances is dispersed, one can further refrain from generating attachment to dharmas; thus, one breaks through ignorance and accomplishes the state of non-arising.
Birth-endurance. Riding this precious vehicle, one proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). This is called the fourth part: possessing all dharmas while possessing afflictions.
It is also called practicing on non-paths while penetrating the Buddha-path. It is also called entering nirvana without severing afflictions.
Nirvana is Prajñā; Prajñā is the Tathāgata. The essence of the Tathāgata, the wisdom of the Tathāgata, and the function of the Tathāgata are equal and without distinction;
they cannot be fully detailed.
Third, regarding the contemplation of the realm of illness: To possess a body is itself a great affliction. Why is this?

It is like four snakes of differing natures, fire and water which are mutually opposed, a vessel of poison, and a heavy burden—a thicket of all sufferings. It is as if four kingdoms are neighbors; when their powers are equal, they may be temporarily at peace.
When one rides upon emptiness, one may launch an attack; the same applies to the cessation of the four great elements. There are two meanings of "sickness": first, actual sickness within the cause;

second, provisional sickness at the level of the fruit. If one reclines in Vaiśālī and propagates the teaching through illness, extensively discussing the sickness of the cause, there are three kinds of subduing.
If one extensively discusses the sickness of the fruit, there are four kinds of consolation. All of these are provisional applications for entering [the path].
The Dharma-gate of Illness: To provide relief from the affliction of sickness, one should understand that such illnesses as these are not what is being examined here.

What is being examined here is the body of karmic retribution, wherein the four great elements arise and function, obstructing the practice of the Noble Path. One must observe this [body] in order to quell its maladies.

Now, chronic illness and long-distance travel are obstacles to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Furthermore, there are those who are indolent while living at ease but, upon falling ill, arouse the resolve for awakening and are able to accomplish various tasks;
since karmic conditions differ, awakening may well occur through illness. For this reason, it is necessary to discuss the realm of illness.

Contemplating this, there are five [sections]: first, clarifying the symptoms of illness; second, clarifying the causes and conditions of the illness; third, clarifying the methods of treatment; fourth, clarifying the harms and benefits;
fifth, clarifying *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Now, the signs of the hundred illnesses cannot be fully investigated;

here we shall briefly state the symptoms of the illnesses of the five viscera. When the liver is ill, the pulse is full and straight. When the heart is ill, the pulse is light and floating. When the lungs are ill, the pulse...
Tight and sharp. When the kidneys are diseased, the pulse flows like a string of pearls. When the spleen is diseased, the pulse is slow and relaxed.

Furthermore, the characteristics of disease caused by earth, water, fire, and wind differ from one another; the way the vital energies of the organs harm one another also varies. A skilled physician must fully understand these matters;
this is called the "characteristics of disease. There are six causes for the arising of disease: either the four great elements (mahābhūta) are in disharmony, or...
Improper moderation in food and drink; or lack of regulation while practicing *dhyāna*; or being invaded by malevolent spirits (*yakṣa*); or the machinations of Māra;

or arising from past karma—these can be clearly known if they are inconsistent or unregulated. If one’s *dhyāna* is unregulated, or if one relies on arrogance and indolence, Māra will watch for his opportunity to cause pain in the joints and bones;
this ailment is called *zhù* (a piercing affliction) and is the most difficult to cure. If [this occurs] frequently...
Irregular breathing causes one to suffer from chronic fever and spleen disorders. Furthermore, there are eight tactile sensations that oppose the function of the breath and lead to illness.
When the mind unites with the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), there arise the four primary and four dependent tactile sensations:

inhalation accords with earth, being heavy; exhalation accords with wind, being light. Moreover, inhalation accords with water, being cold; exhalation accords with fire, being warm. Furthermore, inhalation...
The inhalation is moist and follows the earth; the exhalation is smooth and follows the wind. Furthermore, the inhalation is soft and follows the water;

the exhalation is coarse and follows the fire. If one exhales repeatedly while generating a heavy tactile sensation, and this sensation contradicts [the natural flow], it immediately results in illness.

The others are likewise. If one constantly fixes the mind on the lower part, the disease of excessive movement of the earth element arises; if on the upper part, the disease of excessive movement of the wind element arises.

Furthermore, if one fixes the mind with sudden intensity, the disease of excessive movement of the fire element arises; if one fixes the mind with excessive laxity, the disease of excessive movement of the water element arises.

One should observe that even the practitioner of seated meditation who engages in contemplation suffers much damage to the five viscera, which can be known through examination. Moreover, there are those whose contemplation is deviant, resulting in diseases of movement.

The objects of contemplation are not fixed; if the mind alternates between one object and another, it gives rise to conflict. Due to this conflict, the mind becomes distracted, resulting in the wind disorder (*vāta-vyādhi*).
Alternatively, if one fixates exclusively on a single object while sitting and awaiting success, internal heat will inevitably arise, resulting in the fire disorder (*tejas-vyādhi*).

Furthermore, if one perceives the arising of the mind as its ceasing, or its ceasing as its arising, the mind again becomes stagnant, resulting in the earth disorder (*pṛthivī-vyādhi*). Moreover, if one does not savor [the meditative state]...
One contemplates the object and forcibly applies [the remedy]; when water becomes excessive, it produces disease. Regarding those who fall ill due to ghosts:
formerly, there was a king who was afflicted by a ghost; he was repeatedly subjected to acupuncture and near death. The King of Ghosts came in person and resided upon his heart.

Confucian texts also speak of the two "Upright Ones" (Er Shu) at the *gao* and *huang* points. This is because when a person harbors depraved thoughts and seeks after depraved matters, the *Dhūmrā* ghost manifests.
It manifests as five colors and enters the five sense faculties of humans, shifting into the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) to provoke false understandings in people.
It may cause them to know matters of future fortune or misfortune; if not treated, it will eventually kill the person. Furthermore, regarding demonic afflictions (*māra-roga*):

while ghosts merely cause illness and kill, demons (*māra*) can destroy the contemplation of the mind (*citta-vipaśyanā*). When a practitioner is in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), if they harbor wrong thoughts regarding worldly gain, the demon then...
They arrive through the power of recollective manifestation (*anusmṛti-vikurvaṇa*). Upon arrival, they are received; once received, they become disease. Furthermore, regarding karmic diseases:
some are exclusively the result of past karma, while others arise when current violations of the precepts disturb past karma. For instance, the karma of killing results in liver and eye diseases;
the karma of drinking alcohol results in heart and mouth diseases; the karma of sexual misconduct results in kidney and ear diseases; and the karma of false speech results in spleen diseases.

Diseases of the tongue result from the karma of stealing; diseases of the lungs and nose result from the karma of [sexual misconduct]. If one maintains the precepts in this life, even the movement of such karma will result in illness.
What would have been a heavy retribution in hell is instead a light compensation in the human realm; this is an illness resulting from the exhaustion of karma. The power of karma is manifold;

one must carefully examine it and apply the appropriate remedy. Next, the methods of treatment are discussed. Regarding cold, heat, food, and drink, one should treat them according to the specific circumstances. As for sitting in meditation (*zuo-chan*):

If illness arises, one should instead use dhyāna to regulate the breath. If it is an illness caused by either spirits or demons, one should rely on powerful meditative power and great divine mantras to assist.

If it is an illness resulting from karma, one should employ internal contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) and external repentance to assist. Furthermore, regarding seated meditation, there are five methods of treatment:

namely, using cessation (*śamatha*), using the vital energy (*prāṇa*), using the breath (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*), using visualization (*saṃjñā*), and using contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Regarding "using cessation," there is a master who says:

Bind the mind within the navel, as small as a bean. Close the eyes and regulate the breath to maintain this focus. If, despite mindfulness, it is not seen, one should loosen one's clothing and look at it.
This can cure diseases and can also give rise to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). When performing this visualization, there may be pain or a sense of tension.
Whether cold or hot, such tactile sensations arise. By applying single-minded diligence to avoid these sensations, one gives rise to the various *dhyānas*.

When *dhyāna* arises, all ailments naturally depart, and the spirit and thoughts become tranquil; this is also called the "sign of the lightning-flash concentration" (*vidyut-pradīpa-samādhi-nimitta*).

One who practices this contemplation easily awakens to impermanence, is able to perceive impurity, is able to cease greedy desire, and accomplishes the gateway of the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). Furthermore, [regarding] the navel...
It serves as the *dantian* (elixir field), also called the Sea of Qi (*qihai*). When the qi is regulated, illness is naturally cured. Another master says:

for upper respiratory distress, chest pain, tightness in the back, mental agitation, and heat in the upper body, one should settle the mind in the *dantian*. The *dantian* is located two and a half inches below the navel.
If the pain is excruciating, shift the mind to the third finger from the little toe. If the pain still does not subside, shift it to the big toe; continue until the ailment is cured.
If there is a headache, redness of the eyes, fever in the mouth, deafness, or abdominal pain, then direct the mind to the space between the two feet and focus single-mindedly on that one object.
After a short while, the lower abdomen may become distended and tight; at that point, rest briefly and wait. If the illness...
If it does not cease, one should further imagine a great pit beneath one's feet and move the object of focus into that pit;

thus, one will naturally be cured. Furthermore, by fixing the mind on the feet, one can eliminate all illnesses; this is what is meant by "stopping as the remedy. Regarding the remedy of using the breath (*prāṇa*):
this refers to employing the breath during the process of exhalation and inhalation. If the illness is cold, use *cī* (blowing); if the illness is heat, use *hū* (shouting). As for the illness...

For wind, use *xi*; for pathogenic qi, use *he*; for phlegm and mucus, use *xu*; for fatigue and exhaustion, use *shi*, and so forth. These are what are called "treating with breath" (*qi*). Regarding "treating with respiration":
since form and mind are mutually dependent, there are inhalations and exhalations. The practitioner examines the strength or weakness of the breath to know whether the body is at ease or not;
one should discern and examine this accordingly. Generally, that which has sound is called "wind. If one maintains [the breath], then...

To disperse. That which is knotted and stagnant is called *qi* (vital energy); if one holds onto it, it becomes obstructed. That which enters and exits without completion is called *chuan* (labored breathing); if one holds onto it, it leads to exhaustion.
