That which is neither voiced nor stagnant, with both entry and exit flowing smoothly, is called *xi* (respiration); if one holds onto it, it leads to stability.

One should seek a quiet place and sit comfortably, close the eyes, and harmonize the body before employing this method. If treating illnesses caused by the mutual opposition of the eight tactile objects (*aṣṭaspraṣṭavya*), the earth element is formed through the heavy tactile object.

In cases of major illness, it is appropriate to employ exhalation predominantly as the remedy. If a sensation of lightness arises and results in a wind disorder (*vāta*), employ inhalation predominantly as the remedy.
If a sensation of cold arises and results in a water disorder (*ap*), employ exhalation predominantly as the remedy.

If a sensation of heat arises and results in a fire disorder (*tejas*), employ inhalation predominantly as the remedy. If the breath is regulated and balanced, then employ it according to one's preference. This is the application.

In the constant practice of counting the breaths (*gaṇanā*), if one were to employ various other mental visualizations (*parikalpa*) to direct the breath, such obscurations would be numerous and cannot be fully recorded here.

Furthermore, as for those who treat through visualization, it is like the method of using needles for treating tumors, like the method of using warm ghee as prescribed in the *Āgamas*, or like the methods of swallowing snakes and so forth.
As for treating by contemplating the mind, one directly contemplates the mind to investigate this illness—the cause of the illness and the illness itself.
Conditions and the self are both unobtainable. When illness comes to press, who is it that is pressed? Who is the one who receives the illness? This is called the contemplation of treatment.

Next, we discuss loss and gain; these may be gradual or sudden. If one employs the breath excessively, the five viscera will suddenly overturn. Even if they have not yet overturned, the affliction will gradually increase thereafter.
If a person practices skillfully, there will be a sudden benefit, as if opening up in a flash. Although at present it may merely contend with the illness, later—

There is gradual recovery, or the mind being sharp while the illness is light; or the mind being sharp while the illness is heavy; or the mind being dull while the illness is light; or the mind being dull while the illness is heavy.
Thus, there arise differences between gradual and sudden improvement or deterioration. If one can possess ten dharmas, one will certainly be able to eliminate [the afflictions].
Of these, faith is the foundation. Having faith, one can apply it; applying it, one can be diligent; being diligent, one can be constant; being constant, one can exercise discernment. Only then—

Then practice exhalation and inhalation. Direct the mind so that it attains its proper state; once it has attained this state, maintain it for a long duration. If there is decline, rectify the treatment; if there is progress, apply yourself single-mindedly.
Clearly recognize what is prohibited; do not harbor doubts and do not speak of it. One who practices in this manner will certainly achieve success. This is true if one skillfully cultivates samādhi.

Sustained by the power of the Way, what transgression would not be extinguished? What karma would not be transformed? Next, regarding the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, it is also like contemplating afflictions as ten dharmas;
first, one discusses the conceivable. Indeed, due to illness, one may lose the original mind, giving rise to great false views, slandering the Dharma and disparaging the sages.
Or, when the illness departs and the body is strong, one may commit great evil karma, giving rise to upper, middle, and lower offenses. Thus they are formed.

The realms of the three evil paths. Perhaps because of this illness, one practices with a sense of shame and remorse, giving rise to superior, middling, and inferior goodness, thereby accomplishing the realms of the three wholesome dharmas.
If one fears birth, aging, sickness, and death, one then contemplates how this body is a cycle of suffering and its accumulation, with afflictions never ceasing;
one should then seek the extinction of *nirvāṇa*. This is how the realm of the *śrāvaka* dharma arises from illness. One contemplates that this illness arises from within one's own body.

The body arises from past existence (*bhava*). Existence arises from grasping (*upādāna*). Grasping arises from craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Craving arises from feeling (*vedanā*). Feeling arises from contact (*sparśa*). Contact arises from the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The six sense bases arise from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Contemplating this name-and-form, one sees it arises from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Furthermore, contemplating the four great elements, one does not perceive a creator. One contemplates the five external elements and the five internal organs. Since they possess no fundamental essence, why do they not perish? They are sustained by the four minds.

Vijñāna (consciousness) sustains the earth; saṃjñā (perception) sustains the wind; vedanā (feeling) sustains the fire; and saṃskāra (volitional formations) sustain the water. Therefore, they are indestructible.
Furthermore, as for these four mental states, do they arise spontaneously or not spontaneously? One then knows that volitional formations arise from feeling;

feeling arises from perception; perception arises from consciousness; consciousness arises from past volitional formations; volitional formations arise from ignorance; and ignorance, in turn, arises from past feeling.
One knows that the nature of this birth is originally quiescent, yet through deluded and inverted conceptualization, one speaks of arising and ceasing.

If one does not follow such deluded inversions, then ignorance ceases, and so on until old age and death cease. This is the contemplation of the conditions from which illness arises, which gives rise to the dharma-realm of the pratyekabuddha.

Furthermore, one contemplates that this illness arises from craving, ignorance, hatred, and the like; by extending one's own compassion to others, one immediately gives rise to ethical discipline, meditative concentration, patience, and diligence.
These are the dharmas of equality. Thus, based on illness, the Bodhisattva’s dharma-realm of the six perfections arises.
Furthermore, observing this illness, one knows it arises from deluded thoughts and inversion; yet these deluded thoughts have no reality. Both "self" and "nirvana" are empty.

This is the Dharma-realm of the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Prajñāpāramitā) arising from illness. Furthermore, one contemplates that although this illness is ultimately empty, and though emptiness has nothing to receive, it nevertheless receives various sensations;
as long as the Buddha-dharmas are not yet complete, one should not extinguish sensation to attain realization.

This is the Dharma-realm of the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching arising from illness. Because they arise through a sequential process, they are termed "conceivable and speculatable," and thus do not pertain to the present [ultimate] reality.
Regarding that which is contemplated as inconceivable: the single thought-moment of the diseased mind is neither real nor existent; it is itself the dharma-nature (dharmatā).

It is the destination toward which all phenomena of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) tend, and the disease does not transcend this tendency. It is solely the totality of the dharma-realm, wherein there are no distinctions of the nine realms.

Like a wish-fulfilling jewel, it is neither before nor after; it penetrates the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the illness. When one contemplates in this way, the ailment is suddenly and completely cured.

As the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* states: "Merely hearing these words, the illness is immediately healed. This refers to the meaning of the first contemplation: the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*).
If the illness is not cured, one should further treat it with various other contemplations. All sentient beings are endowed with this principle.
Yet they cannot recognize it; following the influx of views and cravings, they enter into the birth-and-death of segmented existence (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*).

[The Bodhisattva] gives rise to profound compassion for them and bestows upon them the bliss of the Path and Cessation (*mārga-nirodha*), which is non-existence and immediate emptiness. This is how a sick Bodhisattva subdues his mind through the contemplation of emptiness.

Once the actual illness has been removed, the provisional illness arises accordingly, such that he is born within the realm of segmented existence. He regards all people as his own children; because the child is ill, the father [is also affected].

The mother was also ill. Because of her physical illness, he comforted and exhorted her; when the son recovered, she also recovered. This is called "comforting and exhorting through the analysis of the body" for a sick bodhisattva.
Furthermore, one contemplates that although this illness is empty, sentient beings cannot attain liberation solely by means of emptiness.
One should know that there are various dharma-gates for the illness of emptiness; because those of the Two Vehicles do not understand them, they follow along with ignorance.
They wander through the cycle of birth and death characterized by flux and transformation; they are unable to distinguish the various grades of illnesses.

For this reason, the Buddha-dharma does not manifest before them, and they fail to achieve the purification of sentient beings or their own buddha-lands. Thereupon, they give rise to compassion to uproot the suffering of ignorance and bestow the joy of discernment through the knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*).
This is how a sick bodhisattva uses the contemplation of the provisional to subdue the mind. [The contemplation of] the real...
Once the illness has been removed, the provisional sickness arises; one is born within the Land of Expedient Means and regards those of expedient means as if they were one's only child.
When the child’s illness is cured, the parents are also cured. This is called the Separate Teaching for consoling a bodhisattva who is ill.

Furthermore, one contemplates that although this illness is the Dharma-realm, sentient beings do not immediately realize the Middle Way; until this principle is opened, [the illness] follows along with non-...
Illuminating the ocean of change and flux, he immediately gives rise to compassion, uproots the suffering of ignorance, and bestows ultimate bliss.
This is the sick bodhisattva using the contemplation of the Middle Way to subdue his mind. Once the actual illness is removed, the provisional illness arises;
he is born within the Land of True Reward to console and encourage his children. When the child is healed, he too is healed. This is called the consolation of the Perfect Teaching.

For a bodhisattva who is ill, there are three kinds of illness: first, that which arises within the mind; this is tamed by contemplation. Second, that which arises from observation; this is tamed by compassion.
Third, that which arises from universal manifestation; this is tamed by the manifestation of the Universal Gate. Thus does he offer consolation.
He expounds with a single sound; it is only for the sake of easy understanding that he makes such distinctions. To state the essentials: this is nothing other than inconceivable compassion.
Only the Great Being, Vimalakīrti, is able to possess this Dharma: the three realities are perfectly eliminated, and the three skillful means are perfectly employed.
That Superior Person is truly difficult to respond to; only one whose power of the Way is equal to that of Mañjuśrī could even pose such a question.
He asked: "Householder, from what cause does this illness of yours arise? How long has it been present? And how shall it be extinguished? He replied:
"My illness arises from great compassion. Because sentient beings are ill, I am ill. When the illnesses of sentient beings are cured, my illness will likewise cease."
It is healed. This is called inconceivable compassion. Regarding the settling of the mind (*anxin*):

if a person falls ill while at the site of practice (*dōjō*), once they have realized the essence and aroused the bodhicitta, they employ the skillful means (*upāya*) of the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* *siddhānta* to bring about harmony and adjustment. This is the "great medicine," requiring no further application of various treatments.
As for the "pervasive destruction of phenomena" (*pòfǎbiàn*): the practitioner contemplates that the mind of illness arises neither from itself nor from another; it is neither internal nor...
Externally, it is ultimately pure. The mind is like empty space; who, then, could be ill? As Vimalakīrti said: "It is not the earth element, yet it is not separate from the earth element.

It does not combine with the body, because the characteristics of the body are detached. It does not combine with the mind, because the mind is like an illusion. One cannot find illness as arising, nor as non-arising;
nor as both arising and non-arising, nor as neither arising nor non-arising. Whether single or combined, it is fully complete, just as in the [Diamond] Sūtra’s refutation."

This is explained within the context of the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*). This constitutes the universal analysis of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) regarding illness. Regarding "penetration and obstruction":

within the phenomena of illness, one recognizes the principles of the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), understanding them without any doubt or confusion; one realizes that words are non-words, thereby causing all obstructions to be penetrated.
Regarding "the harmonization of the factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣadharma*): if one contemplates that this illness is an illness of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), it is impure.
Sickness. If one is apart from the sickness of the four great elements, that is the sickness of purity. It is neither the four great elements nor apart from the four great elements.

Sickness is neither pure nor impure; it is real, yet neither existent nor real; it is empty and provisional, yet neither empty nor negated; it is withered and flourishing, yet neither withered nor flourishing.
Such meanings as these are all non-dual and indistinguishable from the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). The same applies to the other three foundations of mindfulness.

Thus it is. Even unto the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, one achieves them upon the pillow. Understanding suffering as being without suffering, one enters the cool pond. As for those who assist the Path:

if one employs contemplation to treat an illness and the illness does not subside, then one employs the aforementioned remedial methods. One practices the primary and auxiliary methods in conjunction.

When performing this contemplation, one must have a profound understanding of the successive stages so as not to allow for transgression or confusion, nor to presumptuously compare oneself to the Sages and Worthies. [This concerns] internal and external hindrances.

When illness arises, one should diligently practice patience. When the practice is perfected through the affliction of sickness, do not give rise to attachment to dharmas. By accomplishing these ten dharmas, one swiftly enters the stream of the Dharma;
this is called attaining the realization of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti) amidst illness, thereby riding upon the Great Vehicle.

Fourth, regarding the contemplation of the objective realm of karmic characteristics: A person has, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, performed immeasurable karmas, some of which have already yielded their retribution while others have not yet done so.
This is like the great earth, which contains all seeds; when they encounter conditions, there are differences in their maturation, and those that emerge do so in a sequence of first and last.
While in their ordinary state, their characteristics do not manifest; however, when moved by the power of contemplation, the images of these realms appear clearly.
Some may say that regarding the Mahāyāna’s quiescence (*śamatha*), what characteristics could possibly be discussed? This is certainly not the case. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states:

"When one is about to realize the ten stages (*bhūmi*), all their characteristics manifest before one. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Deeply penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit. And the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:

"Skillfully able to discern the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) while remaining unmoved within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). If they are not manifested, what else could it be? Now, I shall clarify this in four points. First, the place...

I. The Causes and Conditions for Arousing [the Aspiration]; II. The Characteristics of Proper Arousing; III. Detailed Examination and Discernment; IV. Cultivating Śamatha and Vipaśyanā. Now, causes and conditions are of two kinds: internal and external.

The internal refers to the clarity and purity of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*), which illuminates all that is wholesome and unwholesome. Alternatively, one may employ *śamatha* to stifle evil; as the evil is just about to be extinguished, [one applies this method].
Sometimes one contemplates with *vipaśyanā* (insight) so that goodness may arise; sometimes one stills with *śamatha* (calm abiding) so that evil ceases due to stillness.

Sometimes one contemplates with *vipaśyanā* so that goodness is extinguished through contemplation. Immeasurable karmic signs emerge from within *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, just as when a mirror has been polished, the myriad images naturally appear.
This is what is meant by "internal and external. Through the power of their compassion, the Buddhas respond perfectly to sentient beings. There is...
As for this "stimulus," it evokes the Buddhas to manifest the meditations of good and evil, such that all karmic actions appear before one; this is called the "external.

When the practitioner merely disciplines the mind to enter into principle and brings the power of contemplation to fulfillment, then karma will naturally dissipate of itself; how could it depend on the subtle discernment of signs?
Next, the manifestation of karma is explained. Manifestations are of two kinds: wholesome and unwholesome, each having six aspects. First, the aspect of the manifestation of the retributive fruit.
Second, the signs of the cause of habituation appear; third, the retribution appears first and the habituation appears later; fourth, the habituation appears first and the retribution appears later;

fifth, the habituation and retribution appear simultaneously; sixth, their sequence is indefinite. If one understands these six meanings, then the myriad variations of ascent and descent will all be discerned without error.
Regarding what are called the "cause of habituation" and the "fruit of habituation": "habituation" (vāsanā) means continuous cultivation; it refers to the characteristic of its own specific seeds.

Birth: when a subsequent moment of mind arises, it continues the habituation of the preceding one. With reference to the preceding moment as the cause and the subsequent moment as the effect, there are the "causes of retribution" and "effects of retribution.
These pertain to different lifetimes. Both the causal habituation and the resultant habituation of the previous life are termed "causes of retribution.

Because one receives the retribution of the five destinies by virtue of these causes, they are called "effects of retribution. Furthermore, based on this body that is the effect of retribution, one again gives rise to wholesome and unwholesome habituations.

Continued: Regarding the causal habituation and the resultant habituation, viewed collectively in relation to the previous life, this very continuity of habituation constitutes the result. Viewed in relation to the subsequent life, it again functions as the cause.

When a practitioner perceives various signs within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this is called the manifestation of the signs of retributive results (*vipākaphala*). Because they arise from past causes, they may also be termed retributive causes;
these are merely reciprocal designations. For now, let us consider them as retributive results. If one does not perceive [these signs] within meditative concentration...

Various signs arise suddenly in the mind; these are called "habitual causes" (*vāsanā-hetu*) because they can bring about future fruits, and they are also called "habitual fruits" (*vāsanā-phala*). For now, we shall refer to them simply as habitual causes.
Such auspicious signs are numerous, but for the time being, let us consider them in relation to the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).

Regarding the manifestation of the sign of *dāna* (generosity): while sitting in meditation, one may suddenly see images of the Triple Gem, or one's parents, teachers, or friends; or one may see fields of compassion (*karuṇā-kṣetra*) receiving one’s offerings. Or...

One does not see either receiving or not receiving; one merely sees the objects to be relinquished, or sees a pure ground, or sees the donor of the gift deeply praising the act of giving—all of which are signs of the arising of the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*).

If, however, one sees none of these signs and yet the mind is resolute in its desire to practice generosity, or if one has a particular clarity of understanding regarding the gateway of giving, such are the signs of the arising of the causal habituation (*abhyāsa-hetu*). Or, first...
One may first arouse the thought [of awakening] and subsequently perceive the signs of retribution; or one may first perceive the signs of retribution and subsequently arouse the thought;

or both may arise simultaneously; or their sequence may be indeterminate. This can be understood through reflection. The same applies to the signs of precepts, up to those of patience and diligence. Next, the signs of evil are clarified.
Evil dharmas are immeasurable, but for now we shall take the six obscurations as our basis. Regarding the manifestation of the sign of the obscuration of stinginess:
Then, while in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one suddenly sees the forms of one's parents, teachers, or friends looking distressed and haggard; or sees them suffering from hunger and cold;
or sees all things as being sealed shut; or sees beggars shouting insults at objects; or sees a miser appear before one.

These are the retributive fruits of the mark of stinginess (*mātsarya*). The causes of habitual practice can be understood by analogy with what precedes, extending even to the various obscurations such as breaking the precepts (*śīla*).
The retribution of habitual tendencies is also like this. Next, let us examine in detail how the manifestations of good and evil differ as obstacles:

there are those that are not obstacles yet act as obstacles, those that are obstacles yet are not obstacles, those where both non-obstacles and obstacles act as obstacles, and those where both non-obstacles and obstacles do not act as obstacles.

Regarding what is called "not an obstacle yet acting as an obstacle": if a person first gives rise to a virtuous sign and feels joy at the time, but later gives rise to craving and pride, relying upon themselves...

To despise others and, through such a nature prone to regression, abandon the precepts—is this not a case where an initial cause that was non-obstructive to goodness later results in the calamity of a great obstruction?

As for what is called "an obstruction that is not an obstruction": seeing evil and knowing shame, being ashamed and able to practice, thereby relying upon manifold virtues to accomplish great matters—is this not a case where an initial cause that was obstructive later results in non-obstruction? Both are obstructions.

In both cases there is no obstruction; this may be understood by analogy. Generally, when that which is not an obstruction appears as an obstruction, it is because wholesome states are about to perish and their signs appear to indicate the arising of unwholesome states.
When that which is an obstruction appears as non-obstruction, it is because unwholesome states are about to perish and their signs appear to indicate the arising of wholesome states.

In both cases, there is no obstruction. This indicates that the wholesome is not extinguished and the unwholesome does not arise. When both are obstructive, it indicates that the unwholesome is not extinguished and the wholesome does not arise.
Speaking in terms of the wholesome and the unwholesome, the wholesome does not act as an obstruction while the unwholesome acts as an obstruction.

If speaking in terms of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), then both the wholesome and the unwholesome are obstructions. If speaking in terms of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), then both the ultimate and the conventional—both wholesome and unwholesome—are capable of acting as obstructions.

Obstruction. If we speak in terms of the Middle Way, even provisional wisdom regarding good and evil can act as an obstruction; thus, from ordinary beings up to the sages, all possess the affliction of obstructions.
Furthermore, while the causal conditions of good and evil arising from the mind are easy to understand, the manifestation of the characteristics of retributive fruits is difficult to discern.

If the characteristics of a good retribution arise in conjunction with the characteristics of the causal conditions of good practice—whether arising simultaneously or sequentially—it occurs in many instances.
This is the characteristic of innate goodness (*prakṛti-kuśala*). Arising in isolation, it is mostly the characteristic of non-informative goodness (*avijñapti-kuśala*).

If the fruit of an evil retribution and the cause of an evil habituation support one another, or arise sequentially, it is mostly innate evil. If it does not arise supported by habituation, it is mostly contrary to the characteristic of non-informative evil.

Furthermore, when the fruits of good or evil retribution arise in isolation, although they are designated as "non-informative," [they are so called because they do not manifest through physical or vocal action].
Furthermore, the principle is difficult to clarify, yet it is often interspersed with demonic influences. One should examine it by means of ten dharmas: namely, emptiness and existence;
light and darkness; concentration and distraction; good and evil; folly and wisdom; sorrow and joy; misfortune and fortune; suffering and happiness; love and hatred; and strength and weakness.

If these ten deviate from the mean—whether by excess or deficiency—they are all signs of Māra. If they differ from this, there is no activity [of Māra]. Moreover, one should verify them through three further dharmas.

If one dwells on these counts for a long time, and their frequent recurrence further disrupts the meditative mind, they are the signs of a māra. If these three are absent, then there is non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
When wisdom and understanding are authentic, one will not be deluded by various signs; thereafter, one can spur the mind to enter into principle, such that karma cannot obstruct it.
If, however, one originally lacks a mind of understanding, or if one’s resolve is deviant, and one perceives signs and gives rise to attachment, then—

Māra finds his opportunity and enters to show them signs of good and ill fortune; they practice the "ghost-dhyāna" while alive and fall into the realm of ghosts after death—this is an inevitable principle.
Next, regarding the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one first contemplates the "encompassing object of thought.

If karma can summon retribution in the three evil paths or the three good paths, even up to immovable karma summoning retribution in the realms of form and formlessness, all are instances of delusion regarding matter and mind that give rise to inverted afflictions.
Now, observing that karma is without karma, inverted delusions do not arise, leading even to the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava*). This is called the śrāvaka’s observation of karma.

If one observes that karma arises from ignorance (*avidyā*) through to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), such that the cessation of ignorance leads to the cessation of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and so on until the cessation of old age and death—this is called the pratyekabuddha’s observation of karma.
If one observes that karma is a magical illusion (*māyā*), and that what is illusory is itself emptiness (*śūnyatā*)—emptiness...
This is precisely *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, one contemplates karma as being like the great earth, which gives rise to various sprouts; all phenomena of the ten dharma realms arise from karma.

These are called the two contemplations—general and specific—and they both pertain to the realm of the conceivable (*saciṃtya-viṣaya*); they are not what is being contemplated here. Regarding the "inconceivable" (*acintya*):
the Sūtra says, "One who deeply penetrates the characteristics of sin and merit. Sin refers to the three evil realms; merit refers to the three good realms. To understand this...
Regarding "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa): merely knowing good and evil is not profound penetration. To regard both good and evil as evil, and to transcend both good and evil, is profound penetration.
Furthermore, to know that "transcending" and "not transcending" each occupy one side [of a duality] is not yet profound penetration;

it is only when a Bodhisattva of the Separate Teaching can penetrate these two sides—from the shallow to the deep—that it constitutes profound penetration. Moreover, the sequence of shallow and deep is also...

One has not yet deeply penetrated [the truth]. In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), that which is both shallow and deep constitutes true deep penetration. To deeply penetrate this characteristic such that it universally illumines the ten directions is precisely this meaning.
When one contemplates the arising of a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), it is already endowed with the ten dharma-realms (*daśadhātus*).

This is what is called the "ten directions," which refers to the primary retribution (*sambhogakāya*) and the environmental retribution (*bhājanaloka*). It also includes the hundred dharmas, such as the nature-characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth. All such dharmas are the karma of a single thought-moment; therefore—
It is called "one karma" and "all karmas. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* asks: "O Son of the Buddha, the nature of the mind is one;
how can it give rise to all manner of various karmas? It answers: "For example, the great earth is one, yet it can produce all manner of sprouts.
One should know that karma is the totality of all dharmas; this is the inconceivable realm. To penetrate deeply into this realm is to give rise to compassion. A single thought of compassion..."
Compassion is neither prior nor posterior; this is the true arousal of the mind. When the activity of settling the mind is empty, the good proceeds and the evil ceases.

The cessation of evil is called *śamatha* (calm abiding), and the proceeding of the good is called *vipaśyanā* (insight). This is likewise true for the activity of settling the mind when it is provisional, even up to within the activity itself.
This is the settling of the mind through the contemplation of karma. Furthermore, one contemplates that this karma is not separate from the three periods of time.
If it is past, then what has passed is non-existent; how could there be karma? If it is future, the future has not yet arrived. If it is present, the present does not abide.
When sought within the three periods of time, karma is entirely unobtainable. It is ultimately pure; it is only by means of words and provisional names that it is called "karma."
Karma is without agent and without recipient; the three truths are all quiescent. This universally destroys all karma.

Furthermore, regarding karma, non-karma, both karma and non-karma, and neither karma nor non-karma—within each of these phrases, one clearly discerns suffering, its origin, the path, and its cessation.
Upon careful examination, it is established that it is ultimately not the character "insect" (虫). This constitutes the discernment of whether the karma of consciousness is unimpeded or obstructed.
Furthermore, observe that this karma encompasses the ten realms and the five aggregates; this is precisely the possession of all four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

All form is the foundation of mindfulness of the body. This body is neither pure nor impure. Likewise, sensation is neither suffering nor pleasure; the mind is neither permanent nor impermanent; and phenomena are neither... [the text continues].
I am not non-self; this is precisely the nirvana of the twin trees, neither flourishing nor withered. This is called the harmonious adjustment of the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).

As for remedies, nothing is more essential than mindfulness of the Buddha—mindfulness of the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution) Buddha and the *nirmāṇakāya* (response) Buddha—together destroying the habitual causes and evil karma.

Furthermore, one should contemplate the Dharma-Buddha to destroy the evil karma of retributive results. When observing in this manner, one should also deeply recognize the successive stages so as not to overstep or usurp them.
One should also practice patience toward all internal and external obstacles so as not to be hindered by them. Furthermore, one should not give rise to attachment to the Dharma.

Spontaneously flowing into the pool of cool serenity, one attains the supreme retribution and achieves mastery over karma. Returning to the root and restoring the source, the illumination of wisdom reaches its ultimate perfection;
therefore, it is called the "Supreme Manifestation of the Universal Gate. Because there is nowhere it does not respond, it is called "Mastery."
This is precisely the Mahāyāna path leading directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), as previously explained.
Fifth, regarding the contemplation of demonic realms: when a practitioner cultivates the four samādhis and their functional application gradually becomes pure, demons are able to create obstacles.
They fear losing their subjects and followers, and they further dread that the practitioner might attain great supernormal powers (*mahābhijñā*) and incite a great conflict. Furthermore—
Before [the bodhisattva path] is perfected, they destroy those roots of goodness; thus, there is the affliction of Māra.

The Bodhisattva knows that the suchness of the realm of Māra and the suchness of the realm of the Buddha are one suchness without duality, a single mark of equality, resting in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). If one can act in this way, the heterodox cannot harm the orthodox.

Otherwise, there will undoubtedly be affliction. This is clarified in three parts: first, distinguishing similarities and differences; second, clarifying the characteristics of arising and the methods of treatment;

third, the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Regarding the distinction between the similarities and differences of the *māras*, there are four kinds: the *kleśa-māra*, the *skandha-māra*, and the *maraṇa-māra*.
They have already been subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and so forth; now, the text specifically clarifies the celestial Māra (*devaputra-māra*).

If one is outside the realms, there are the perversions such as impermanence, which likewise constitute the afflictions (*kleśa*), aggregates, birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), and so on; even at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), there is still the death-māra (*mṛtyu-māra*).

As long as the red-colored samādhi has not reached its ultimate consummation, it may also be termed the celestial māra. Only when the principle of wondrous enlightenment reaches its limit is the work of the māras finally brought to an end.
The *Avataṃsaka* speaks of ten māras; this is precisely what is meant here. Next, the manifestation of signs is explained:

if, when a person is sitting, they see ghosts clinging to their body, falling away and then climbing back up, departing and then returning, with four eyes and two mouths, emitting sounds that deafen the ears.
Furthermore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states that twelve animals dwell among the jewel mountains as lords of malevolent spirits (*piśāca*).

They may appear as young boys or girls, or in the forms of birds and beasts, with extraordinary shapes and diverse appearances, engaging in various playful transformations. Moreover, there is Māra’s delight, which enters through the five sense faculties;
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* refers to this as the "flower-arrows" and so forth. When ordinary eyes behold pleasing forms, or those that are terrifying—
Regarding form: if it is a neutral form, the other five sense-faculties combine to form eighteen arrows, which are also called the eighteen sensations (*vedanā*).

Attachment to them obstructs meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and at death, one falls into the path of Māra. Alternatively, if the arrow is shot inward but does not enter, then externally the teacher and disciples will be subjected to slander and praise from the sidelines.
Such causes and conditions are explained in detail in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Furthermore, those who are skillful at enticing others cause them exclusively to fall into unwholesome dharmas;

they encourage the construction of stupas and temples, which distracts people and hinders meditative concentration; or they convert people to enter a "void" that lacks skillful means, thereby repudiating cause and effect.
All such various paths lead to affliction and harm. One must forge their minds with firm resolve, for those who dwell in mountain forests are often many [in number].
One should keep a square mirror and hang it behind one's seat; when the *meihuo* (a type of spirit) looks into it, its form will be fully revealed.
Furthermore, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Do not accept any external things. The method of non-acceptance can cure all demonic activities concerning both self and others.

Next, regarding the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, there are ten dharmas as a general rule. As for the "contemplation of the realm" (*sīyì jìng*), if one follows the demons in giving rise to evil, or follows the demons in cultivation...

"Excellent. There are superior, middling, and inferior [levels], which are the māras of the six dharma-realms. Furthermore, they transform people so that they enter nirvāṇa prematurely, without the need for further deliverance;
these are the māras of the dharma-realm of the Two Vehicles. Moreover, they cause people to wander in circuitous and clumsy ways, preventing them from swiftly attaining the fruit of Bodhi.
Such gradations of shallow and deep are called 'conceivable and speculatable' (siyi). If this very matter is a demonic activity..."
The ten realms and hundred dharmas are fully present within a single thought-moment. All dharmas tend toward Māra; they are neither one nor many.
Not departing from the realm of Māra is precisely the realm of the Buddha. One who contemplates in this way finds that Māra is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Taking Māra as an attendant, one feels no fear of Māra. Holding the world without awakening, Māra’s stratagem says: "Welcome! You have obtained the seal of reality. Thus he knows it.

Māra is not Śakra. The Separate Teaching (biejiao) does not accept that which is contrary to the Dharma; therefore, it says, "This is not suitable for me. The Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) abides in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi);
therefore, it says, "As I am, I should accept this. Not fearing non-human beings, one possesses courage within birth-and-death (saṃsāra). This is called the inconceivable object (acintya-viṣaya).
The essence of Māra is identical to that of the Buddha, yet sentient beings do not know this; they perversely give rise to [distinctions] within the realm of the Buddha.

Within the realm of Māra, afflictions arise within awakening; therefore, one gives rise to compassion (*karuṇā*). Desiring to cause sentient beings—who are themselves Māras—to attain Buddhahood, one gives rise to loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
This is what is called "unconditioned" (*apratihata*) compassion and loving-kindness. It is to fulfill this vow and to manifest this principle that [one acts].
One should subdue this Māra; its inability to move one is what constitutes cessation. To penetrate Māra is to contemplate it as the Buddha.

Furthermore, when the activities of Māra momentarily stir, one should immediately employ the four logical propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) to analyze and destroy them. At the outset, the Tripitaka Master subdued the four Māras while seated at the site of enlightenment:

he destroyed the Māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*) to attain the path of Bodhi; his Dharma-nature body destroyed the Māras of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), as well as the Māra of death (*mṛtyumāra*). Thus, beneath the Bodhi tree—

Having attained the Immovable Samādhi (*acala-samādhi*), one is able to destroy the celestial Māras. In the Shared Teaching (*p’ung-hsiao*), one first attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*);

reaching the sixth stage (*bhūmi*), one attains the path of Bodhi as previously explained. At the eighth stage, the path and contemplation flow together; this is the Immovable Samādhi that destroys the celestial Māras.

In the Distinct Teaching (*pieh-chiao*), one has already destroyed the four Māras within the realm of desire by the ten stages of abiding (*daśa-vihāra*); at the first stage, one partially destroys the afflictions and partially attains the Dharma.
The body destroys the *skandha-māra*; by attaining the crimson *samādhi*, one partially destroys the *deva-māra*. The *Yingluo jing* states:

"In the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*), the three *māras* are already exhausted; only a portion of the *maraṇa-māra* remains. Speaking according to principle, it is not fitting that the three should be exhausted beforehand, nor that one alone should remain;

one should know that this refers to the provisional path (*upāya-mārga*). In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the eight *māras* are destroyed simultaneously at the first *bhūmi*; only upon reaching Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*) are they fully investigated and eliminated.

Ultimately, it is forever detached. Furthermore, although it is destroyed at the initial dwelling, it is not destroyed by the initial dwelling; although it is destroyed by the final awakening, it is not destroyed by the final awakening.

Yet, it is also not separate from the destruction of the beginning and the destruction of the end. Moreover, within each and every māra, one recognizes the suffering and its origin, the obscuration of ignorance, and the crossing over [to liberation];
one knows that characters are non-characters. Furthermore, within a single māra, all forms are present; form is itself emptiness, itself the provisional, and itself...
It is neither pure nor impure. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this; this is called the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
One who contemplates in this way opens the three gates of liberation.

For those whose gates have not yet opened, they will long remain under the influence of Māra, giving rise to demonic generosity, demonic precepts, demonic patience, demonic diligence, demonic meditation, and demonic wisdom. Due to these false obscurations, the true path is blocked.
Now, employ right measure to govern obscuration. When obscuration is removed, measure is perfected. Alternatively, use other contemplations as aids—whether to subdue or to shatter them.
Illuminate them without confusion; with single-minded patience, do not give rise to attachment to dharmas. Then you will not be moved or disturbed by Māra, and shall immediately enter the true stage.
Taking Māra as your attendant, you will proceed directly to the site of enlightenment (the end of the fifth fascicle in the original text).

Regarding the sixth contemplation on the states of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*): once the practitioner has contemplated the five preceding objects and successfully entered the Cool Pond, they need no longer contemplate the states of *dhyāna*.
However, even if the demonic states have passed, if latent habitual tendencies suddenly arise, various *dhyānas* will manifest in confusion.

Although one may escape the harm of Māra, one may still be bound by meditative concentration (*samādhi*). For this reason, it is necessary to contemplate the objects of dhyāna. The *Abhidharma* and *Tattvasiddhi* clarify the four dhyānas and eight concentrations;

the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* and *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* further clarify the nine dhyānas of intrinsic nature. It would be impossible to record them all exhaustively; here, I shall briefly discuss their names and meanings.
Next, I shall discuss the causes and conditions for their arousal and the signs of their arousal. Next, the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā... [The] so-called "name" (nāman) is as follows:
Regarding the meaning, it shall be treated according to ten gates: first, the four fundamental dhyānas; second, the sixteen special victories (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa*);

third, the universal clarity (*sāmānya-vidyā*); fourth, the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*); fifth, the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*); sixth, the great impurity (*mahā-aśubha*); seventh, loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*); eighth, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*);
ninth, mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*); and tenth, the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). These ten types correspond to the meditations discussed in various sūtras and śāstras.
The enumerations may be expanded or condensed, but the general meaning is limited to this. The essential nature and characteristics of these ten dhyānas are with-outflow (sāsrava).
They are all mundane dhyānas (vastu-dhyāna) and must also be distinguished accordingly. The four dhyānas exist inherently in the world; they are shared by ordinary persons and non-Buddhists alike.

Those who practice them exclusively can only develop mundane *viśeṣa* (special attainments) and *abhijñā* (superknowledges). Even if a Buddha does not appear in the world, those of sharp faculties among ordinary persons are still able to cultivate them.
[These practices] do not give rise to outflow-free (*anāsrava*) states on their own; however, if they are based upon the Buddha’s teaching, they do give rise to outflow-free states.

Compared to the fundamental [realizations], their power is superior; therefore, they are described as being "both with outflows and without outflows. Although the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*) and so forth belong to the category of mundane phenomena (*dharma*), they can serve as causes for transcending the world.

They do not, however, depend upon the wisdom of the Truths (*satya-jñāna*) to give rise to outflow-free states; therefore, they are all collectively termed "without outflows" (*anāsrava*). This is clarified according to their sequence.
The four *dhyānas* are fundamental, dark, and relishing meditations (*āsvādana-dhyāna*). They are common to both ordinary beings and sages;

by practicing them even slightly, one attains specific excellence (*viśeṣa*), yet they possess little insight (*vipaśyanā*) and are neither relishing nor dark. Therefore, they follow the fundamental [meditations]. The general illumination (*sāmānyaprabhāsa*) involves the realization of insight that is profound and subtle, and thus follows the specific excellence.
These three are all actual contemplations (*bhūtadhyāna*), but their power to counteract afflictions is weak. The nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*) are precisely conceptual (*prajñapti*) [contemplations].
The first gateway of perception begins the subduing of craving and desire; therefore, next, the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*) are explained in general.

Furthermore, while the nine perceptions merely engender revulsion toward external objects, they have not yet disciplined the mind itself; therefore, next, the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) are discussed.

Moreover, although the liberations destroy both internal and external greed and desire, they do so in a general way rather than specifically, and one does not attain mastery over the various conditions; therefore, next, the great impurity (*mahāśubha*) is discussed.
Furthermore, although one may have treated the mind both generally and specifically, one has not yet attained great merit; therefore, next, compassion is discussed.
Moreover, although one may externally treat heavy greed and internally cultivate supreme practices, if one does not contemplate causes and conditions, it is not the right view of the world;

therefore, next, causes and conditions are discussed. Furthermore, although one may have attained right view, if one relies on inferior persons, the power of one's merit will be weak; next, [the superior person] is relied upon.

Because the merit and power of the supreme fruit are vast and great, the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha is discussed next. Furthermore, although there are various meditative concentrations as previously described, they have not yet attained sovereign power and function;
therefore, the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are discussed next. As for what is called "arousing" [these powers], it occurs through their successive and reciprocal development.
For example, regarding the external conditions that trigger the arising of dhyāna, there are internal and external factors.

Just as within the great earth all types of seeds are fully present, and upon receiving rain they sprout and grow into distinct, individual fruits, the *Jingdu jing* states: "Sentient beings save themselves;
the Buddha provides no benefit to them. The Bodhisattva Jingdu said: "If sentient beings do not hear the Buddha's words, how could they [attain liberation]?"
"Crossing over" (du) and "arousing" (fa) are two words that seem contrary yet together form a single meaning; this is the simultaneous arising of both the internal and external.
I shall now distinguish the signs of the arousal of dhyāna. Among the four types of samādhi, the constantly seated samādhi most frequently arouses dhyāna.

If, while sitting, the physical constitution and vital energy are harmonious and well-adjusted, one perceives that the path of the mind becomes submerged in clarity and stillness, becoming profoundly peaceful and secure. One then binds the object of focus to that which has been practiced.
That which does not scatter or disperse is called "coarse abiding" (*audārikasthiti*). When this mind becomes further superior, it is called "subtle abiding" (*sūkṣmasthiti*).
Between these two states of mind—before and after—there must necessarily be a factor that sustains the body. The body remains upright, neither lax nor weary, as if supported by some external aid.
This may last for one or two periods, or one or two days, or even for ten or twenty days; it gradually deepens and becomes increasingly subtle.

It is luminously empty and pure. One maintains the mind without movement; yet, despite this emptiness and purity, the marks of body and mind are still perceived, and the various branches of merit have not yet arisen.

This is called the concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*). Abiding in this concentration for perhaps one or two years, one is sustained by the power of the meditative state itself and feels no weariness.
Following that mental state, the mind further becomes vacuous and expansive, and the concentration of the desire realm is no longer seen.
The characteristics of body and mind therein are like empty space; this is called the sign of the "not-yet-reached" stage (*anāgamya-bhūmi*).

Worldly fools may attain this concentration and claim it is the "patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), yet they do not realize that their innate obstructions remain entirely intact and that they have not yet entered the first dhyāna.

It is like fire covered by ashes; the ignorant tread upon it lightly and thereby injure and scorch themselves. From the stage of coarse abiding up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there are generally four divisions:

namely, decline (*hāna*), protection (*anurakṣaṇā*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and progress (*viśeṣa*). Decline is further twofold: first, spontaneous decline; second, decline due to external conditions.

Conditions are of two kinds: internal and external. External conditions consist of twenty-five types of improper exhalation and inhalation among various skillful means; these constitute external conditions that cause regression.

Internal conditions consist of the arising of the three obstacles and four maras within a state of meditative stillness, giving rise to sorrow and attachment; these constitute internal conditions that cause regression.

"Guarding" means protecting and sustaining the concentrated mind through skillful means. "Abiding" means either remaining in peace through such protection and assistance, or the concentration itself abiding naturally.

"Advancing" means that from the stage of "not-yet-attained concentration," one gradually perceives the body and mind as empty and tranquil; internally one does not see the body, and externally one does not see objects.
Within this concentration, one perceives the body and mind moving subtly and continuously; thus, one gives rise to the Form Realm.

The pure and subtle four great elements—motion, itching, lightness, heaviness, cold, warmth, roughness, and smoothness—are collectively termed the eight tangibles (*spraṣṭavya*). These tangibles contact the body within the desire realm.

Thereupon, the qualities of the causal forest arise from this. There are ten such qualities: namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), clarity (*prabhāsvara*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*jñāna*), a virtuous mind (*kuśalacitta*), suppleness (*mṛdutā*), joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), liberation (*vimukti*), and correspondence with the objective sphere (*viṣayapratyupasthāna*). Regarding "emptiness":

when various contacts arise, the empty mind is vast and open, no longer being of the same nature as when the obscurations have not yet been removed. Regarding "clarity": it is pure, wondrous, and resplendent. Regarding "concentration": it is... [not disturbed].

Furthermore, "scattered and moving" refers to the agitation of the mind. "The wise" refers to those who understand tranquility and benefit. "Those with a virtuous mind" refers to those who have deep faith in the sublime Dharma.

"Gentle" refers to being free from the coarse and harsh characteristics of the desire realm. "Joyful" refers to rejoicing in the Dharma attained. "Blissful" refers to abiding in this exquisite beauty.

"Liberated" refers to being free once again from the five hindrances. "Conjoined" refers to the mind being conjoined with the merits of various contacts (*sparśa*) without distraction. Furthermore, one maintains mindfulness.

One maintains this through application and does not forget it. However, these eight tactile sensations do not exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Furthermore, regarding the eight tactile sensations of the first dhyāna, one must carefully distinguish between the false and the correct.
Why? Because it is close to the desire realm; if the mind still carries the tendencies of the desire realm, then the false can easily enter along with it.

This refers to ghosts entering into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); yet, meditative concentration itself is not a ghost. Therefore, this is further clarified by means of the eight tactile sensations (*spraṣṭavya*) and the ten merits (*guṇa*).

Whether one exceeds [the proper measure] or falls short of it, both constitute what is deviant (*mithyā*). To examine the origin of correct meditation (*samyak-dhyāna*), it should not contain anything deviant.

As for why such things occur, it is like taking *chángpú* or *huángjīng*: while these medicinal substances are intended to provide benefit, they may cause one to become prone to anger and desire; thus, they are not the medicine itself.

It is so. This is the method for removing coarse factors. When coarse factors are removed, the principle is indeed thus; one must distinguish them with precision. Regarding the five factors of formal meditation (*dhyāna*):

when the initial contact touches the body upon the object, it is called the factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). The subtle mental discernment of the eight types of contact and their ten attendants is called the factor of investigation (*dharma-vicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Rejoicing that what was previously unattained is now attained is called the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Serene pleasure is called...

The factor of joy (*prīti-aṅga*). Tranquility is called the factor of one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā-aṅga*). The characteristics of these five factors are fully explained as in the separate commentary.

Furthermore, when first moving, the eight contacts are still coarse in their qualities; however, if they are repeatedly aroused, they become increasingly profound and sharp. When about to abandon them, one simply censures applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
Once the first dhyāna has passed away, the intermediate state (*dhyānāntara*) is immediately produced. Having already departed from the lower stage, yet not yet having reached the higher, this—

At times, regret or remorse may arise; if there is no remorse, inner purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) immediately manifests. The eight tactile sensations (*spraṣṭavya*) cease to exist, and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived forms (*upādāyarūpa*) merge into a single pure form (*śubharūpa*).

This illuminates the mind, which becomes increasingly pure. Joy (*prīti*) arises together with this state, and from joy, bliss (*sukha*) is born. When bliss subsides, one enters one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*).

Because the joy and movement of bliss in this dhyāna are unstable, one then censures that joy. As joy subsides, one enters the stage of *anāgamya* (the threshold), where suddenly [the factor of] equanimity (*upekṣā*) arises.

In the third dhyāna, material phenomena become increasingly subtle. Right pleasure is experienced throughout the entire body; it is only the noble ones (ārya) who are able to relinquish it, whereas for ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), this is difficult.

This [dhyāna] possesses five factors: equanimity (upekṣā), mindfulness (smṛti), discernment (prajñā), pleasure (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (cittaikāgratā). As stated in the sūtras and śāstras, these may appear either before or after [one another].

These differ only slightly in their practice. This pleasure is a counterpoint to suffering; when suffering is censured, the pleasure immediately subsides. There are also cases where it has not yet arrived;

once it has arrived and then subsided, one gives rise to the immovable concentration (*āniñjya-samādhi*). As for "immovable," it means being unmoved by suffering or pleasure. The state of concentration is peaceful and secure;

inhalation and exhalation cease, and there is neither suffering nor pleasure. Equanimity and mindfulness are purified. Although the factors of single-mindedness (*ekāgra*) are thus, they still belong to the realm of form (*rūpa-dharma*).

Having rejected the three kinds of form, one attains concentration by taking emptiness as the object and no longer perceives form, like a bird escaping from a cage; this is called the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).

When this concentration has ceased, one likewise enters the threshold state (*anāgamya*). Taking consciousness as the object, one gives rise to concentration; this is called the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). When this concentration has ceased—
Because there is nothing to be relied upon, one enters the state corresponding to the dharma of non-existence; this is called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Furthermore, having transcended this, one suddenly gives rise to the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This meditative absorption is called "neither-perception" because it does not rely on the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, and "nor-non-perception" because it does not rely on the Sphere of Nothingness.

It is the meditative dhyāna at the summit of the three realms, beyond which there is no further dharma. Non-Buddhists reckon this to be *nirvāṇa*. This is [the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception].
The Hidden Witness: Fully endowed with suffering and its accumulation, one again falls into the three miserable realms. 2. Clarifying the Extraordinary Excellence of the Arising:
When this contemplation arises, one suddenly perceives the breath entering and exiting as long or short; one knows that it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
Upon entering, it does not accumulate; upon exiting, it does not disperse. One sees the thirty-six components within the body as impure, impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.

I have traversed these sixteen dharmas from beginning to end; they may be correlated with the four foundations of mindfulness, or their degrees of depth may be discussed in terms of the fundamental dhyānas and their constituent factors (*dhyānāṅga*).
However, while the fundamental merits are coarse and thin, the particularly superior merits are deep and thick.
The names, meanings, and detailed explanations regarding the arising of these sixteen types are as set forth in the separate commentary. (3)

Regarding "the development of the clear and penetrating illumination of dhyāna" (*abhijñā-pratisaṃvid-vyutpatti*): during the cultivation of the *uttara-manasikāra*, one perceives the thirty-six objects collectively, and the signs of realization (*pratyakṣa-lakṣaṇa*) are likewise collective.

During the cultivation of the *abhijñā-pratisaṃvid*, the subtle and wondrous signs of realization are also wondrous. Because it can give rise to the three knowledges (*tri-vidyā*) and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), it is called "clear and penetrating illumination.

The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* explains these five branches as follows: namely, the great awakening of the mind (*citta-mahābodhi*), the great contemplation (*mahāmanasikāra*), and the observation (*vipaśyanā*).

This nature of mind is called the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Contemplating the activity of the mind, its great activity, and its pervasive activity is called the factor of enlightenment of investigation (*dharma-vicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

Knowing as it truly is, having great knowledge, and the movement of the mind reaching joy is called the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). When body and mind are both at ease and one experiences a touch of bliss, this is called the factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The mind abiding in great abiding, undisturbed by objects, is called the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*). These are the first three matters of contemplation.

At the time of universal integration and realization, these three matters are all one; therefore, it is called "awakening to the mind as such" (*yathā-citta-bodha*). One awakens to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and also cognizes the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

"Contemplation" (*cintā*) and "great contemplation" (*mahā-cintā*) refer precisely to this contemplation of the ultimate and the conventional. To contemplate the nature of the mind is itself emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Whether ultimate or conventional, they all enter the nature of the mind. As the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra* says: "Each and every one enters the limit of reality (*yathābhūta*).

Such factors of awakening (*bodhipakṣa*) differ twofold from the previous factors of awakening. Regarding the "mind-practicing great practitioner": because the mind practices within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is called "practice" (*caryā*);

because it practices the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is called "great practice" (*mahācaryā*); because these three matters are practiced together, it is called "universal practice" (*sarvacaryā*). Regarding the "abiding of the mind": in...
The attainment of one-pointedness through conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is "Great Abiding. This means that regarding ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one attains one-pointedness;

it is to remain undisturbed by conditions, meaning that the illumination of the realms of both the conventional and the ultimate is free from error. One who gives rise to this concentration perceives that the perception of the body, the perception of cessation, and the perception of the mind are like a plantain tree—lacking any solid core.
This is the sign of the Stage Not Yet Reached (*anāgamya-bhūmi*). One perceives these three things as being identical.
The appearance of foam is the sign of the first dhyāna. Seeing the three matters as like floating clouds is the sign of the second dhyāna.

Seeing the three matters as like shadows is the sign of the third dhyāna. Seeing the three matters as identical to reflections in a mirror is the sign of the fourth dhyāna. By ceasing these three matters, one conditions emptiness;
by ceasing emptiness, one conditions consciousness; by ceasing consciousness, one conditions nothingness; by ceasing nothingness, one conditions the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

It is not the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). By extinguishing these three types of feeling and perception of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one personally realizes (*kāyasākṣin*) the dharma of the cessation of feeling and perception, thereby accomplishing liberation.
Because it possesses conventional observation, it is called "also with outflows" (*sāsrava*); because it possesses true observation, it is called "also without outflows" (*anāsrava*).
This meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is complete in both principle and phenomenon. A detailed discussion of its characteristics is also as explained elsewhere. 4. Clarifying Impurity (*aśubha*)

Regarding the arousal of dhyāna: "impurity" refers to the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*). If a person who destroys the Dharma practices this dhyāna up to the eighth notion of bones and the ninth notion of burning, this person seeks in both cases the cessation of suffering;
by burning away the person consisting of bones, they seek to attain the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

Thus, they destroy the dharmas that constitute the merit of the various dhyānas. If it is a person who does not destroy the Dharma, they [practice] the nine notions from the beginning, ceasing at the eighth.
One does not advance to the ninth [liberation]. One attains the liberation of the "flowing light" (*ābhāsvara-vimokṣa*) and the spheres of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*).

Through contemplation, refinement, cultivation, and repeated practice, one becomes fully endowed with all meritorious qualities. If the practitioner perceives an excess of internal [defilements], they contemplate the body; if there is an excess of craving, they contemplate external objects.
When one perceives craving and so forth, one contemplates both internally and externally; it is the same when they arise.

If, while in meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), one suddenly sees a single corpse or many corpses filling the entire land—where the number of corpses is great, this is the sign of the contemplation of the greatly impure (*mahā-aśubha-bhāvanā*).

This continues until the eighth stage, the perception of bones (*asthi-saṃjñā*), where all signs transform and the concentrated mind follows along, becoming joyfully pure and sublime. Having seen these signs, all sensual desires [cease] of their own accord.
Go! Not only does it eliminate desire, but it also gives rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*) and accomplishes the Mahāyāna.

Fifth, explaining the characteristics of the arising of the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*): The first three types are the fundamental "flavor-purity" (*rasa-śuddhi*). From the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*) up to the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), they are called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).

The nine successive [attainments] are called "refinement" (*pariśodhana*). The lion’s bound (or leaping) is called "perfuming" (*vāsana*). The transcendence is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). These four matters constitute meditative concentration (*samādhi*); we shall now explain them first.
The "reversals" (*prātikūlya*) have both general and specific aspects. The general aspect is shared with the two vehicles (*dviyāna*); the specific aspect belongs to the Bodhisattvas.
"Reversal" (*prātikūlya*) refers to the loathing of the lower stages and the pure five desires of one’s own stage. "Abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) means the relinquishing of this attached mind.

If it involves the destruction of craving, it predominantly gives rise to external signs, such as the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*) mentioned previously. If it involves the destruction of views, it predominantly gives rise to internal signs; these are the eight reversals (*aṣṭaprātikūlya*). First, internally...

One contemplates external forms, continuing up to the eighth liberation, the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha-vimokṣa*). The details of these meditative signs (*nimitta*) are fully explained in other commentaries. Regarding the sign of "arousing" (*udbhava-nimitta*):
suddenly one sees one's own body, from head to foot, completely disintegrate and scatter, leaving only a standing skeleton.

Having produced this sign, one deeply loathes the body; internally, one no longer conceives of a self, and externally, one has no attachment to things. This is what the Great Sūtra refers to as "contemplating with precision."
The white bones are called "having internal perception of form while externally perceiving forms. This is like the impurity observed in the nine contemplations;
this is called "externally perceiving forms. As this dharma progresses, one sees the bones arise in four colors—blue, yellow, white, and pigeon-colored—each with its own radiance.
Because of the blue light, it eclipses the ten directions, causing them all to become blue, and so on, until they all become pigeon-colored.

It illuminates the ten directions, becoming vast and brilliantly clear. This single color also possesses ten merits, eight tactile qualities, five branches, and characteristics such as correctness and error.
These gathered merits differ from the fundamental [attainments] and are distinct from the *viśeṣa* (special) and *abhijñā* (super-knowledge) attainments.

If these characteristics arise, the first *parivartana* (turning away/renunciation) is accomplished; its stage is the first *dhyāna*. Second, regarding internal formlessness, one contemplates external forms with a mind focused on impurity.
This skeleton is a composite formation and must be condemned and extinguished. One should analyze the skeleton into its four subtle elements (*mahābhūta*).
According to the principle of the Mahāyāna, one knows that the bone arises from the mind; since the mind is like an illusion or a magical transformation, the bone itself naturally perishes.

Furthermore, with a mind focused on impurity, one should contemplate only external forms. "External forms" refers to external impurities and the eight colors emitted by the skeleton. When the skeleton is extinguished, [the practice is complete].

The temporal stage is intermediate. Furthermore, one observes the eight forms arising simultaneously with the internal purity (*adhyātma-śubha*), while the light of blue, yellow, and so forth becomes increasingly radiant, and the merit of internal purity is further enhanced;
this is the second stage of liberation (*vimokṣa*), situated in the second dhyāna.

Regarding "the purification of the body through the realization of the three purities" (*śubha-vimokṣa-kāyena sākṣātkaroti*): as for "purity," the *Śāstra* states that it is because it takes the pure as its object (*ālambana*). Since the eight forms are already pure...
Regarding the pure dharmas: although they have not yet been purified by purifying conditions, the refined and pure matter reaches its ultimate state in the fourth dhyāna.

When this matter arises, it refines the entering matter, causing the matter to become increasingly bright and pure; therefore, it is said that "it is pure because the conditions are pure. There is pervasive bodily bliss that can serve as proof;

because of this bliss, its stage is the third dhyāna, while its position of ultimate purity is in the fourth dhyāna. As for the liberations of the four formless realms (*ārūpya-vimokṣa*), they transcend...
Regarding all forms: one eliminates obstructive form, does not attend to various forms, and through the critique of form, takes emptiness as the object.

There is no other distinct dharma; one simply enters the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*). If ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are heavily defiled, they cling to this concentration of emptiness;

however, because the sages possess sharp wisdom, they relinquish it without turning back. Therefore, it is called the "emptiness liberation" (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*). If one relies too much on emptiness, the mind becomes distracted, empty, deceptive, and unreal. Thus, one relinquishes emptiness and takes consciousness (*vijñāna*) as the object.

The association with the dharma of consciousness is called the liberation of the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana-vimokṣa*). Furthermore, because consciousness arises and ceases and is impermanent, there is no longer an object of perception (*ālambana*), but only a perceiving subject;
therefore, it is called the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). The sphere of consciousness is like an abscess, and the sphere of nothingness is like a sore.

To abandon these two is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). This state of non-perception still possesses subtle afflictions (*kleśa*); now, one abandons the perceiving subject.

Taking the sensations and perceptions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as their object, there is also no perception capable of extinguishing them. The dharmas of meditative concentration sustain the body, and one becomes utterly devoid of perception;
therefore, it is called the "liberation through the cessation of sensation and perception. This is explained in detail in other commentaries.

Regarding the nine successive concentrations, the leap-over concentrations (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*), and so forth, according to the Tripiṭaka, there are no ordinary persons who cultivate these concentrations; thus, they do not arise again. If, however, we speak from the perspective of the Mahāyāna meaning...

Thus it exists. ○6. Discourse on the Great Contemplation of Impurity. This is also called the Great Liberation. There is nothing among the two types of retribution—the primary (the body) and the secondary (the environment)—that one does not find loathsome.
If, while in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one suddenly perceives these signs, this is the manifestation of the Great Contemplation of Impurity. However, things have no fixed characteristics;
they appear pure or impure according to what is evoked by one's wholesome or unwholesome karma. If one clings to pure forms and cherishes them with attachment...
One must certainly use the power of the Great Contemplation to break this clinging mind and achieve the Great Contemplation of Impurity.

Indeed, even the methods of illusion can transform and manifest things to people; they are like flowing gold turning into ice, with transformations that are manifold, all brought about by the power of meditative concentration.
This is logically appropriate. Furthermore, these small and great liberations (*vimokṣa*) are not yet untainted (*anāsrava*).
If they were to be permeated by the untainted, then what attachment would not be abandoned? As for the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), one further matures this method of liberation;

depending on the central point of reliance, there is a circular and transformative transition—whether as one or many—in which the direction taken is sovereign. However, this has not yet reached universal pervasiveness. Until...
Only through the ten *kṛtsnāyatanas* (totalities) can one achieve such pervasiveness. That is to say, by pervading the ten directions with blue, all ten directions become blue;
this applies to all other colors as well, which is why they are called "totalities" (*kṛtsna*).

As for the "single entrances" (*ekatyāyatana*), when one pervades [the field] with blue, if yellow enters into that blue, it can likewise transform into yellow, yet the two appearances remain distinct and do not obstruct one another; this is also the case for the other colors. Therefore, they are called "single."

Enter into this contemplation. If this contemplation is clear, one should relinquish even the body, let alone other things; this is called *dāna* (generosity). Being unstained by what is unrighteous is called *śīla* (ethical discipline).
The absence of anger and contention is called *kṣānti* (patience). The non-retrogression of the concentrated mind is called *vīrya* (diligence).

This contemplation, when fully observed, refined, cultivated, and practiced, constitutes *dhyāna* (meditation). The non-apprehension of any phenomenon is *prajñā* (wisdom). All dharma-gates are perfected within this excellence.
Regarding the accomplishment of the dwelling: those who practice samādhi will give rise to and attain this dharma, frequently advancing into the five stages (pañcāvasthā).

This is because the power of the auxiliary path is great. Seventh, concerning the arising of a compassionate mind: from the fundamental stage onward, one is able to give rise to compassion both before and after all meditative absorptions (dhyāna).
If one suddenly takes all sentient beings as the object of focus and perceives their aspect of happiness—being without resentment or affliction—one should skillfully cultivate it.
One attains understanding; the concentrated mind becomes clear and pure. There is not a single sentient being who does not obtain happiness.

This understanding becomes increasingly deep, and this practice becomes increasingly subtle, able to give rise to the five factors of virtue (*pañcāṅga-guṇa*). Their names are the same as the fundamental [meditations], yet their flavor of the Dharma (*dharma-rasa*) is distinct.
