If one gives rise to them by relying on the "Special Excellence" (*viśeṣa*), they are further enhanced. The other three immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) may be understood accordingly. Regarding the eight causes and conditions for their arising, within the sitting meditation...

Suddenly, one contemplates the objects of the mind, whether they be wholesome or unwholesome. The subject that perceives and the object perceived are themselves the *bhava-aṅga* (the link of existence).

Because the mind grasps and clings, there is the arising of *bhava* (existence). Thus, it is known that *bhava* arises from *upādāna* (clinging); *upādāna* arises from *tṛṣṇā* (craving); and *tṛṣṇā* arises from *vedanā* (feeling).
As the Sūtra says, "The six types of contact (*sparśa*) as conditions give rise to various feelings," one knows that feeling arises from contacts, and contacts arise from the sense bases (*āyatana*).

Entry occurs by means of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). The discernment of this form is consciousness (*vijñāna*); the experiencing of this form is sensation (*vedanā*); and the arising of conceptualizations such as greed and hatred is volitional formation (*saṃskāra*).

Because of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), there is contact (*sparśa*). Thus, it is known that contact arises from name-and-form, name-and-form from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), and consciousness from prior karma;
karma is itself volitional formation, and volitional formation arises from ignorance (*avidyā*). From the past into the present, [the cycle continues] through the present...
Grasping at existence further invites future birth and death; the causes and conditions of the three periods of time have no fixed master.
Contemplating in this way, the false view of a self naturally collapses. The concentrated mind gradually becomes subtle, and the various branches of merit arise in succession.

The ten dharmas of emptiness and luminosity are each fully accomplished. From the fundamental [dhyānas] up to the special excellences (viśeṣa), the universal luminosities (abhijñā), and the liberations (vimokṣa), all arise from causes and conditions;
they are also able to give rise to causes and conditions based upon them. The gates of causes and conditions vary according to the capacities of beings.

The *Āgama-sūtra* (瓔珞經) clarifies ten types [of recollection], while the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* clarifies the karmic fruits and retributions. In Nāgārjuna’s *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is established as the first chapter.
Regarding the ninth type, "recollection arising through cultivation": it may arise through meditation giving rise to recollection, or through recollection giving rise to meditation.

While the practitioner is in the midst of seated meditation, they suddenly contemplate the great supernormal powers, great wisdom, great merit, and the great marks and signs of the Buddhas. Thereupon—

Regarding the essence of the marks, the fruits of the marks, and the activities of the marks: one deeply understands the ocean of marks without doubt or stagnation, and the mind remains serene, unmoving, and undisturbed.
Suddenly, the merits of the branches of the coarse and subtle dwellings, up to those of the four dhyānas, arise; these arise simultaneously with the mindfulness of the Buddha.
Perfumed by the power of these virtues, they become doubly supreme and absolute. The samādhis thus produced are likewise immeasurable, even unto the ultimate.
The same applies to the [meditations on] the superior, the supernormal knowledges, the impurity, the liberations, and the mind of loving-kindness.

One achieves the Mahāyāna through the gateway of mindfulness of the Buddha, just as Sadāprarudita attained immeasurable Dharma-gates upon seeing the Buddha. If a practitioner has not yet recognized these Dharma-gates:
To see only the radiance of light overflowing the eyes is precisely the work of Māra; it has nothing to do with the Buddha. One should take the Dharma as the standard.
If one focuses exclusively on physical forms, Māra can manifest them all. Are images carved from clay or wood any more than they are the Buddha?
Furthermore, why must the Tathāgata’s manifestation be sixteen feet tall? A height of sixteen feet is merely a manifestation as a handsome man. The Buddha manifests in whatever form people prefer.
The body universally manifests bodies as appropriate; it universally manifests bodies for remediation; it universally manifests bodies for deliverance.

All forms and images arise simultaneously with the Dharma-gates; this is called the Buddha-remembrance Samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*). Anything beyond this is not [it]. Regarding the manifestation of the ten supernormal powers (*abhijñā*):
there are five supernormal powers—divine eye, knowledge of others' minds, divine ear, recollection of past lives, and the power of the body. One attains only the cause...

Dhyāna gives rise to supernormal powers (abhijñā), but one cannot give rise to dhyāna by means of supernormal powers. Why? Because dhyāna is the essence (svabhāva) and supernormal powers are its function (vṛtti).

Since a function does not arise in isolation, how could it give rise to its own essence? Although each individual dhyāna can give rise to supernormal powers, within the fundamental [dhyānas] their arising is slight.

Specifically, the *viśeṣa* (special) and *abhibhvāyatana* (bases of mastery) frequently give rise to the supernormal power of levitation (*laghiman*), while the *vimokṣa* (liberations) and *abhibhvāyatana* frequently give rise to the supernormal power of the body (*kāyābhijñā*).

The supernormal power of mastery over the body at will (*kāya-vaśitā-abhijñā*): if, within the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), one takes the appearance and voice of a person as an object and apprehends the aspect of bliss, then through such seeing and hearing, it penetrates the mental consciousness;
thus, the supernormal powers of knowing others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) and the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*) are frequently produced.

By observing the three periods of time through causal conditions, the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*) is frequently produced. Through the concentration of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*), the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) is frequently produced. All these supernormal powers are subtle and refined.
These are the three types of knowledge (*vidyā*), though they are not yet the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-vidyā*). Within each of these, there are five factors of merit and so forth.
Generally, regarding the essence of dhyāna, either the internal mind attains liberation or external signs are not clear. That which is not clear is called "obscured" (*antarhita*);
that which is clear is not obscured. If supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are the function of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), then their function must necessarily be clear and distinct.
Thereafter, there is no longer any sense of concealment or disappearance. Next, regarding the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*:

if a practitioner lacks skillful means and becomes greedily attached to the flavor of *dhyāna*, they will take birth according to that *dhyāna* and wander through the cycle of birth and death. If one seeks liberation, one should contemplate ten points of meaning.
Even if one initially attains concentration and tames the body and mind—like a snake entering a tube and straightening out due to the *dhyāna*—one must emerge from contemplation.

Regarding the objective realm, afflictions are as they were at the beginning; one breaks the precepts and turns away from the Way, or becomes self-exalting through dhyāna, giving rise to various evil karmas.

Even if one does not lose meditative concentration, once the retribution for that dhyāna is exhausted, all karmas will arise again. This is how one uses dhyāna as the cause to create the dharmadhātu of the three miserable realms.
If, after emerging from concentration, one gives rise to a mind of compassion, benevolence, propriety, and the ten wholesome actions, this constitutes the realm of humans and devas. If...
If one exclusively cultivates the meditative liberation of impurity (aśubha-vimokṣa), one can give rise to the untainted (anāsrava) and accomplish the Dharma-realm of the Śrāvaka.

If one uses dhyāna to break through obscurations, one accomplishes the Dharma-realm of the Bodhisattva of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā). If one contemplates all dhyānas as phenomena produced by causes and conditions that arise and perish, this is the Dharma-realm of the Pratyekabuddha.

Furthermore, if one contemplates these causes and conditions as being empty, and that emptiness as being non-arising, this is the Dharma-realm of the Three Vehicles according to the Shared Teaching (sāmānya-yāna).
If one contemplates that the causes and conditions of dhyāna are themselves empty, provisional, and the Middle, then the ten realms of existence arise from dhyāna and likewise perish within dhyāna.
By extinguishing the nine realms to realize the single realm, the King Samādhi encompasses all samādhis, thereby perfecting the pāramitā of dhyāna.

Transform that concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) into objectless loving-kindness; transform the recollection of the Buddha into the recollection of the ocean of nature; transform supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) into skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) free from deliberation.

All Buddha-dharmas are fully contained within the King Samādhi (*Rāja-samādhi*). This is the realm of the conceivable (*cintya-viṣaya*), not what is currently being contemplated. As for what is called the inconceivable (*acintya*):
whether it be the arousal of a single thought of concentrated mind, its flavor, or its purity—even down to...

Through supernormal power, one immediately knows that this mind is the dharma-nature and the dharma-realm of ignorance. Infinite concentration and distraction are fully present in a single thought-moment.
Why is this? Because of delusion there is distraction; because of understanding there arises concentration.

Since concentration and distraction are identical with ignorance, and ignorance is likewise identical with the dharma-nature, the nature of delusion and understanding, as well as concentration and distraction, is non-dual. It is subtle and difficult to conceive, transcending the path of language. Although...
It transcends ordinary conceptions yet does not depart from the multitude of sentient beings. A sutra states: "All sentient beings are themselves the samādhi of cessation.
Although this mind is designated as "samādhi," sentient beings have never been that [samādhi], nor have they ever not been it.

Why? Because apart from sentient beings, there is no separate samādhi; therefore, it is said they have "never been" it. Yet, since samādhi is not something other than sentient beings, it is also said they have "never not been" it. This is...
This is precisely non-separation; the wondrous lies within it. Only a Buddha can fully investigate all meditative concentrations and all realms, which are all thus.
If one’s affliction were removed simply by hearing these words, there would be no further need for the nine methods.

If one does not awaken, one should again give rise to compassion, knowing that ignorance is itself the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and that afflictions are themselves awakening (*bodhi*). This is intended to cause sentient beings...
To transform delusion into awakening and extract suffering to achieve bliss, one must be free from poisonous admixture and partiality, giving rise to a mind of true correctness.

If the mind is not yet settled, one should skillfully practice *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). If one contemplates that within a single thought-moment, both meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and its opposite are quiescent, this is called "True Stopping" (*tattva-śamatha*).
To illuminate the purity of the *dharmatā* without obstruction is called the "Contemplation of Emptiness" (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Furthermore, one contemplates the meditative mind...

It is both empty and provisional; it simultaneously illuminates the two truths without wavering from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). This is called "stopping according with conditions" (*suiyuan zhi*).

To penetrate the correspondence between medicine and illness, adapting to the capacity and meeting the occasion, is called the "contemplation of the provisional" (*jia guan*). Furthermore, one contemplates that this meditative mind is empty, provisional, and the Middle Way.

Non-dual and undifferentiated, one penetrates the true reality; this is called the cessation of the Middle Way. The three cessations and three contemplations are unified within a single thought-moment.
To shatter the two extremes, it is called "One"; to shatter biased attachment to arising and ceasing, it is called "Perfect" and "Quiescent."
Use this calm abiding and insight to settle the mind. Furthermore, if one does not enter [the state], one should know that everything prior to the arising of true reality is delusion and confusion;
one must universally shatter it with the inconceivable threefold contemplation. When delusion departs, wisdom arises; when confusion ceases, concentration is perfected.

Furthermore, for those who do not yet awaken, one must carefully examine this state of being obstructed or unobstructed. If it is obstructed and does not become unobstructed, then one should employ the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) to bring about adjustment.

Why is this? A single thought-moment of meditative mind (*dhyāna-citta*) encompasses the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the ten realms. By destroying the inversions, one achieves witheredness; by destroying witheredness, one achieves flourishing.

By destroying both types simultaneously, one achieves that which is neither withered nor flourishing. In this way, the four foundations of mindfulness open the three gates of liberation. Furthermore, for those who do not yet awaken...

One should be obscured by past karmic hindrances; therefore, one employs the six perfections as an aid for their remedy. Alternatively, there may be attachment to the flavor of dhyāna, relying on meditation for self-indulgence and resenting those who do not practice it.
Such obscurations arise simultaneously with dhyāna itself; the method for their counteraction requires diligent self-reflection.
For the practitioner, the ultimate limit of observing the Dharma lies herein. Furthermore, those who do not awaken to this are of great dullness and darkness, possessing great...

It is a hindrance of affliction and cannot be remedied. If one enters from this point gradually, using the successive stages to guard against internal [defilements] and patience (*kṣānti*) to guard against external ones, and removing attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) to prevent falling from the "summit" (*mūrdhan*), then by accomplishing the ten dharmas, one attains the One Vehicle Mahāyāna and realizes the King Samādhi.

Thus, both practice for oneself and the transformation of others are fully perfected in terms of both phenomena and principle (and so forth). Furthermore, regarding the previously discussed causal *dhyāna*, its intent may be...

It is not yet exhaustive; let us further elaborate upon it. According to the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, the twelve links of dependent origination are observed by those with inferior, middling, superior, and supreme-superior wisdom, thereby accomplishing four types of bodhi.
Now, we shall expound this as a contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). First, regarding the "contemplable realm" (*cintya-viṣaya*):
when past ignorance gives rise to wholesome, unwholesome, superior, middling, and inferior karma, the six dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*) are formed. If one employs...
When the clarity of arising and ceasing transforms this ignorance, it becomes the bodhi of the śrāvakas.

When contaminated actions (*sāsrava-karman*) transform into supramundane auxiliary practices for the path, those practitioners whose residual delusions are not yet exhausted still take birth among humans or devas.

If those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) employ uncontaminated karma (*anāsrava-karman*) and the attachment to reality, which merges with fundamental ignorance, they are born in the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*) and receive the name "Expedient."

To take up existence through the grasping of form is the wisdom of the lower grade. If one regards ignorance itself as the clarity of non-arising and non-ceasing, one attains the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
with the exhaustion of fetters and karma, yet not exhausting the [concept of] lands, this is the same as the śrāvaka. As the *Avalokana-sūtra* says:

"Contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination as being like a dream or an illusion constitutes the path of a pratyekabuddha"; this is the wisdom of the middle grade. If one transforms ignorance into *parinirvāṇa*...

If one transforms unwholesome conduct into the five perfections, because true realization has not yet arisen, they possess the causes and conditions of the realm within; this is called the "realm of the six perfections.
If, in the sixth or seventh stages, the severing of delusions is not yet complete, it is the same as the previous teaching. Those who have exhausted the severing of delusions are born there;

their power of wisdom is merely slightly superior. If one transforms ignorance into sequential clear practice, it constitutes distinct practice and thus becomes the Separate Teaching (Pṛthagvidha-śāsana).

Bodhi is supreme wisdom. If, from the moment of generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one understands that the twelve links of dependent origination are themselves the three Buddha-natures—namely, ignorance, craving, and grasping are the *nirvedhabhāga* (the cause of realization);
volitional formations and existence are the *pratyaya-bhāga* (the causal condition);

and the branches of consciousness, name-and-form, and so forth, are the *mūla-bhāga* (the fundamental cause)—then these are called the "three natures" in the state of cause and the "three virtues" in the state of fruition. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Sentient beings are themselves bodhi; they are themselves nirvāṇa."
Cultivating such contemplation, one attains the Bodhi of the Buddhas; this is called the supreme wisdom. This wisdom is inconceivable.

It achieves perfect severance at the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) and reaches total exhaustion at the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbuddha*). It is a severance that is not severing, a realization that is not realizing. It exhaustively investigates the source of ignorance (*avidyā*).
This is a great divine mantra; this is a great illuminating mantra. One should know that these causal conditions are the ocean of immeasurable Buddha-dharmas;
they are the realm of the inconceivable. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "All dharmas tend toward ignorance, and so on, up to tending toward old age and death;
there is no going beyond this tendency. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The twelve links of dependent origination are within a single thought-moment. As for this "single thought-moment":
What is called "neither one nor different" is designated as "one," yet it is not like the fixed attachment to "oneness" or "difference" held by ordinary people.
Having understood this realm, one proceeds through the ten dharmas: the arousal of the mind, settling the mind, breaking through pervasiveness, penetration and obstruction, and the aids to the path.
All of these are clearly visible within the context of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). Thus, what dharma is not complete? What practice is not subsumed?
What stage is not established? What place is not included? For a student who wishes to contemplate according to reality, the essential point lies herein.
The seventh contemplation concerns the objects of various views (*dṛṣṭi*). Generally speaking, "view" refers to a distorted understanding.

Because one reasons incorrectly yet perceives with clarity, forming a definitive conviction, it is termed a "view. That which gives rise to such a view may be due either to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) or to hearing (*śruta*);

of these two, that due to meditative concentration is more prevalent. It may arise after meditation has already seen [the object], or it may arise simultaneously with the vision produced by meditation. As for...

For this reason, next is the treatise on views (*dṛṣṭi*). This examination of views is fourfold: first, clarifying the persons and dharmas of various views; second, clarifying the causes and conditions that give rise to views;

third, clarifying the faults; and fourth, the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. First, clarifying the persons and dharmas of various views refers to the heterodox persons and the dharmas they grasp.
There are three types of heterodox persons: those outside the Buddha-dharma, namely the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and furthermore...
Attached to the Buddha-dharma, there are those who study the Buddha-dharma and yet become non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Among the external non-Buddhists, there are three patriarchs:
the Kāpila non-Buddhist calculates that the effect exists within the cause; the Ulūka-Sāṃkhya calculates that the effect does not exist within the cause;

and the Leśava calculates that the effect both exists and does not exist within the cause. Furthermore, the *Ru Dacheng Lun* (Treatise on Entering the Mahāyāna) states: "The Kāpila calculates [the principle of] unity."
Ulūka maintains the doctrine of difference; Kāśyapa maintains the doctrine of both identity and difference; Sañjayin maintains the doctrine of neither identity nor difference.

All non-Buddhist schools have branched out from these origins, being transmitted and taught through successive generations. During the time of the Buddha’s appearance in the world, there were six great teachers, namely:
Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, who maintained the doctrine of neither arising nor ceasing; and Makkhali Gosāla.
Pūraṇa Kāśyapa reckoned that the suffering and happiness of sentient beings have no causes or conditions and occur spontaneously.
Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra reckoned that when the time for sentient beings has ripened, they attain the Way.

Ajita Keśakambalin reckoned that the suffering of karmic retribution for sins could be replaced by throwing oneself from cliffs or plucking out one's hair. Kakuda Kātyāyana reckoned that things both exist and do not exist. Nigaṇṭha... [text fragment]
The son of Kātyāyana, Gaṇḍatīputra, maintained that what is produced by karma is fixed and absolutely cannot be altered. These [views] are recorded as compiled by Kumārajīva;

their names are identical to those in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (the Great Scripture), though the doctrines they maintain may differ, perhaps due to errors in translation or because they possess distinct underlying intentions, which remains undetermined at present.
For the most part, they do not deviate from the three types, such as Kāśyapa and others. Next, [the views of] the Buddhajīvas are appended.

The Dharma-heretics originated with the Vātsīputrīyas. The Vātsīputrīyas studied the *Śāriputra-abhidharma* and composed their own distinct interpretations, asserting that the "self" exists outside the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*) within the "ineffable treasury.
As for the four propositions, these heretics maintain that form (*rūpa*) is the self.
There is a self apart from form; there is a self within form; form is within the self. The same applies to the other four aggregates (*skandhas*).

These constitute twenty types of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). As the *Mahā-śāstra* states: "By destroying the twenty types of the view of a self, one becomes a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). This is precisely that meaning.

Now, the Vātsīputrīya school’s conception of a self differs from those views and is not part of the Buddha's teaching. Alternatively, it is said that [the self] is comprised of the three times and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
This forms four propositions; such individuals are then non-Buddhists who merely attach themselves to the Buddha-dharma.

Furthermore, there are those of the Vaipulya school who, upon reading the Buddha’s ten parables, formulate their own doctrines, claiming that "non-arising and non-ceasing are like illusions and transformations," taking emptiness and illusion as their primary tenet.

Nāgārjuna rebuked them, saying this is not the Buddha-dharma, for it is the dharma of heterodox persons. Next, regarding those who study the Buddha-dharma and become non-Buddhists: this refers to those who cling to the teachings.
Delusions arise, and one cannot enter into the principle. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If one lacks the skillful means of Prajñā, entering the Abhidharma leads to falling into existence;
entering emptiness leads to falling into non-existence; entering the *Kun-le* (Vaiśeṣika) leads to falling into both existence and non-existence.

The *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* states: "To cling to 'neither existence nor non-existence' is the discourse of the deluded; it is a perverted grasping of the True Dharma that results in the dharma of a heterodox person. If...
To study the four gates of Prajñā is to be consumed by the fire of perversion, whereby one instead produces perverted dharmas.

Furthermore, each of the six teachers attained the dharma of omniscience; this was because they gave rise to views regarding their own calculations, and through these views, their knowledge pervaded all dharmas.

Moreover, they all attained the dharmas of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*); that is, having developed the five supernormal powers, they transformed cities into salt marshes and turned Śakra into a sheep.

They can cause rivers to stand still at their ears and reach for the sun and moon with their hands; these are their supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). Furthermore, they have all attained the Vedas and are proficient in every worldly script and calculation.

Whether it be the Vatsiputriyas, the Vaipulya followers, or even those who study the Buddha-dharma through the four teachings and four gates—when compared to those non-Buddhists, each of them possesses these three kinds of qualities. It is only that their depth and subtlety differ.
The same applies to the ear. Regarding the clarification of the causes and conditions for the arising of various views:

if sentient beings have not practiced certain views in the past, yet their current hindrances are thin, they may be able to give rise to various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). Then, either the meditative absorption and the view arise together, or the view arises after the absorption, or the view suddenly arises upon hearing another’s teaching.
As the dark hindrances are gradually removed, that which was grasped as real becomes permeable; and regarding that which was not grasped, [it likewise becomes so].

It collapses of its own accord. Such insight arises from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Since concentration possesses the factor of investigation (*vicaya*), one might occasionally become negligent and fail to restrain oneself while investigating phenomena.
From this factor of investigation, one reasons that all phenomena contain their effects within their causes.
This understanding becomes so sharp and penetrating that no one can challenge it or refute it; one considers it supremely subtle and wonderful. Yet, if one examines it closely, it is merely...
This is the view of meaning (Arthadarśana). It is fully possessed of the eighty-eight latent proclivities (anuśaya) and the net of inverted delusions;

one should know that this is the manifestation of the Sāṃkhya view. Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of the factors (aṅga), one investigates how effects do not exist within causes. This view is fierce and sharp;
its followers convert others from themselves, asserting that their ultimate resort does not transcend this interpretation. This, then, is the manifestation of the Sāṃkhya view. Moreover—

Within contemplation, one reflects on the principle that within causes there exist both the presence and the absence of effects. The *Mahā-śāstra* states: "Existence contends with non-existence; non-existence contends with existence.
One who clings to the view of both existence and non-existence contends with those who hold to existence and non-existence respectively.
If one enters into such views, the resulting inquiries are inexhaustible; this is the manifestation of the *Lokāyata* (Leshabha) view. The calculations of the six teachers differ from one another.
If one skillfully grasps the underlying intention and examines it against the views that have arisen, they will be largely similar; this is the arising of the views of the six heretical teachers.

If, within the factors of contemplation, one reckons that there must necessarily be a self, yet it does not reside in the body—nor does it reside among the four positions of the tetralemma, nor in the three times or the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) among the four positions of the tetralemma—but rather resides within the fifth, the "unspeakable treasury" (avaktavyakośa)—then when this view arises:
When the mind’s understanding is clear and sharp, one refutes others and establishes oneself; this resolve is unshakable. This is the arising of the Vātsīputrīya view.

If, within the factors of contemplation, one regards all phenomena as illusory transformations and gives rise to the perception of emptiness and exhaustion, such that neither the liberating mind nor any phenomena are perceived—[this is the correct path].
All return to illusion; this is the manifestation of the Vaipulya (fangguǎng) view.

If, within the branch of contemplation, one infers that phenomena are impermanent and that abiding ceases without persisting, and that the self and person are as unobtainable as the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit, such that only substantial dharmas remain—though these are analyzed until they become empty—then whether coarse or subtle, observing them collectively as impermanent and selfless, and reckoning this [emptiness] as real, one’s spiritual understanding becomes a hundredfold.

Twofold. Although such an understanding may arise, if the afflictions (kleśa) instead flare up more intensely, one should know that this is the arising of the view of the gate of existence (bhāva-mukha).

If, during the branch of contemplation, there suddenly arises an understanding of emptiness (śūnyatā), asserting that impermanence and the two types of arising-and-ceasing are merely provisional, floating, and hollow, and that the skillful means of analyzing phenomena into emptiness are clear and sharp—this is the arising of the view of the gate of emptiness (śūnyatā-mukha).
The same principle applies to the views of "both existent and non-existent" and "neither existent nor non-existent."

Know this: one should know that when the four gates penetrate the principle, right view is established. If one loses these skillful means and falls into the four views, then one is a heterodox person within the Buddha-dharma.

Furthermore, let alone the four views regarding the Tripiṭaka, even regarding the Mahāyāna—whether in its universal, particular, or perfect aspects—if one grasps at the four extremes, one will be consumed by the fire of heterodoxy.
Amidst the branches of contemplation, one may suddenly give rise to former understandings, like a dream.
The existence of flowers in the sky is like an illusion. Some say it is the unreal basis of an illusion; because it is unreal, it is empty.
Others say that, like an illusory transformation, it is seen yet cannot be seen. Still others say it is neither an illusory existence nor an illusory non-existence.

These four interpretations are sharp and clever, yet their shifting movements constitute mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); these are the four views of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*). Furthermore, within the contemplation of the branches, one engages in reflection.

The four interpretations of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) hold that these are merely illusions and dreams within the realm of conditioned existence (*dhātu*). These dreams arise from ignorance (*avidyā*).

Contemplating how ignorance enters into the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) also involves four gates: some say the dharma-nature is like the seven treasures within a casket; others say it is like empty space.
Some say it is like a jar of wine or curd; some say it is the Middle Way. These four interpretations and attachments constitute the four views of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*).

Regarding the branch of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), one might suddenly realize that ignorance (*avidyā*) transforms and immediately becomes clarity (*vidyā*), and that this clarity encompasses all phenomena.

Or one might say that neither ignorance nor clarity can be apprehended. Or one might say that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is both apprehendable and non-apprehendable, yet it is not [merely] apprehendable.
To attain that which is non-attainable; for one gate is the three gates, and the three gates are the one gate. This understanding becomes increasingly refined:

there is nothing that cannot be destroyed by what is refuted, and there is nothing that cannot be established by what is preserved. One claims this is the very patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);

this is the emergence of the four views within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). To give rise to these views of the four teachings and fall into perverse attachments constitutes internal false views (4).
View is the root of all views; self and other are likewise the roots of conjunction and disjunction. Therefore, Nāgārjuna refutes both self and other, clarifying only self and other;
the rest may be understood by implication. If the Tripiṭaka masters claim that great arising and small arising both arise from ignorance, [it is as follows].

It does not arise from the Real. If ignorance ceases, then the formative forces cease; this has no bearing on the cessation of the Real. To cling to such a view constitutes the false view of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
In the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-sāmānya-yāna*), it is clarified that the Real is non-arising; because it is non-arising, it gives rise to all things.
If all delusions were to cease, these delusions would likewise result from non-arising. To cling to such a notion constitutes the false view of other-nature (*parabhāva*). Within the realm...

Taking delusion as "self" and taking the True [Dharmadhātu] as "other," one speaks of others. Regarding the realms beyond [the threefold world], taking *dharmatā* as "self" and ignorance (*avidyā*) as "other," the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*) calculates that the *ālayavijñāna* gives rise to all delusions; it holds that by cultivating wisdom through conditions, this ignorance is extinguished. That which can give rise to and can extinguish [delusion] is not related to *dharmatā*. This attachment to the arising of other-nature constitutes a false view. "The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) gives rise to all phenomena; the nature of phenomena extinguishes all phenomena. This is the false view of calculating an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Now, as for the distinctions between ordinary beings and sages, or the heterodox and the orthodox, these must all be determined in terms of persons and teachings.

From the three patriarchs and six masters of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) downward, they all developed the power of omniscience (*sarvajñā*), the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), and the *Veda*; since what they have developed is distinct, their applications [must also differ].
It is also different. Next, one approaches the Buddha-dharma; furthermore, one gives rise to views based upon the Dharma. What is thus attained is likewise boundless.

If one is not meticulous and thorough, then errors of right and wrong will arise, and the heterodox and the orthodox will become confused. A deviation of a mere hair’s breadth leads to a loss of billions.
There would be no way to discern the true Dharma; therefore, one must verify it by its primordial source and examine it with...
Returning to the source, the Jing and Wei rivers flow separately, and jade and stone follow distinct paths. One must not err oneself or lead others astray, lest both fall into ruin.
Regarding the discussion on the faults arising from views: there are many such faults that arise from views. Here, I shall briefly resolve them by examining two factors:
the origin and the basis. First, regarding external influences: this includes the four propositions of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), up to the four propositions of the Perfect [Teaching].
The views of the non-Buddhist paths—from the Vedas up to the Perfect Gate—share the same names and numbers as the three stations of mindfulness and the three gates of liberation.
Yet, the faults and fetters arising from these views are no different; though gold and iron differ, their function as locks and shackles is one and the same.
Furthermore, the afflictions arising from the four propositions of the non-Buddhists up to the four views of the Perfect Gate all lead back to the same defilement; though jade and a rat may differ...

The difference lies solely in the raw jade itself. Furthermore, from the four propositions of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) up to the four views of the Perfect Gate, although both involve refinement, one succeeds while the other does not, like the milk of a cow and a donkey.

Moreover, from the four propositions of the non-Buddhists to the four views of the Perfect Gate, one is harmful while the other is not, like the *kāra* and *ciñcā* fruits. The self (*ātman*) conceived therein is entirely a phenomenon of bondage.
They are not the self-mastering Lord. Their mutual disputes over right and wrong have nothing to do with reality as it is. Looking toward Nirvana, they instead sink into birth and death.

Where there is attachment, love arises; where there is aversion, hatred arises. Though they give rise to compassion, it only results in views of attachment. Whether applying ointment or inflicting cuts, [they remain bound by their own afflictions].

In the end, one merely practices forced endurance. Although the All-Knowing One does not employ speculative reasoning, and although his supernormal powers are all transformations within the realm of outflows, the Vedas he has studied are not the power of *dhāraṇī*.
Though he has severed the dull afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), he is like a centipede that falters; though treated by worldly physicians, the illness recurs after recovery.
The ocean of the eighty-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) is vast and boundless, and the net of suffering of the twenty-five realms of existence is without end.

All such limits are produced by various views and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). How could they be grasped as truly real dharmas? Furthermore, regarding the difference in the dharmas upon which [the views] rely:

those outside the three [vehicles] are outsiders (*bāhyaka*) who are possessed of outflows (*sāsrava*). They give rise to outflowing dharmas and, with an outflowing mind, become attached to objects of attachment.
The dharmas upon which they rely are not true, and the views they produce are likewise false. Nevertheless, in their secret intent, they [employ] the perverse...

The mutual entry [of phenomena] is their true characteristic. If the Three Pitakas and Four Gates belong to supramundane sages who have attained supramundane dharmas, then their essence is pure and they abide in the cessation of afflictions.
Knowing that these gates are universal paths, they no longer give rise to contention. Where there is no contention, there is no karma.
Without karma, there is no birth and death. When only the Path of cessation exists, one achieves right view and is no longer subject to false views.
If one becomes attached to this gate, it immediately turns right into wrong; with hatred and craving surging forth, one differs from the external non-Buddhists by no more than a hair’s breadth.

This arises from a mind attached to the dharma of non-attachment, thereby giving rise to false views. This applies to the Distinct, Shared, and Complete [teachings], as well as the false and the correct, which can be understood through reflection.
Generally, because one practices *śamatha* (calm abiding) through the Shared [teaching], the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) are elicited;

because one practices *vipaśyanā* (insight) through the Shared [teaching], the various views are elicited. If, previously, one did not recognize the faults of these views and thus felt fear toward them, striving to sever them quickly, yet now indulges them...
Accomplishing the power that assists the Path brings certain great benefit. If one enters the Two Vehicles, one moves through the factors of the Path (mārga-aṅga) during the cultivation of insight;
if one enters the Mahāyāna, one does not move through the factors of the Path during their cultivation.

If one gives rise to the clumsy four-gate views of the Tripiṭaka Teaching or the skillful four-gate views of the Shared Teaching, although these views are obstacles, those who realize their underlying intent awaken to the Path very swiftly, just as [the practitioners of] external paths first [do].
There are those with the capacity for vision who, upon being transformed by the Buddha, attain awakening immediately—like a swift horse that sees the shadow of a whip and leaps at once.

For those without such vision, the Buddha does not appear in the world; instead, he may manifest divided forms or dispersed bodies to act as their teachers and friends, guiding them to perceive the Dharma.
When the sun of the Buddha first rises, the provisional leads to the ultimate, and upon hearing the Dharma, one attains awakening. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "He secretly dispatched two..."

Regarding the person: their finger points here to the circle (○). As for those who practice *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, just as with the various views mentioned previously, in principle there is not a single person capable of giving rise to them all simultaneously.
Even if they were all to arise, they would ultimately devour one another and return to a single view. For now, let us distinguish the many by means of one.
Among all views, the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*) is able to destroy all phenomena; yet all phenomena cannot [destroy it].

The emptiness that destroys [views] is the most potent blade for leading people to form attachments; therefore, we shall first take this as our object of contemplation. We shall apply ten points of reflection. Regarding the "object of contemplation through deliberation":
the view of emptiness gives rise to the dharmas of the ten dharma-realms. The *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* states:

"If a mind of viewing arises even for a single kṣaṇa, it is unwholesome. The *Abhidharmapada* states: "If a mind of viewing arises even for a single kṣaṇa, it is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; it is called..."
It is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). It is the mind that acts as the causal motivation (*hetu-samutthāna-citta*), for all wholesome and unwholesome states arise because of it.
Now, the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*) is likewise. Why is this so? By means of emptiness one commits evil and performs unimpeded actions, which result in the three evil realms;

by means of emptiness one performs good, which results in the three good realms. Furthermore, the fundamental [meditations] of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) also arise because of emptiness. The Śrāvaka contemplates this emptiness.

[Long-nailed] sees that the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas) are themselves the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya). That eighty-eight proclivities (anuśayas) arise from the view of emptiness is the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya).
Origination arises from delusion regarding suffering; suffering is produced by origination. Thus suffering and origination circulate together. Long-nailed does not recognize this.

If he were to recognize emptiness, he would see suffering and origination. All suffering and origination depend upon form (rūpa). All phenomena of form are called the body (kāya); the body is impure. Wisdom—

That which is loathed is called the foundation of mindfulness of body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). One accepts this view of emptiness and reckons sensation as pleasure; if one knows there is no pleasure, that is the foundation of mindfulness of sensation (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*).
When empty objects confront the mind, they can give rise to consciousness; though arising and ceasing and impermanent, it is falsely reckoned as permanent.

To recognize this impermanence is called the foundation of mindfulness of mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*). One grasps the forms and appearances of emptiness and performs good or evil deeds; within these actions, one reckons a self. If...

Knowing there is no self, one immediately breaks through perception and mental formations; this is called the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). This constitutes the arising of the foundations of mindfulness from the view of emptiness.

Through contemplation and diligence, one breaks through perversions; this contemplation is then perfected as right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*). Cultivating within a concentrated mind is called the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

Thus, up to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, these constitute how the view of emptiness can give rise to the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*). When the four perversions are extinguished, ignorance and craving are extinguished. When ignorance and craving are extinguished, then...
Hatred is extinguished. When one knows that emptiness is not the path, pride is extinguished. When there is nothing further to grasp, doubt is extinguished.
Since the view of emptiness entails both suffering and its origin, it is not ultimate emptiness. If the grasping at emptiness is shattered, then the self cannot be found.

When the self is destroyed, the view of a body is destroyed. When the view of a body is destroyed, the view of a self is destroyed. When the view of a self is destroyed, the view of extremes is destroyed. The view of emptiness is not...
When the path is realized, the clinging to precepts (*śīlavrata-parāmarśa*) is destroyed. When emptiness is not [mistakenly taken as] nirvana, the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) is destroyed.

When emptiness does not accord with the principle, false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are destroyed. When the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) are destroyed, the eighty-eight proclivities are destroyed. When the eighty-eight proclivities are destroyed, the fetters of the "son" (*putra-bandhana*) are destroyed.

When the fetters of the son are destroyed, one is able to realize the first fruit and advance to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). When the fetters of the fruit are destroyed, one enters nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
This is the view of emptiness that gives rise to the Truth of Cessation; it is the Dharma-realm of the Śrāvakas.

If one clearly recognizes the Four Noble Truths within emptiness, then one knows the true path for exhausting suffering. Through this true path, by subduing and severing [afflictions], one becomes a noble one (ārya).

Thus, whether views are single, paired, or complete—including the "ineffable" and other such views—one recognizes them all as the true path. Among all views, one is able to move and transcend them. If it were not so, [one would remain bound].
Such a person does not perceive the Four Noble Truths; therefore, they have long wandered through the great ocean of suffering in saṃsāra.
Furthermore, regarding those who clarify the view of emptiness and give rise to the realm of the Pratyekabuddhas: their view of emptiness is not true emptiness, yet they falsely claim it to be so.

This is inverted discrimination, and inversion is itself ignorance (*avidyā*). If one knows that ignorance does not arise, then grasping at existence is exhausted and no new karma is created. If there is no ignorance, then...
One achieves the light of wisdom. Therefore, when there is wisdom, there are no afflictions (*kleśa*); when there are no afflictions, there is no ignorance (*avidyā*).
When ignorance ceases, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) cease, and so on, up to the cessation of old age and death. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* asks:
"How does a śrāvaka contemplate the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination? It then explains that [the notions of] permanence and impermanence are both ignorance; one should know this.

When ignorance does not arise, grasping for existence ceases; this is precisely the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination within the Śrāvaka teachings. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Delighting in solitary tranquility, they seek natural wisdom.
This wisdom is the tranquility that transcends the sixty-two views. Furthermore, one contemplates the emptiness of each moment (*kṣaṇa*).

Once the view of emptiness is fully established, it encompasses the Four Noble Truths. As for whether this mind of the view of emptiness exists or does not exist: since it cannot be said not to exist, it is itself a link of existence (*bhava-aṅga*).
Grasping arises from clinging; clinging arises from craving; craving is caused by feeling; feeling is caused by contact; contact arises from the sense bases;
the sense bases arise from name-and-form; name-and-form arises from consciousness; consciousness arises from past karma; and karma arises from ignorance.

Ignorance consists of all inverted views regarding existence and non-existence in the past, which are able to produce the physical body in the present, and which now further give rise to views that bring it into being.
Wholesome and unwholesome formations serve as the causes for future name-and-form; they mutually produce and sustain one another without end.

If one knows that the essential nature of ignorance is fundamentally unreal and exists only through the conjunction of deluded thoughts and conditions, then once this inversion is understood, ignorance subsides.
Because it subsides, everything up to old age and death also subsides. Thus, ignorance, old age, and death—along with the view of emptiness—all subside.
In this state, all views, ignorance, old age, and death are completely stilled, and one further erases the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).

When Nāgārjuna first brought about its revival, he observed that as the time since the Buddha’s passing had gradually increased, non-Buddhist paths were flourishing;

Master Huiwen of the Northern Qi relied upon this treatise to establish his contemplative practice (*guan*), which he orally transmitted to Master Sengzhao of Mount Nanyue.
